#6347. Why You Should Pack Your Hiking Boots on a Trip to St. Croix

The smell hit me out of nowhere: an uncanny whiff of sweaty socks. I instinctively glanced around for another hiker. My guide, local naturalist Olasee Davis, laughed and pointed to a thick brown seed pod lying on the trail. It had fallen from a West Indian locust, more commonly known as a stinking toe tree.

The culprit loomed farther down the trail, its massive limbs weaving a vaulted canopy overhead. “It tastes better than it smells,” Olasee said, picking up the pod and cracking it open on a rock to reveal the powdery pulp inside. I watched him take a bite but decided to pass. I suspected stinking toe fruit was an acquired taste, and with only a few days remaining on my trip to St. Croix, I'd save the acquiring for a future visit.

As we continued along, Olasee introduced me to other tropical evergreens, including the soursop, laden with spiky fruit, and the red manjack, much shorter and shrubbier, with brownish-red berries. Around the next bend he pointed out nonnative fruit trees: papaya from South America and mango from India. But he hadn't brought me here just for the botany. He'd brought me to understand why this forest matters.

As an ecologist, historian, and assistant professor at the University of the Virgin Islands, Olasee helped lead the effort to establish Maroon Sanctuary Territorial Park in 2025. Encompassing 2,469 acres in the northwest corner of St. Croix, the park protects part of Maroon Country, the island's steep, forested interior where people who had escaped slavery found refuge during the 1700s and early 1800s. The new park also safeguards former sugar plantations and mill sites, which have been slowly returning to nature since Denmark ended slavery in the Danish West Indies (present-day US Virgin Islands) in 1848. By that time more than 100,000 enslaved Africans had passed through the port of Christiansted on St. Croix, the largest of the islands, to be sold to plantation owners in the Danish Caribbean sugar economy.

Olasee and I were following an old plantation trail through one such former estate when he suddenly stopped and then scrambled up a steep embankment into the trees. I followed, brushing aside slender branches. Hidden beneath the understory, almost swallowed by spider lilies, was a burial ground. Most graves were marked with conch shells. Some were covered by low, weathered concrete slabs. One was marked by a headstone, its inscription softened by decades of moisture and lichen. The hidden cemetery wasn't an isolated discovery. For more than 40 years, Olasee has bushwhacked his way through Maroon Country to search for burial grounds and other traces of those who escaped slavery, documenting sites that would otherwise disappear beneath the forest. Now that it's been conserved as a territorial park, that work can continue in a more systematic, permanent way. Or as Olasee put it, “I could die in peace now.”

Travelers have traditionally come to the USVI for beach vacations and sailing charters; now Maroon Sanctuary is opening up another side to the islands. The park's founders are also building out an official trail network. The roughly 10 miles of trail that I explored with Olasee were a patchwork of former estate roads, plantation footpaths, and forgotten forest routes that he'd pieced together over decades. Soon these trails will be easier to navigate without needing someone like Olasee to lead the way. The next morning I met Kristina “Kitty” Edwards, director of the US Virgin Islands Division of Territorial Parks & Protected Areas, at a trailhead on the slopes of 1,165-foot Mount Eagle, the island's highest peak. We were about to hike the first official segment of the trail, a three-mile loop designed for hiking and mountain biking, which opened this past May. When completed, the trail system will wend 30 miles through the forested backcountry.

As excited as Kitty was to show off the new path, a first of its kind on the island, she wasn't in a hurry. “I'm a meanderer,” she said with a shrug and a smile. In the shirt-soaking heat of the tropics, I was grateful to take it slow. We ascended amid white-winged butterflies and yellow-breasted bananaquits. After an hour we reached the stone remnants of the old watchtower that marked the summit. A spur trail led us to an overlook where we paused to take in the 270-degree view, bookended by emerald peaks to our right and the inviting turquoise waters of Cane Bay to our left. It occurred to me that Maroon Sanctuary wasn't just about the land. The park's protected boundary extends all the way to the sea, helping shield Cane Bay's coral reefs and the nearby Annaly Bay tide pools from pollution and sediment.

A green sea turtle in the warm waters around St. Croix

I spent the next day reveling in those crystal waters. At Sweet Bottom Dive Center, I rented a mask and fins, and went snorkeling among the parrotfish, angelfish, and wrasse that inhabit the shallow reef just offshore. After watching a sea turtle munch on seagrass, I flipped over onto my back. Above the beach the densely forested peaks of Maroon Country rose in layers, a physical reminder of the many lives and histories held within.

The Waves at Cane Bay, an 11-room boutique hotel built into the rocky shoreline overlooking the bay, was reimagined in 2021 as a stylish oceanfront retreat with private patios, two bars, and the sustainable seafood restaurant Ama. The hotel is a four-minute walk to the beach at Cane Bay and a nine-minute drive to the new Mount Eagle trailhead.

Located directly across the road from Cane Bay, the Landing Beach Bar serves up Caribbean specialties like jerk chicken and fried plantains in a fun, convivial setting. Leatherback Brewing Company is St. Croix's first craft brewery and an unofficial headquarters for the island's mountain-biking community, complete with a full-service bike shop inside.

#6346. These 7,400-Year-Old Cave Drawings Were Hiding in Plain Sight for Decades. They’re Finally Getting Their Due.

Buried under centuries of graffiti, a trove of Paleolithic art only appears when light hits it just so.

Known for its ancient artifacts, the Catalonian village of Espluga de Francolí has been one of the most recognized troves of Paleolithic cave finds in Spain. Even the “Espluga” in its name translates to “cave.” The village is surrounded by mountains with limestone caves or covas whose human history reaches back thousands of years, and while Cova de la Font Major has been a tourist attraction since 1957, something that almost should have been obvious went unseen.

Cova de la Font Major had already been investigated by archaeologists by the time it was converted into a museum in 1993. By then, it was thought that the cave had been thoroughly scoured for artifacts and other evidence that it was inhabited, and that its irregular walls had been unsuitable for cave art because of their uneven coloration and texture. Part of what became known as its Adventure Route is the Gatoneres de cal Palletes, a series of smaller galleries branching off from the main gallery. Visitors filed past for decades, never noticing the engravings concealed in the dark. Cut into the pale limestone were animals and abstract symbols, each one made by human hands.

Part of the reason that these drawings had never been observed is that they have to be illuminated from certain angles in order to be visible. An archaeological team led by Josep Maria Vergès and Míriam Salas-Altès of the Catalan Institute of Human Paleocecology and Evolution (IPHES-CERCA) identified 280 motifs scratched into the soft rock, which now make up the highest known concentration of Paleolithic figures found on a cave wall in Catalonia. It’s also the third largest cave art assemblage on the eastern Iberian Peninsula. It was unexpectedly discovered during a 2019 excavation campaign, although it was obscured by modern graffiti left behind by tourists and others who’ve visited the site since explorers first crept in through the well of a townhouse courtyard in 1853. It also seems that the art incorporated stone variations.

“While the intentional integration of these natural features remains interpretative and cannot be definitively demonstrated, their proposed use is supported by precise anatomical alignment with some features and the recurrent use of similar elements across the corpus,” Vergès and Salas-Altès said in a study recently published in Antiquity.

Some of the animal figures, including horses, deer, goats, and aurochs, appear to trot along the seams between different types of rock. They share the walls with abstract motifs, which make up most of the cave art. Researchers also documented parallel lines, some of them cut across the animals, as well as convergent lines and tangles of loops. The meanings of these symbols can only be guessed at, and so can their age. Direct dating of material from Cova de la Font Major is difficult, though the team thinks uranium dating may work on calcite deposits that formed over at least one figure. Even then, a date for one drawing won’t necessarily reveal the age of the others. For now, the closest anchor comes from radiocarbon dating, which places the cave’s earliest Neolithic occupations between 7,050 and 7,400 years ago.

The cave was also used for late Neolithic burials on the cusp of the Bronze Age. Right before it was opened to the public in 1957, archaeologists unearthed a human femur that was radiocarbon dated to 5,600–5,700 years old. Also found near the entrance was a hoard of later Bronze Age artifacts that included pins decorated with sun imagery, an axe, a dagger, and fragments of a blade that could have been a dagger or sword. Deeper in the cave, charcoal dated to 26,000 years ago may be the oldest sign of human presence, aided by similar charcoal discovered near the prehistoric shrine known as Sala del Llac and in other spots inside the cave. Much later, in the Iron Age, people used another part of the cave for rituals. They left behind ceramic vessels that may have been offerings to deities, along with metal artifacts and food remnants.

“[This discovery is] a substantial advance in the understanding of Paleolithic rock art in the eastern Iberian Peninsula,” the researchers said. “Gaps in the Paleolithic record may reflect limitations in research strategies, visibility conditions or preservation factors, rather than the actual absence of rock art practices.”

Elizabeth Rayne is a creature who writes. Her work has appeared in Popular Mechanics, Ars Technica, SYFY WIRE, Space.com, Live Science, Den of Geek, Forbidden Futures and Collective Tales. She lurks right outside New York City with her parrot, Lestat. When not writing, she can be found drawing, playing the piano or shapeshifting.

#6345. 2026 Full Moon calendar: When to see the Full Moon and phases

The phenomenon of a Full Moon arises when our planet, Earth, is precisely sandwiched between the Sun and the Moon. This alignment ensures the entire side of the Moon that faces us gleams under sunlight. Thanks to the Moon’s orbit around Earth, the angle of sunlight hitting the lunar surface and being reflected back to our planet changes. That creates different lunar phases.

The next Full Moon will be the November Beaver Moon, which occurs at 9:54 a.m. EST on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. It will also be a Super Moon.

We’ll update this article multiple times each week with the latest moonrise, moonset, Full Moon schedule, and some of what you can see in the sky each week.

Here’s the complete list of Full Moons this year and their traditional names.

(All times Eastern; * denotes a Super Moon.)

The images below show the day-by-day phases of the Moon in November. The Full Moon this month will be on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026.

The times below for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location. All other times are Eastern unless otherwise specified. For more details on upcoming sky events, check out our full Sky This Week column.

Sunrise: 6:43 A.M.Sunset: 4:45 P.M.Moonrise: 10:54 A.M.Moonset: 7:55 P.M.Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (21%)

The phases of the Moon are: New Moon, waxing crescent, First Quarter, waxing gibbous, Full Moon, waning gibbous, Last Quarter, and waning crescent. A cycle starting from one Full Moon to its next counterpart, termed the synodic month or lunar month, lasts about 29.5 days.

Though a Full Moon only occurs during the exact moment when Earth, Moon, and Sun form a perfect alignment, to our eyes, the Moon seems Full for around three days.

There are a wide variety of specialized names used to identify distinct types or timings of Full Moons. These names primarily trace back to a blend of cultural, agricultural, and natural observations about the Moon, aimed at allowing humans to not only predict seasonal changes, but also track the passage of time.

For instance, almost every month’s Full Moon boasts a name sourced from Native American, Colonial American, or other North American traditions, with their titles mirroring seasonal shifts and nature’s events.

Wolf Moon (January): Inspired by the cries of hungry wolves.

Snow Moon (February): A nod to the month’s often heavy snowfall.

Worm Moon (March): Named after the earthworms that signal thawing grounds.

Pink Moon (April): In honor of the blossoming pink wildflowers.

Flower Moon (May): Celebrating the bloom of flowers.

Strawberry Moon (June): Marks the prime strawberry harvest season.

Buck Moon (July): Recognizing the new antlers on bucks.

Sturgeon Moon (August): Named after the abundant sturgeon fish.

Corn Moon (September): Signifying the corn harvesting period.

Hunter’s Moon (October): Commemorating the hunting season preceding winter.

Beaver Moon (November): Reflects the time when beavers are busy building their winter dams.

Cold Moon (December): Evocative of winter’s chill.

In addition, there are a few additional names for Full Moons that commonly make their way into public conversations and news.

Super Moon: This term is reserved for a Full Moon that aligns with the lunar perigee, which is the Moon’s nearest point to Earth in its orbit. This proximity renders the Full Moon unusually large and luminous. For a Full Moon to earn the Super Moon tag, it should be within approximately 90 percent of its closest distance to Earth.

Blue Moon: A Blue Moon is the second Full Moon in a month that experiences two Full Moons. This phenomenon graces our skies roughly every 2.7 years. Though the term suggests a color, Blue Moons aren’t truly blue. Very occasionally, atmospheric conditions such as recent volcanic eruptions might lend the Moon a slightly blueish tint, but this hue isn’t tied to the term.

Black Moon: A Black Moon is a recent, unofficial term that can describe one of two situations. Either the third of four New Moons in a single astronomical season or the second of two New Moons in a month is a Black Moon. As its name suggests, the Black Moon is completely dark, as it is a New Moon that occurs when the Moon is between the Sun and Earth. The New Moon cannot be observed except during a total solar eclipse.

Harvest Moon: Occurring closest to the autumnal equinox, typically in September, the Harvest Moon is often renowned for a distinct orange tint it might display. This Full Moon rises close to sunset and sets near sunrise, providing extended hours of bright moonlight. Historically, this was invaluable to farmers gathering their produce.

What is the difference between a Full Moon and a New Moon? A Full Moon is witnessed when Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, making the entire Moon’s face visible. Conversely, during a New Moon, the Moon lies between Earth and the Sun, shrouding its Earth-facing side in darkness.

How does the Full Moon influence tides? The Moon’s gravitational tug causes Earth’s waters to bulge, birthing tides. During both Full and New Moons, the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in alignment, generating “spring tides.” These tides can swing exceptionally high or low due to the combined gravitational influences of the Sun and Moon.

#6344. This may be the best evidence yet that dinosaur blood can fossilize

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Minerals may have preserved remnants of ancient blood in a dinosaur bone, but some are skeptical

Using a technique called scanning electron microscopy to peer inside an 115 million-year-old dinosaur limb bone, researchers captured images of tiny ellipsoid structures, about 20 micrometers in diameter, that may be fossilized red blood cells. Molecular analyses found preserved heme — the oxygen-carrying component of hemoglobin — in the bone.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The life and times of a dinosaur may be written in its blood — if blood can be preserved in bone.

Tiny microstructures found in the limb bones of a fossilized 115-million-year-old specimen are the remnants of red blood cells, researchers report November 2 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The team says these are both the oldest red blood cell structures yet identified and the first to be chemically proven. But not everyone is as sanguine about that conclusion.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The ability to identify such structures could offer a powerful molecular window into the physiology of long-extinct animals, including their metabolism and even activity levels, says paleontologist Kliti Grice of Curtin University in Bentley, Australia.

The bone, from a fossil-rich site in northeastern Brazil called Mina Pedra Branca, belonged to the dinosaur Aratasaurus museunacionali. Grice and her colleagues used a variety of chemical and imaging analyses to study the Cretaceous Period specimen.

Maurilio Oliveira/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)

The team prepared thin cross-sectional slices of bone and imaged details of the limb bone’s internal structure with focused electron beams. That revealed ellipse-shaped microstructures within the limb’s fossilized network of blood vessels.

A map of the ellipsoids’ chemical element composition revealed that they were full of iron, carbon and nitrogen, all components of a biomolecule called heme. Heme is an iron-bearing, ring-shaped molecule found in hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen throughout the body.

Then, the researchers used a technique that identifies molecules by how they scatter laser light. Those analyses suggested the presence of porphyrins, ringlike organic compounds found in blood — and the precursors of heme. Finally, they ruled out contamination from other porphyrins, such as the pigment chlorophyll, by separating and identifying the molecular contents of a bone extract. That experiment also suggested heme.

Taken together, these findings point unequivocally to the preservation of molecular traces of ancient blood, the team says. They also offer a clue to a novel pathway that might preserve those traces for so many millions of years.

Blood cells decompose within days of the death of an organism. Only unusual and fast-acting environmental and biochemical conditions could have stopped decay and held those tissues in place as the organism fossilizes.

In this fossil, the secret ingredient was a manganese oxide mineral called hausmannite, the researchers say. The team’s analyses had found the mineral within the ellipsoid structures. That mineral, they propose, may have acted as a time capsule, preserving the cellular structures and protecting the molecules within, including collagen amino acids.

Distinguishing fossilized blood cells from nonorganic minerals that formed within a fossil after the organism’s death is a tricky task. During fossilization, mineral-rich fluids seep in and around the bones, and the minerals that form within the fossil can bear a strong resemblance to bodily structures.

In a 1997 study, two paleontologists analyzed tiny spheres found inside the limb of a fossil, possibly a pterosaur. The spheres were once thought to be the fossilized remnants of ancient blood cells, but the duo determined that the spheres were instead pyrite, an iron mineral that had been deposited in the bones after death.

Those paleontologists suggested that, going forward, several criteria should be met before proposing a blood cell origin for fossilized structures, including comparing the shape of the structures with that of living related organisms and identifying certain biomarkers in the structures. One of those biomarkers is heme compounds.

Grice and her colleagues say that their study meets these criteria. Unlike the pyrite, hausmannite was crucial to preservation, “rather than simply a mineral that replaced biological material after it had disappeared,” she says. The close spatial relationship between the hausmannite, the blood cell-like structures and the chemical signatures of heme “raises the possibility that mineralization helped stabilize, entomb and protect components of the original biological material during fossilization.”

But Mary Schweitzer, a paleontologist at North Carolina State University in Raleigh who was not involved in the new study, says she doesn’t think these findings do fully meet those criteria.

The heme biomarkers, for example, don’t appear to be localized to the round structures alone, as would be expected in fossilized blood cells, but come from analysis of the entire bone. The proposed red blood cells also differ in size and shape compared with red blood cells from living birds and reptiles, she says.

Schweitzer is no stranger to skepticism over the discovery of ephemeral tissues in fossils. In 2005, she and her colleagues reported the first recovery of flexible, soft-tissue blood vessels from the 68-million-year-old fossilized leg bone of a Tyrannosaurus rex. It was a landmark study that sparked debate, including over how it would even be possible to preserve such tissues through deep time, as well as the most surefire way to detect them in the present.

“I am not convinced” that the research team has definitively identified heme compounds, Schweitzer says. “I do applaud them for bringing a plethora of methods to the study. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and that does require state-of-the-art technology.”

No one really knows what a dinosaur’s red blood cell shape would be, let alone how the process of fossilization might distort the original shape of the structures, or allow heme-related molecules to escape their cellular confines over time, Grice says.

And, she says, her team’s interpretation of the evidence doesn’t just rely on the observations of those structures. “[It] rests on the convergence of anatomy, morphology, mineralogy, elemental analysis and molecular chemistry,” she says. “That combination is critical.”

As for whether other fossils might have molecular traces that have been preserved by hausmannite, “we simply don’t know yet,” Grice says. “But this type of preservation may not be quite as rare as we currently think.”

D.M. Martill and D.M. Unwin. Small spheres in fossil bones: Blood corpuscles or diagenetic products? Palaeontology. 1997.

#6343. The 23 Best Gaming Gifts, According to Our Editor With 15 Years in the Industry

Whether they play on PlayStation, Switch 2, or PC, these are the items that are sure to bring joy.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

With rising memory and GPU costs, the gamer in your life may still be wishing for a new laptop, gaming rig, or console this holiday season—or even something small like a keyboard or a high-end controller. And let’s not forget: At $70 for the biggest new releases, the games themselves are not small purchases.

All of which is to say, there’s even more reason to give your loved ones something gaming-related. More often than not, the best gear is a bit of a splurge, but there’s a lot of cool stuff out there that’s worth the spend.

I’ve been writing about games and gaming gear for 15 years, and I test new and exciting gear all year. Here are some of the best, coolest, and most useful bits of kit out there that are sure to light up their faces. (And their desks… And their couches.)

With no new consoles announced, all of the core consoles will make for great gifts, but the Switch 2 is the newest kid on the block, and thus the one that will likely stay active the longest. The Switch 2 was a significant tech improvement over the original Switch when it launched last year, and Nintendo has launched a substantial number of exciting exclusives over the past year, many of which are truly all-ages experiences: kid-friendly, so families can play worry-free, but with the innovative gameplay and polish that will hold an adult’s attention.

Lately, I’ve been playing Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave, the latest entry in the long-running strategy RPG franchise. That’s on the niche side for a Nintendo game, but there’s a wide array of fun, distinctive games, like Pokopia, the Pokemon habitat-builder; Donkey Kong Bananza, a platformer you can literally break apart piece by piece; and Mario Kart World, which brings some huge changes to the long-running classic racer.

And, while the Switch 2 will not be able to play GTA VI (at least not at launch), it will get its mega-blockbuster this November: a remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, a game that most critics and fans of a certain age put up among the best games of all time.

Earlier this year, HP folded its two gaming PC brands—Omen and Victus—into HyperX, the PC gaming peripherals brand it purchased back in 2021. That means HyperX makes PCs now! I’ve always been a huge fan of the brand, which was best known for headsets but also made good keyboards and mice, among other things, so I was excited to see what the first HyperX PCs could do.

The HyperX Omen 15 is a capable mid-range gaming laptop equipped with either a Ryzen 7 or Intel Core i7 CPU, an Nvidia 5060 GPU, 16 GB of RAM, and 1TB SSD. The display is a 2.5K (2560 x 1600p) IPS panel with a 180Hz max refresh rate, which is more than enough to handle what a 5060 will throw at it. At a time when gaming PC prices are shockingly high (note the conspicuous lack of a desktop or GPUs on this list) I think this is a solid machine from a trustworthy brand, which is really all you can ask for at a time like this.

All gaming PCs are expensive this year, but the handheld gaming PC market has gotten especially out of control. If you want to be nice to someone and splurge nearly $2,000, the new model I’ve seen this year is MSI’s Claw EX AI+. It’s the first handheld furnished with Intel’s Arc G3 Extreme processor, a chip made specifically for handhelds instead of laptops. That has made it both more performant and, crucially, power-efficient than most of the handhelds I’ve seen and tried. And, unlike a Steam Deck, it is Windows-based out of the box, which makes it easier to use Steam, Xbox Game Pass, and all the other storefronts without any tinkering.

If you’re willing to spend top dollar to buy the most bonkers version of a gaming peripheral, SteelSeries is usually a good brand to look at. After designing and redesigning its impeccable multiplatform headset, the Arctis Nova Pro, the brand has turned its attention back to the controller, and released a new, equally impressive Xbox-style gamepad, the Aeon Pro.

SteelSeries took a lot of the features from the Arctis Nova headset and ported them over to the Aeon Pro. There’s a charging dock with multiple inputs so you can hot-swap between Xbox and PC on the fly. It also comes with a pair of replaceable batteries (the same ones in the Nova Pro/Elite), so you can always switch batteries and keep playing. Even if you forget to use the dock, you will never run out of battery with this controller.

You also get all the standard features you’d expect on a premium controller—swappable Hall effect analog sticks, four customizable rear paddles, adjustable trigger travel—it features sublimely clicky mechanical buttons and balanced weight in your hand. At $260, this is the very definition of a giftable controller: It’s more money than anyone would want to spend on a controller themselves, but a daily player will absolutely appreciate the luxury of owning one.

Low-profile gaming keyboards, which feature less “travel” or a smaller distance from unpressed to fully bottomed out, are an acquired taste. Mechanical keyboards, with longer travel, tend to be more comfortable, but many players are comfortable with low-profile keys because they feel more like a laptop keyboard and/or because the keys are optimal for “hair trigger” settings that cater to twitch reflexes. When a quick action is all that stands between you and certain death, a low-profile keyboard might be the difference between a dodge and your demise.

Razer does well with just about everything, but I find myself recommending the brand’s keyboards about as often as anything, and its newest low-profile option really worked for me this year. With adjustable actuation and other features that allow you to really optimize for the fastest possible response, it’s a high-performance keyboard for players who want to go all in on multiplayer performance.

In the same vein as the Aeon Pro, SteelSeries has reinvented its mouse line with a four-pack of new mice: The Rival Pro, Rival Pro Mini, Sensei Pro, and Sensei Pro Mini. That sounds like a lot of mice, but really it comes down to two shapes: The more ergonomic Sensei and the more streamlined Rival, both of which come in a standard or lighter “mini” size. (Mini mice are better for small hands, of course, but also preferred by “claw” players who hold their hand above their mice for quick-clicking.) While they are different, I’d say both Sensei and Rival have a decidedly competitive build, which is why I’d specifically recommend Rival Pro.

Like the Aeon Pro controller, Steelseries has ported over its swappable battery system (though the mice have smaller puck-sized batteries), but the big innovation is a new, faster wireless connection, which they call “Ultra 8K wideband.” 8K polling—the number of times the mouse sends signals back to your PC per second, sort of like a “refresh rate” for mice–is now a common claim among high-end gaming mice, but not every mouse delivers it consistently. Steelseries claims that Ultra 8K Wideband, which relies on line of sight between the mouse and a small base station (that also charges the backup battery), ensures a steady 8K connection. And, like all esports mice, it’s incredibly light, about 53 grams.

It ain’t cheap, but if your gamer plays a lot of competitive online multiplayer games, like Call of Duty, Fortnite, Valorant, or Marvel Rivals, this is the kind of mouse they’re looking for to get a competitive edge (and show off to their friends).

I’ve been known to recommend some incredibly expensive gaming headsets in the past, so this year my most gift-worthy option is a little more reasonable, if not cheap. The newest riff on Logitech’s flagship gaming headset, the Pro X3, offers a great balance of audio quality, mic clarity, comfort, and style. I’ve long been a fan of the advanced EQ and post-processing work that Logitech manages to pull off via G Hub, its companion app, though it still sounds clear and sweet on PS5, where you don’t have access to those fine controls. It’s also the most stylish new headset I tested this year. The black aluminum and faux-leather-coated padding look great on a stream, or even a video call at work.

I haven’t played Grand Theft Auto VI yet, but I don’t need to touch it to know that it’s at the top of every gamer’s wish list this holiday season. It’s been more than a decade since Rockstar Games released the last Grand Theft Auto game, but in that time, the series’ popularity has only grown. With the game launching November 19, the hype has reached a fever pitch as release day approaches. Houston Rockets center Steven Adams joked that NBA productivity will drop on launch day. There are a couple of stories out there with advice on how to ask for time off to play.

If you haven’t watched the Netflix special about the game, GTA VI follows a Bonnie and Clyde-esque criminal couple in Vice City, which is loosely based on Miami. Like past games, it seems to boast incredibly detailed and cinematic visuals, particularly for an open-world experience where you can go anywhere, do anything, and, per the name, steal anyone’s car.

Speaking of which, I feel like most people are aware of GTA and its adult themes because of various satires and news stories about the rest of the series, but just in case: This game has a lot of violence, and seemingly some sexual content as well. If you are shopping for a kid, treat access to this game the same way you would an R-rated movie.

Released in 1998 on the Nintendo 64, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is often touted as the pinnacle of the franchise, bested maybe only by the original Switch’s Breath of the Wild. After nearly 30 years, Nintendo has rebuilt this classic from the ground up. I’m normally not easily swayed by pure nostalgia, but it’s incredible to return to Ocarina of Time and realize how deeply ingrained it is in my mind. It’s been a very long time since I played the original, but I breezed through the first few hours as if it had been yesterday. And the things that have changed—new graphics, voice acting in cutscenes, and an orchestral score, to name a few—all bring the game to life in a new way, without detracting from my memory of playing it before.

Obviously, I’m approaching it as an old-head and a fan, but I do think the game still holds up quite well for new audiences as well. So much of the Zelda gameplay that younger fans know and love is built on a foundation created here, and that essential sense of adventure is still very much alive.

If the Ocarina of Time remake is not enough for your favorite Nintendo fan (or if they’ve already pre-ordered it), there is a lot of new Zelda merch coming out alongside the new game this fall. My personal fave is this backpack, which I checked out at a Nintendo event earlier this year. It’s surprisingly big, 18 by 22 by 4 inches (w x h x d), with a built-in laptop sleeve. Most importantly, it looks just like the shield, and the exterior is made from polyurethane with rubber details, rather than simply painted on, so they won’t rub off or fade.

Everyone’s heard of GTA VI. Everyone’s heard of Zelda. When you give a gamer either of these gifts, you’ve done right by them, but you’ve also picked the most obvious choices. They aren’t going to know you read this guide. That you put in the work to find a great game for them. One of the biggest surprise hits in a crowded fall game calendar, Blood of the Dawnwalker, on the other hand, shows that you’ve been paying attention to what critics and players have been talking about.

This action-RPG about medieval vampires comes from developer Rebel Wolves, which is led by senior staff from CD Projekt who worked on The Witcher 3 and Cyberpunk 2077. As Coen, a daywalking vampire, you have to save your human family from a vampire lord. Like The Witcher, this game has a compelling narrative with nuanced writing. There’s a lot to dig your teeth into, so your gamer will be telling you about it for a while.

We’ve been talking about OLED TVs for a long time, but manufacturers have only put OLED panels in PC monitors for a couple of years. OLED gaming monitors are here, but are generally pretty expensive. If you don’t shop for PC monitors often, you might be shocked when I tell you that this 27-inch, 1440p display is “relatively affordable at only… $570!?

But making the jump to an OLED display, like switching to an OLED TV, can be a game changer. Organic light-emitting diode (OLED) technology allows for dynamic brightness control to generate more accurate colors, sharper contrast, and maximize HDR output. Put another way, they make games “pop” in a way that your average LED display just won’t. Alienware has put out a few well-made and relatively obtainable options, including the AW2725DF.

I always rankle a bit at the concept of a “gaming TV”: All of the best TVs handle games well. But there are a couple of features that go from “nice to have” to mandatory when I go to recommend a new big screen with games in mind. In addition to the usual attention to color, brightness, and display technology, a higher refresh rate is a must, as is variable refresh rate support. And if there’s a good “game mode” in the settings, that’s a nice plus, too.

Giving someone a TV, any TV, is a hugely generous act, but in the spirit of “giving them what they wouldn’t buy themselves,” I’d recommend going all out and giving your gamer the Samsung S95H, the true best OLED of the year when you take price out of the question. It’s expensive, but makes games look absolutely incredible, with tremendous color accuracy, brightness, and the “perfect” blacks of an OLED screen.

All of the consoles (and desktop gaming PCs) give you a way to add more storage to your system so you can store more games at a time. Games take up more space than ever, so having the extra storage is convenient: It gets annoying when you have to delete a game every time you want to download something new. I’ll admit, it’s a utilitarian gift—basically the equivalent of buying someone a pair of warm socks—but one that will make any player’s life more convenient.

On PC and PS5, we’re talking about an M.2 SSD hard drive, which loads games at high speeds. Xbox has a proprietary expansion card system, which is easy to install. Finally, the Switch 2 relies on high-speed micro SD cards for extra storage. There are many brands for each option, but the differences in performance aren’t huge. The most important thing is compatibility: If it doesn’t specifically state that it works with your gamer’s console of choice, you need to check the specs and make sure. (Or pick any of the options below.)

Shop PS5 Storage Shop Xbox Storage Shop Switch Storage

IKEA launched a fun new line of Xbox-inspired gaming furniture and housewares earlier this year, and there are some great, utilitarian pieces if you’re looking to spruce up your setup. One thing that caught my eye, a potential stuffer, is this controller display box, which gives you a cool way to store your gamepads or use them as decoration. Especially if you’re picking up limited edition controllers, these give you a cool way to show them off rather than simply leaving them next to your TV.

While I haven’t tested any of these, I think a lot of the YXSTABY line looks pretty fun. There’s a neat gaming side table, which features built-in storage underneath, an easel-style TV stand, and a D-pad-shaped throw pillow. All of these are relatively affordable, too, so they’re great choices if the tech’s looking a bit too pricey.

Once upon a time—maybe a decade ago or so—the Blue Yeti was the USB microphone that launched a million podcasts. A long time has passed since then: Blue was acquired by Logitech, and the Yeti fell out of vogue. Well, Logitech has relaunched the iconic audio starter kit under its gaming banner, Logitech G, with new focus on streaming video games and, more specifically, helping streamers automate the technical side of things.

The Yeti 2 upholds the original model’s legacy as a stellar starter mic (for streaming, podcasts, or any deskside audio you need to capture), but the new and improved model has some fascinating features, including the ability to detect and adjust your EQ settings based on your proximity to the microphone, and an LED screen that lets you manually change audio settings without digging into menus on your PC (where you already have a lot going on). This is a great pickup for someone who’s thinking about getting into streaming, or is looking for an easy plug-and-play upgrade that doesn’t require too much finicking to figure out.

If you have someone in your life who can’t stop talking about GTA VI, chances are they’ve already preordered the game. To meet them where they are in their fandom, you have to jump to the next step and get them something that allows them to show off the depth of their fandom.

There’s a ton of unofficial GTA merch out there, but realheads accept no substitutes, and PS5 players will be stoked to get a new Vice City-themed DualSense with the “VI” on the touchpad. (Also, depending on how long they’ve had their console, it may be time for a controller refresh, anyway. Analog stick drift is a problem we all learn to live with, but sometimes it’s just better to start fresh.)

Not every gaming gift needs to be electronic. Sometimes it can be a toy where you build a scale model of electronics. The latest in a now long line of game console–based sets, Lego just released a scale model of the original PlayStation, in honor of “over 30 years of play,” according to Sony. Whether you have a gamer in your life who’s a die-hard PlayStation fan, a collector who’s been decorating their space with hand-assembled consoles, or just someone who loves to tinker, building a 1,911-piece PlayStation brick by brick seems like a fun, relaxing way to spend a weekend.

Press Reset is the only item on this list that wasn’t released in 2026, but I think it’s a very good time to read it if you or the gamer in your life hasn’t yet. This series of longform nonfiction stories from Bloomberg video game industry reporter Jason Schrier provide detailed histories of how some major games from the last 20 years were made. The connective tissue between the stories, which are woven together in surprisingly personal ways, have a common theme: The development houses that made the games shut down afterwards.

The video game business has been in a bit of a transitional period for the past few years: A wide realization that rising costs, both for developers and consumers, has led to projects getting cancelled, companies downsizing or closing, and more. For gamers, who often like to think they have much better understanding of what’s going on in the game world than they really do, these stories illustrate the many ways that making a video game can go wrong, whether you’re working with a small independent team or one of the biggest, most well-funded companies in the business. It’s a fascinating book, and a must read for anyone interested in how games are made.

If you’re a fighting game fan playing on Xbox or PC, HyperX has a really interesting new Hitbox-style “leverless” fight stick called the Clutch Tachi. It’s compact, with snappy mechanical switches under the buttons and customizable RGB lighting. It’s also tournament-ready with a competition “lock” switch and the ability to switch between up to four different control settings for different games.

The thing I find most intriguing, though, is the fact that HyperX has released 3D printer files for the buttons and top plate so you can design and print your own custom parts. Some hardcore players like to assemble or customize their fight sticks, but that kind of work generally requires a fair bit of research and technical confidence. Having a brand encourage and enable this kind of customization makes it a lot easier for folks to try tinkering, and I think that’s really cool.

Mike Epstein is a Senior Commerce Editor at Hearst Enthusiast Group, producing reviews for buying guides Popular Mechanics, Runner’s World, Bicycling, and Best Products. Prior to joining Hearst, he was a video game and technology critic for over 10 years, with bylines at IGN, Gamespot, Variety, Lifehacker, Kotaku, GamesRadar, Flavorwire and Digital Trends, among others. Now, he’s a jack of all trades, helping reviewers share everything they know about all kinds of technical gear, from snowblowers, to running shoes and bicycles, and every kind of gadget imaginable.

#6342. Editor's Letter: Introducing Our Winter Travel Issue

It was a long and hot summer, and I welcomed the cooler weather as soon as the leaves started to turn. My closet full of coats and jackets had sat sadly neglected for many months; the new boots I bought in April on a clearance rack are only now about to get their moment. I'm excited for the Christmas lights in London and New York, the festive trees, chestnuts roasting on street corners—and yes, my Christmas wish list (featuring a dangerous number of watches and pieces of jewelry) is ready too. There is something about the winter that still feels exotic and enthralling to me. I saw snow a few times in Kashmir as a kid, but the first real blizzard I encountered was when I was a freshman in college in Pennsylvania. It was late at night, but my roommate dragged me out of bed to make snow angels. I still remember lying on my back, waving my arms around—the sensation of cold all along my body was surreal, as was the way in which white feathery bits floated down from the sky. I recall thinking, What a strange but wonderful feeling! I discovered two things quickly: One, I was a terrible skier. And, two, I loved après-ski—to be nursing hot chocolate by crackling fireplaces and snuggled in blankets.

Our story on Banff perfectly encapsulates the promise of winter: the adventure, the exhilaration, the romance of a landscape transformed overnight. But equally seductive is the prospect of winter sun. Come January I'll happily trade snow boots for sandals and fly to Tenerife, Spain, or Boracay, in the Philippines, or Brisbane, Australia. That dose of vitamin D is essential by then, when the Christmas lights have come down and everything seems gray and empty. At that point I need a beach—and something colorful and sparkly to wear on it. So often I close my eyes and return to the end-of-year trips I've made to Maldives, Indonesia, Mexico, and remembered the sunrises, the sound of the waves, the palm trees swaying in the breeze, the fiery red chiles, and fresh coconut water. It's been a strange year. But as we navigate the final months ahead, this issue is filled with reasons to feel excited about what comes next. I hope it gives you plenty to dream about—and somewhere to go.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6341. Nov. 12, 2014: The Philae lander touches down on a comet

The European Space Agency’s Rosetta mission launched March 2, 2004, on a 4-billion-mile (6.4 billion kilometers) path to Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko. The mission consisted of the Rosetta orbiter and the Philae lander, both designed for in-depth study of the comet. The spacecraft arrived at 67P/C-G on Aug. 6, 2014, and began orbiting the body a month later; on Nov. 12, 2014, the Philae lander descended to the comet surface. Both the spacecraft orbiting a comet and the landing on the comet’s surface were firsts in space exploration history.

Unfortunately, there were some complications with the landing: The harpoon system that was designed to hold the lander in place didn’t work, causing Philae to bounce and to float and drift above the surface. When it finally came to rest, it was in a shadowy location now known as Abydos, limiting to the sunlight its solar panels received.

Despite these challenges, Philae was able to operate for three days on battery power, and still sent back photos and data about the composition of the comet’s dust and its analysis of the body’s magnetism. (In short, the comet didn’t have a magnetic field.) Additionally, the orbiter transmitted data about water and oxygen in the tail that led to new understanding of such comets’ makeup.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

A man's appendix had to be removed, but not for dangerous inflammation, as you might expect.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The symptoms: The man went to the emergency room because he had a sharp pain in his lower-right abdomen.

What happened next: When doctors examined the man, the type of pain and the location of his discomfort suggested that he might have appendicitis, or inflammation of the appendix.

Appendicitis can be dangerous because it can cause the appendix to burst and release bacteria from the bowels into the abdominal cavity, thereby infecting the cavity's lining. This infection, called peritonitis, can spread to the bloodstream and cause the life-threatening condition sepsis, which kicks the immune system into overdrive.

Even though the patient had acute pain in his lower-right abdomen, he did not show signs of peritonitis, such as fever, nausea, symptoms of dehydration and an elevated heart rate, according to a report of his case. His doctors then performed abdominal ultrasound scans and found that the man's abdominal organs, including the appendix, appeared normal, with no signs of inflammation.

The report's authors did not include details about the man's treatment after this examination. But eight months later, he was still in pain and returned to the hospital for further evaluation, they noted.

The diagnosis: This time, when medical personnel questioned the man, he recalled that approximately 15 years earlier, he had accidentally swallowed a piece of a long bone containing edible marrow. The report does not mention if the man sought treatment immediately after swallowing this bone.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

At this second visit, doctors performed an abdominal X-ray and found a round object near the upper right of the man's pelvis. It measured about an inch (2.5 centimeters) long and a little over an inch (3 cm) wide.

According to a subsequent CT scan, the object contained bone tissue and was near the appendix. When the doctors looked inside the patient's abdomen with a laparoscope — a long, flexible tool with a camera at one end — they saw that the appendix was enlarged.

The treatment: Surgeons performed a laparoscopic appendectomy, which uses small incisions in the abdomen to insert instruments for removing the appendix. Inside the appendix was a hardened mass of fecal matter, called a fecaloma, which surrounded a long bone.

The organ's muscular walls had been stretched out by the mass, but there were no signs of inflammation. No complications developed after the surgery, and the patient was discharged two days later. The report does not describe any follow-up visits or treatments.

The appendix (orange) is a small, thin pouch of tissue attached to the colon.

What makes the case unique: It's relatively uncommon for people to accidentally swallow something indigestible and then require a medical visit for it. In the United States annually, about 120,000 people — roughly 90% of whom are children — are treated for ingesting foreign objects, and most of the objects are swallowed accidentally. Most commonly, the adults requiring treatment have ingested jewelry, while children are more likely to swallow coins, toys and batteries.

Typically, small, swallowed items pass harmlessly through the intestines within 48 hours; less than 1% require surgical intervention. Some objects, however, need immediate attention. For example, sharp items can tear the esophagus or puncture digestive organs. Batteries are hazardous if swallowed, as they contain corrosive acid that can leak into the gut. And small magnets are a big risk, especially if two or more are involved, since they may stick together through intestinal walls, which can tear holes in tissues or cause blockages and contortions in the intestines.

Swallowed foreign bodies rarely affect the appendix. Whether they enter the organ depends on the size of the opening into the appendix where it connects to the colon (which can vary between individuals), the dimensions of the ingested object, and the appendix's position in the body at the time. These objects cause approximately 0.005% cases of appendicitis, according to the man's case report. Such items recovered by surgeons through appendectomies include pieces of coal, nails, bits of enamel and glass, shells, dental crowns and bullets.

When a foreign body migrates to the appendix, it typically generates appendicitis within a few months, at most. However, this is not always the case. One report described a man who had eaten pigeons as a child and discovered more than 30 years later that he had 27 lead shot pellets in his appendix. Despite containing these pellets from the birds' flesh, his appendix was not inflamed.

"It is therefore possible, although rare, that a foreign body in the appendix even after many years (in our case, 15 years) does not lead to an authentic appendicitis either histologically or clinically," the authors of the marrowbone case report wrote.

They added that their patient was the first record in the scientific literature of a sizable bone lingering inside an appendix for more than a decade without causing significant inflammation. His pain was likely caused by physical shifting of the hard mass. His experience presented "a unique clinical picture," the doctors wrote.

"This case could offer a possible diagnostic and therapeutic option for appropriately treating patients with foreign bodies within the appendix," they said.

For more intriguing medical cases, check out our Diagnostic Dilemma archives.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Antonacci, N., Labombarda, M., Ricci, C., Buscemi, S., Casadei, R., & Minni, F. (2013). A bizarre foreign body in the appendix: A case report. World Journal of Gastrointestinal Surgery, 5(6), 195–198. https://doi.org/10.4240/wjgs.v5.i6.195

#6339. In Winter, Canada's Banff National Park is So Much More Than a Skiers' Paradise

My view from the foot of gleaming Victoria Glacier was straight out of a snow globe. Two shaggy ebony draft horses pulled a vintage sleigh along a powdery path that hugged the shores of frozen Lake Louise. Lycra-clad Nordic skiers glided across the snow-dusted ice, navigating around life-size snowmen. In the far distance a ray of sun glinted off the turret of an ice-sculpted castle, a mini version of the grand Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise hotel, which stands sentinel over this unbelievably pretty patch of wilderness in Banff National Park. A soft gust of wind swirled a flurry of flakes across the scene. The winter wonderland in front of me was magical enough to make even the most die-hard snowbirds reconsider the season.

I've always felt winter could be approached in two ways: You could be lazy and binge Netflix for three months, or you could be sporty and get after it in the mountains. But a weeklong trip to the Banff and Lake Louise region of Alberta opened my eyes to a gratifying middle ground. This area is a true winter playground, where you could downhill-ski or engage with the elements in so many other ways: snowshoeing, going for a horse-drawn sleigh ride, or watching the snowflakes fall while you're soaking in an outdoor hot tub. My time ended up being more about appreciating nature than conquering it on the slopes.

A seat with a view inside Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise

I arrived in early January on the tail of one of the area's snowiest Decembers on record, though you couldn't tell from the landscape around Calgary airport. Umber-hued prairies and agricultural land surround the gateway city, and it wasn't until 40 minutes into my 90-minute drive west on the Trans-Canada Highway that the Great Plains transitioned to the Canadian Rockies and the sky started nuking snow.

Home to SkiBig3—a trio of resorts that include Banff Sunshine, Lake Louise Ski Resort, and the mom-and-pop Mount Norquay—Banff National Park was the place to be during a winter in which most of the American West suffered a snow drought. In my 20s I would have driven straight from the airport to the ski slopes. Now in my mid-40s, with an unpredictable knee, back-to-back, bell-to-bell days have lost their appeal. But the childlike joy of playing in the snow has not. And Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise was the perfect base for “soft” winter adventure.

The resort's address, in the heart of Banff National Park overlooking glacier-fed Lake Louise, envelops guests in nature. No surprise—Lake Louise was originally developed for outdoor tourism. In 1885, after the last spike of the Canadian Pacific Railway was driven in, future company president William Cornelius Van Horne built hotels along the route. Among the first, the Banff Springs Hotel was designed for horseback sightseeing. The Chalet at Lake Louise, a humble log cabin, was marketed as a destination for fishing, canoeing, and alpinism. Van Horne hired Swiss guides to teach his guests to safely navigate the mountains, and they are partially responsible for introducing locals to the sport of skiing.

A horse-drawn sleigh ride around Lake Louise

In 1925 the original Chalet, which had been damaged in a fire, was reimagined as Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise, a grand, Renaissance Revival–style resort with 539 rooms and suites. Today, a century after opening, some characteristics—like its staff dressed in lederhosen-inspired uniforms and its fondue-focused restaurant, Walliser Stube—nod to the original Swiss influence, and the lobby-level Guide's Cabin, decorated with vintage photos and stocked with books on alpine living, continues the property's mountaineering legacy. Through the hotel, guests can sign up for snowshoe hikes or Bavarian curling lessons and rent ice skates and Nordic skis.

My first morning, I met guide Kevin Kirkpatrick at the cabin for an activity called Powderfest Snowshoeing. I've long found snowshoeing a little snoozy and worried how we'd fill the allotted three hours. The activity's name, it turned out, wasn't a cutesy marketing ploy. The resort has seven snowshoe trails, but because there was a base of 61 inches and another foot of fresh powder, we went “off-roading.”

Leaving behind the groomed lakeshore trail, we trekked up the shoulder of Fairview Mountain, and all signs of civilization disappeared as we entered a frosted forest straight out of a Dr. Seuss story. “Really get in there and explore,” he encouraged as we wandered past fir and larch trees bent at cartoonish angles, their limbs heaving with snow. I followed him up a massive mound of powder only to catch the metal cleat of my snowshoe on a branch and topple backward, leaving an imprint like a gigantic snow angel.

Time flew as Kirkpatrick shared wisdom on everything from the current weather anomaly to how, in 1882, Edwin Hunter, a member of the Stoney Nakoda, first led a young European wrangler, Tom Wilson, to what the Indigenous people of this area called Ho-run-num-nay (Lake of the Little Fishes). He chose to ignore the name and anointed it Emerald Lake for its jewel-colored waters. Two years later the government changed the moniker to Louise to honor a daughter of Queen Victoria, Princess Louise Caroline Alberta.

An ice climber on the Lake Louise Lakeshore Trail

I returned to the hotel thoroughly exhausted from hours of high-stepping and grateful that I was booked for a session at Basin Glacial Waters, Fairmont's new, guests-only thermal bathhouse. Designed by Italian architect Matteo Thun, the building, with floor-to-ceiling windows that frame the lake and towering peaks at every turn, feels like part of the landscape. This is the epitome of nature bathing, I thought as I took in the views from the hot-stone room, silent salt chamber, and indoor-outdoor vitality pool.

I didn't think it was possible to distract me from the dramatic vista, but Basin's signature Aufguss sauna ritual, the conclusion to my multisensory journey, was impossible to ignore. This choreographed sauna performance popular across Europe has only recently been introduced to North American spas. For 15 minutes our sauna master, Kyan Van Haasteren, a young, blond Dutchman, theatrically waved a towel over scorching sauna stones to waft steam toward me and 32 other guests. He danced around the 185-degree-Fahrenheit space to an upbeat soundtrack of Luis Fonsi while smashing snowballs scented with aromatic oils over the hot stones to release the fragrance of Siberian fir. It felt more like a Vegas show than a wellness ritual, but the entertainment took my mind off the discomfort of the heat. I exited in a sweaty daze and willed myself to follow Van Haasteren's lead and dunk myself into the outdoor cold plunge. In seconds the tingling numbness gave way to a heady euphoria. I looked up to see the start of a steady snow spiraling down, one that wouldn't let up until late the next day.

I may not be a first-to-last-chair skier any longer, but I'm still motivated to score fresh tracks on a powder day. By 8 a.m. the next morning, I was on the complimentary Fairmont shuttle with a throng of stoked skiers for the 10-minute transfer to Lake Louise Ski Resort. With three ways up the front of the mountain, there's rarely a line. And once you're on the mountain, it's easy to spread out. With this season's addition of Richardson's Ridge, 200 acres of beginner- and intermediate-friendly glades and groomers, the resort owns bragging rights as the third biggest ski area in Canada, with 4,200 acres of skiable terrain. Throughout the day I experienced moments that felt more like backcountry than resort riding, especially in the rowdy inbounds steeps of the West Bowl.

Gearing up to snowshoe at Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise

I spent the morning lapping bowl runs off the Summit Chair, but in the afternoon the visibility disappeared, making a drop down black diamond Rodney's Ridge downright vertigo-inducing. I'd gotten my fix of SkiBig3's “Prosecco Powder” (wonderfully light, dry snow), and I won't lie—the other incentive that got me up and out early was the promise of lunch at Whitehorn Bistro. The acclaimed views from this upscale, on-mountain restaurant were obscured, but that didn't damper the deliciousness of its farm-to-table dishes, like pickled beet carpaccio with goat cheese and crispy duck with black cherry jus.

With a solid half day of riding under my belt, I left the resort to work off my lunch on the Nordic trails of the Lake Louise campground with Clare McCann, the high-energy owner of Bikescape. Her lighthearted guiding philosophy was an ideal match for my novice cross-country ski skills and the tricky conditions. Heavy wet snow would cement our skis to the ground the minute we stopped propelling forward. “Shimmy, shimmy, shimmy, glide,” she repeated like a mantra as we haltingly made our way around the four-mile Bow River Loop. The trail was so silent that the only sound was my retro SkiBig3 pass flapping on the side of my jacket.

Those words stuck with me as I drove 50 minutes southeast to the town of Banff. Compared with Lake Louise, it's a bustling tourism hub, but thanks to strict design guidelines, the businesses downtown—even the Starbucks and the McDonald's—are housed in intentionally rustic spaces built from local stone and wood. Over the last few years, new businesses have enlivened the downtown area. Some of these arrivals include locavore-focused restaurants Good Folk and Farm & Fire, and the 67-room boutique Kenrick Hotel, a hip remodel of the former High Country Inn that added a third-wave coffee shop, a thermal circuit spa, and a stellar Italian restaurant, The Fat Ox. Even the classic sticky-floored late-night club, the Dusty Boot Saloon & Dance Hall, has been reinvented as Banff's take on Jackson Hole's Million Dollar Cowboy Bar, complete with a shiny, boot-shaped disco ball and a karaoke room.

I kept things old-school and checked in to Fairmont Banff Springs, nicknamed the Castle in the Rockies for its Scottish-baronial-style architecture and perch overlooking the town. The hotel was another vision of railway executive Van Horne, who famously said, “If we can't export the scenery, we'll import the tourists.”

Today Banff National Park sees more than 4.25 million visitors every year; nearly two thirds come during summer. But a week into my trip, I began to think that winter might be the more enchanting season. On my final day I joined Discover Banff Tours on an excursion to Johnston Canyon for its Icewalk experience. In the parking lot our guide, Jeff Doherty, outfitted our group of six in Yaktrax—ice-gripping cleats that attach to shoes—then had us briskly hike a half mile over slick paths and bridges to the lower falls before the big bus tour groups arrived.

The canyon was pure quietude, and we had it to ourselves. When the pace slowed, I was able to admire the feathery moss suspended in frost on the forest floor, the icy old man's beard lichen dangling from the trees, and, most of all, the frozen ribbons of electric blue cascades. About a mile of slippery uphill trail led us to the upper falls, a stream of water plunging behind a veil of ice. I stood in front of Mother Nature's ice sculpture in awe. “It's like seeing the Mona Lisa alone in the Louvre,” said Doherty. “In summer you'd be elbowing iPhones out of the way for a view, let alone a photo.”

A few weeks after I'd returned home to Colorado, I read that Alberta had been hit by a warm spell that doused the mountains in rain, turning the slopes into sheets of ice. Some friends had taken their family on a ski trip per my recommendation. When I asked about their vacation, they told me they hadn't skied once, but they had the best time dogsledding, night tubing, and ice-skating. In an age when weather is unforgivingly unpredictable, Banff, with its buffet of activities, might be the closest thing to a guaranteed winter escape, no matter your preferred pace of adventure. My trip showed me that winter isn't just about high-voltage powder days at the ski resort. It can be enjoyed at a slower pace. I was even inspired to buy a pair of my own snowshoes.

Direct flights to Calgary International Airport are available from more than a dozen major US hubs. Banff National Park is an easy 90-minute drive west on the Trans-Canada Highway.

Lakefront grande dame Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise offers every imaginable snowy activity, from horse-drawn sleigh rides to curling. In winter an outdoor bar built from 240 blocks of ice serves mulled wine and spiked cocoa. Only hotel guests have access to Basin Glacial Waters, a sprawling thermal bathhouse. Don't miss the excellent hotel bookshop, curated with out-of-print editions on the area's mountaineering history.

One of the park's first hotels, Fairmont Banff Springs, recently added a new wing of larger, family-friendly suites with bunk beds and adjoining rooms. An on-site skating rink has a pop-up sugar shack that serves maple treats, and the adventure center rents fat-tire bikes and arranges guided evening snowshoe tours. Of the 13 dining venues, 1888 Chophouse, known for its Alberta Wagyu, is a standout.

A refreshing boutique alternative to Banff's palatial resorts, the reimagined Kenrick Hotel has an outpost of Calgary's Analog Coffee, a guests-only hydrotherapy spa that stays open until midnight, and one of the town's top tables, Alpine Italian–inspired Fat Ox.

Tucked away on Sulphur Mountain, 320-room resort Rimrock Banff, Emblems Collection debuted a sleek makeover last summer. The first property in Accor's new über-luxe Emblems Collection features a bathhouse of saunas, glacial plunges, and infinity pools, plus a cocktail-forward vinyl listening room and in-house guides who can take guests on glacier treks and ice canyon walks.

Reservations are a must at white-tablecloth Dining Room at the Post Hotel and Spa, known for its 25,000-plus-bottle wine cellar and European-inspired menu of dishes like roasted chateaubriand and Dover sole with saffron beurre blanc.

The house-made sourdough alone makes it worth pausing on a powder day for lunch at ski-in, ski-out restaurant Whitehorn Bistro off the Grizzly Gondola of Lake Louise Ski Resort. On a bluebird day request a patio seat.

The Dusty Boot Saloon and Dance Hall was recently spiffed up and turned into an Old West saloon with a stage for live music and a menu of excellent cocktails, like the Cattleman's Old Fashioned, and elevated bar food, including addictive popcorn chicken and shrimp spiked with wasabi peas.

At Good Folk, hearty breakfast dishes like banana caramel French toast will fuel your day's adventure. In the evening the menu showcases the local bounty in dishes like Alberta wild boar chop and a decadent bison burger topped with smoked cheddar and pepper bacon.

Johnston Canyon, a labyrinth of limestone rocks and cascades, sees a fraction of the visitors in winter than in summer. But to make sure you have the frozen falls to yourself, book the morning Icewalk experience with Discover Banff Tours.

Local outfitter Bikescape runs beginner-friendly Nordic ski tours on the trails within Banff National Park as well as electric fat-tire bike tours that include a backcountry lunch.

Sit back and enjoy the views of Lake Louise from the seat of a horse-drawn sled. Brewsters Lake Louise Stables runs hour-long trips that follow the lake path; evening tours under the stars are extra special.

SkiBig3's resorts offer something for everyone. Family-friendly Mount Norquay has night skiing and a thrilling tubing park. Every chairlift on the front side of Lake Louise Ski Resort has both an easy (green) and challenging (black) way down. Sunshine Mountain Lodge at Banff Sunshine Village has the area's only ski-in, ski-out lodging, and its big alpine views make you feel like you're downhilling in Europe.

For the perfect detour en route to Calgary International Airport, Everwild Canmore, a new Nordic spa at the Everwild hotel in the town of Canmore, features a DIY outdoor thermal circuit as well as five-elements rituals, ranging from an herbal steam cleanse to an Aufguss ceremony. The spa lounge serves a shareable charcuterie and cheese board for two along with cocktails.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.
