#6273. 13 Travel Slippers That Are Comfier Than the Ones From Your Favorite Hotel

After a full day of sightseeing—or an even longer one spent in and out of airports—few things feel better than kicking off your shoes and sliding on a cozy pair of slippers. The complimentary slippers at a luxury hotel are always tempting to take home, but if we're honest, they rarely last beyond a few wears. Fortunately, plenty of more durable—and more comfortable—options exist, from plush, shearling slides and classic wool slip-ons to lightweight travel slippers that barely take up any room in your suitcase. Some have cushioned footbeds and rubber soles sturdy enough for a quick trip outside; others feature soft, suede soles better suited to padding around the house.

Whether you want a warm, fluffy pair by your bed or a foldable option for your next long-haul flight, there’s a slipper for everyone on this list. Read on for the very best pairs to pick up this season from Bombas, Cozy Earth, Ugg, and more.

⁠These lightweight, fuzzy slippers feature a soft, wool-like polyester upper, a breathable lining, and a memory foam footbed for a cushy feel underfoot. The nonslip soles are sturdy enough for quick trips outside to grab the mail or take out the trash, but they're best suited for indoor wear. Even better, they're machine washable, so you can easily keep them in pristine condition all season long. Available in five colors and backed by more than 10,000 Amazon reviews, they're an affordable option for wearing around the house or packing for a weekend away.

It's easy to see why this under-$25 Amazon find has racked up more than 23,000 five-star ratings. Not only are these slippers ridiculously soft (and just the right amount of over-the-top), but they're also pretty practical, thanks to the thick memory foam insole that retains its shape even after daily wear.

While your winter wardrobe likely contains a cashmere sweater or two, don’t sleep on these cashmere slides from Garnet Hill. Thanks to the slip-on slides’ sumptuous cashmere construction and breathable, thermal-insulating fibers, they’ll keep your feet warm and toasty—but not sweaty—all winter long. The padded footbed provides an extra layer of pillowy-soft comfort.

After a long day on your feet, you'll be glad to have these Quince slippers waiting by your bed. They have a soft suede leather upper and thick Australian shearling lining that feels plush against bare feet. And unlike some fuzzy slippers that leave your feet sweaty, the shearling material naturally wicks away moisture and regulates temperature, so you can wear them year-round.

The soft, moisture-wicking sheepskin wool lining of this classic shoe has made it an all-time favorite from the nostalgic Australian brand. The Scuff comes with a thin rubber sole that has just the right amount of support and stability for being on your feet in the kitchen or just puttering around the house on the weekend. Colors include the popular chestnut (shown above), dark gray, and black.

This luxury slide keeps your feet dry and cool, thanks to its moisture-wicking and temperature-regulating design. They're fluffy and warm, and so easy to slip on when you first wake up in the morning. Plus, they feature a slip-resistant sole, making them one of the sturdiest picks on the list.

One of the little luxuries of a hotel stay is slipping into the plush robes and slippers hanging in the closet. Now you can capture that vacation-level comfort at home with The Ritz-Carlton Frette slippers. Crafted from ultra-soft microfiber, they feel cozy and spa-like, while the nonslip soles make them practical for everyday wear around the house. The embroidered hotel logo adds a touch of opulence, and when they need a refresh, simply toss them in the wash.

These striped slippers from Parachute look like something you'd find at a cool boutique hotel. Made in Turkey from thick, absorbent cotton terry, they're soft underfoot and comfortable to slip on after a shower or while lounging at home. The stripes add a little more personality than your typical spa slippers, and the rubber soles grip slippery floors effortlessly. They're durable enough for everyday wear, too, though you may want to size up for a roomier fit.

Made with ultra-soft sheep fur and a plush shearling lining, these chic slippers provide plenty of warmth on chilly fall and winter mornings. As warm as they are, they're also naturally odor-resistant and breathable, so you don't have to worry about your feet getting too hot. They offer a grippy, durable outsole, so while they're best suited for lounging indoors, they can also be worn outside if necessary; you'll feel a little more secure wearing them out on the Airbnb's deck or down to the hotel lobby than in other pairs. They come recommended by commerce editor Meaghan Kenny, who regularly turns to them for extra warmth on cold weekend mornings at home.

Bombas has quite a few solid slippers from which to choose—including the Gripper Slipper that really blurs the line between sock and shoe. But the Sunday Slipper, with its super-soft faux fur and slip-on, slip-off capability, sits at the top of the heap when it comes to versatility. If you're stumped on what to gift someone for the holidays, the best-selling style is foolproof.

Birkenstock manufactures footwear of fabulous durability and quality, from the popular sandals and clogs that you can wear here, there, and everywhere to the more indoor-friendly Zermatt shearling slipper. Despite being supremely soft, the latex sole offers a boost of support, which is why they make such a great house shoe. They come in men's and women’s sizes, and you can pick between wide or narrow fits for optimal comfort.

The Ugg Tasman slipper might be the most recognizable slipper on this list, and it's popular for good reason: The closed-back design makes it a more practical alternative to the brand's classic Scuff slipper; the plush sheepskin lining and durable suede upper ensure coziness and durability; and the Fair Isle–inspired Tasman braid around the trim adds a hint of character.

L.L.Bean fans rave about these clog-like slippers for their arch support, heel cushioning, and playful patterns, featuring designs ranging from turtles to moose to ombré forest trees. They have a fleece lining and rubber anti-slip sole, and are roomy enough to wear your thickest socks underneath in colder months, making them our top pick for cold feet.

What are the best brands for travel slippers?

Bombas and EverFoams design lightweight slippers that are conveniently packable, while Ugg and Quince offer cozy shearling options that take up a bit more suitcase space. If you love the slippers you usually find at luxury hotels, The Ritz-Carlton also sells its signature Frette spa slippers online, so you can bring five-star comfort right to your home.

Slippers can be a welcome change from sneakers or boots on a long-haul flight, especially if you’re hoping to get some sleep. Choose a lightweight, packable pair with nonslip soles, but switch back to shoes when walking around the cabin or using the bathroom.

What should you look for in the best indoor slippers?

When shopping for indoor slippers, fit and material matter most: Wool and shearling provide warmth without trapping too much heat, while memory foam adds cushioning. Look for a soft, flexible sole with enough grip to keep you from slipping on hardwood or tile floors.

#6272. Holafly Plans: The Best eSIM Plan for Long Term Travelers

There are a lot of eSIM companies in the world. They all work a similar way: you download their app, pick your package, install the eSIM into your smartphone, and off you go. There’s many I like.

But one I like more than the rest is Holafly and I’ve been using their eSIMs for years. I find their app to be easy to use and their rates really competitive.

So when Holafly launched Holafly Plans, a single eSIM that works as an ongoing subscription across 160+ destinations, I was excited. It’s a great option for those who are looking for more data and flexibility than a traditional eSIM. (An eSIM is a digital SIM built directly into your phone’s hardware, so there’s no physical card to insert or swap. Instead of visiting a shop for a plastic SIM, you activate a plan by scanning a QR code or installing it through an app, and you’re connected within minutes. Because it’s software-based, a single phone can hold multiple eSIMs, letting you switch between a home number and a local or global travel plan without touching your device. I have like 10 installed. lol)

In this post, I’m going to explain what the product is, how it’s different than a traditional eSIM, and who I think this option is for!

Holafly Plans is a single global eSIM that covers more than 160 destinations on one ongoing subscription. You buy it once, install it once, and it just keeps working as you move from country to country. You don’t reswap SIMs, you don’t redownload anything, there’s no re-purchasing, and no hunting for a new QR code every time you land somewhere new.

It automatically reconnects you when you land in a new place. Think of it as like a traditional mobile carrier – but a lot cheaper.

You can buy it monthly or annually and it comes in two tiers: Light and Unlimited. There’s no annual contract and you can cancel any time.

The Unlimited Plan includes no data caps and an unlimited hotspot so you can tether your laptop on the go. If you’re a digital nomad uploading video, doing video calls, or just someone who doesn’t want to think about data ever again, this is a great add-on. This tier also comes with a local phone number from the US, UK, or Canada, which lets you receive SMS messages.

The Light Plan gives you 25GB of data a month, still includes a hotspot, and still covers the same 160+ destination coverage. For someone who mostly uses maps, messaging apps, and the occasional Instagram scroll, this package is probably the best option.

Additionally, with both Holafly Plans, once your plan is active, you get their “Always On” feature which is 1GB of backup data every month, automatically for life, even if you eventually cancel your subscription entirely.

Pricing varies a bit by region and currency and depending on how long you purchase, so check out their current rates on the Holafly Plans page. However, as an example, their unlimited plan is only $55 USD per month for 1 year, which is a lot cheaper than any US based carrier charges for their base option that includes unlimited 5G data overseas.  You can get monthly, quarterly, or yearly plans. Quarterly plans save approximately 10% while yearly plans save 15%.

Use the promo code NOMADICMATT at checkout to get 10% OFF Holafly Plans and 5% OFF all standard Holafly eSIMs.

Classic Holafly eSIMs are built for a single trip. You pick a country or region (there are 200+ available), choose how many days of data you need, and it covers just that trip. If you’re flying to Portugal for two weeks, a classic eSIM is still the simpler, cheaper option. It’s a one-and-done purchase. If you only take a couple trips per year then this is still the best option.

On the other hand, if you’re a digital nomad who is gone from your home country most of the year and moving between different countries all the time, then the Holafly Plans fly is the much better option. It’s a standing global subscription designed for people who are more or less always somewhere. Instead of buying a new eSIM every time your itinerary changes, you have one number, one connection, one bill that follows you across borders indefinitely. Plus, you can get a phone number, unlimited data, and a hotspot. In the US, if you were to get T-Mobile’s plan, which caps data and is the closest thing we have to “affordable” international plans, you’re going to spend over $100 USD a month (I know because I used to use this plan!). Holafly Plans costs less and gives you more.

Holafly also recently launched a new tier called The Ultra Plan by Holafly, and it’s a bit different from anything else in the eSIM world.

For comparison, Unlimited is $64.90 monthly, $58.65 quarterly, or $52.41 yearly. Quarterly saves you about 10%, and yearly about 20%. (Use my code NOMADICMATT or MATTK gets you another 10% off on top of whichever plan you choose.)

So, is the upgrade worth it? Ultra costs about $26 a month more than Unlimited if you pay monthly, $24 more on quarterly, and $21 more on yearly. Here’s how I think about it: one lost bag gets you $150, which covers roughly six months of the difference, whichever way you pay. And that’s before you even factor in the language barrier and the stress of figuring out where to go. With Ultra, you get unlimited access to all that support included in your plan.

If you’re heading out for a few months, quarterly is the sweet spot. You get the savings without committing to a full year. If you’re taking a two-week vacation, skip it and stick with a standard Holafly eSIM.

Just to be clear, this doesn’t replace travel insurance. It won’t cover hospital bills, theft, or emergency situations, so you’ll still need proper travel insurance for all of that but if you want small trip related coverage, this can be a cheaper option.

If anything goes sideways during setup, real people are on the other end of support 24/7.

Holafly Plans isn’t for everyone. If you’re taking a single two-week vacation, a classic destination eSIM will cost you less. #6271. Frontier Airlines Starts Selling First Class From $129. I Am Seriously Considering Booking It.

Frontier Airlines is now selling its new first class seats, with wider seating and no middle seats in the first two rows. Extra-legroom seating, USB-C power, and Starlink internet are also part of the cabin transformation. I welcome the investment, though a better seat will only get Frontier so far if the rest of the experience does not improve alongside it.

Installation is underway, with completion expected March 5, 2027. Reservations are open for travel beginning that day.

Promotional pricing requires purchasing the flight and bundle together by November 16, 2026, at 11:59 pm ET, for select nonstop domestic departures March 5–April 5, 2027. Availability is limited.

USB-C power is planned for the first eight rows. Both power and Starlink installations begin in 2027 and progress aircraft by aircraft throughout the year. Booking the new seat does not mean every other advertised improvement will be available on your flight.

For me, reliable internet and the ability to keep a laptop charged substantially determine how useful a flight is. A comfortable seat is welcome, but on a daytime trip I also must get work done…it is an essential part of the package.

I have to say, I’m quite excited about these developments.

As much as I loved warmed mixed nuts, a hot meal, and sparkling water saved with lime and ice in a glass…the Frontier network is respectable and a comfortable seat with Wi-Fi and power are more important. If Frontier can charge half or what American or United are asking on the same route, I’m totally up for flying Frontier more.

The bigger question is whether Frontier can persuade passengers to pay more and then give them a reason to come back.

A first class seat loses much of its appeal if a cancellation leaves you with poor alternatives or resolving an ordinary problem becomes an ordeal…two areas where traditional network carriers still have a huge advantage. Selling a premium product raises expectations even when the price is relatively low.

I do not expect Frontier to become a full-service airline simply because it installs eight larger seats. But I would expect the airline to understand that passengers purchasing those seats are buying some relief from the compromises associated with budget travel, again myself included.

That makes this an opportunity. If Frontier can offer a comfortable seat at a sensible total price and deliver dependable transportation and maybe a little bit more service than the “Big Front Seat” on Spirit Airlines, I think there is a market for it.

Frontier Airlines is moving forward with first class, and I welcome more choice at the front of the aircraft. The new seats could make the airline more attractive to passengers who value comfort but remain sensitive to price, like me. Even the extra legroom seats are something I would consider, with Starlink being an even bigger game-changer.

While I would happily try it, the real test will be whether Frontier delivers an experience that makes me want to book it again. A larger seat with Starlink can get someone through the door…but Frontier must deliver that.

#6267. What’s Your Airport Dwell Time? A Metric Businesses Think A Lot About

Dwell time, simply, is how long you spend in an airport, or airport space, before a flight. For most people, it’s not something they’ve ever actively really thought about.

For businesses in air travel and airports, like lounge operators, credit card companies or airlines, it’s one of the main things they think about. So what’s yours and what does it say about you?

Well, a lot. More importantly, the tracking of that dwell time has contributed to quite a lot of innovation in lounges and airports, with hopefully much more to come.

Build it and they will come. Who knew Kevin Costner knew so much about lounges?! In truth, if someone builds a lounge, everyone will come and ensuring it’s a good experience is an art form requiring math. Crowds can be hard to predict and most lounges are “too” full these days.

Knowing the average dwell time of a customer, and even a specific customer profile is one of the best tools lounges have to predict the flows of customers, including how much they’ll need to stock in food and drinks and everything else during peak times.

Even outside of lounges, knowing how long an air traveler spends in the airport is vital to understanding what kind of businesses, restaurants or concessions to offer. There’s a reason grab and go places do really, really well and get away with charging $12 for water.

Surprisingly to some, top tier frequent flyers typically have a really low dwell time compared to lower ranks or leisure travelers.

If an airline knows their lounge is full of top tiers that day, they can expect many people who won’t stay long. Whereas, if it’s a day with full flights and mostly leisure travel passengers, you can predict people will dwell far longer.

It makes sense. If you’re not used to the delights of a great airport lounge you come earlier, stay longer and take advantage of more. You also have less confidence in timings of the check in and security process, so you pad time in, in addition to the natural, “treat yourself” vibes.

If you do it all the time, every minute not in the airport is often seen as the win, so lounges are just a place to quickly reset and refresh before carrying on.

The first time I experienced a true first class lounge I think I got to the airport at the earliest possible interval. I had hours in there and of course, tried everything.

But I’ve been very lucky, I’ve experienced most lounges many times, been spoiled by the best many times, and unless there’s a real wow factor moment, I’m happiest spending as little time waiting in an airport as possible. Don’t get me wrong, I still indulge from time to time, but I’ve seen a huge dip in my own dwell average.

As I strolled through T2 at Heathrow this week en route to the United Club, it occurred to me that most of my recent lounge visits averaged about 30 minutes in total. In that 30 minutes I’d say I have a maximum of one drink, often little or no food, and mostly take advantage of the wifi and nice calm facilities.

I’ve gotten my time from curb to security at Heathrow down to a decent science and I like it that way. At other airports with even more predictable security and check in patterns, I’ll shave even more time off, often leaving no time for lounges at all.

And this raises a fair question: if everyone could truly model out their time from curb to airside, would they spend as long? Things like TSA PreCheck and CLEAR have been monumental in adding a layer of certainty to this process and I’d expect we’ll see more of it. Will more passengers change habits as they have better confidence in making their flight while cutting it fine?

Now of course, all bets are off when I travel with my kids. And that’s kind of the point. We think we’re very unique in our travel habits, but there are many variables of our travels which drop us into a fairly predictable pattern … and dwell time.

When lounge access is a marquee benefit of being a frequent flyer, but most top frequent flyers hardly leave any time for lounge dwelling, is that a real selling point?

In response, we’ve seen really clever pivots lately, including from Air Canada and Capital One. Each brand has created curated “grab and go” offerings in their lounges or lounge-like areas to offer passengers complimentary things which have tangible value — a nitro cold brew latte, or a nice pastry — for “free”, which they’re totally able to take on the road with them.

That’s a huge departure from the days of lounges with signs everywhere saying no outside food and drinks and no removing food or drinks from the lounge. People never paid attention anyway, and this now just creates a formalized and better thought out approach to catering to all traveler needs.

The big question is: what’s next for adding value to a travelers airport journey? Be sure to share your lounge and travel habits as well.

#6266. United Airlines Finally Plans Boeing 757-300 Makeover With Seatback Screens And Bigger Bins

United Airlines plans to give its Boeing 757-300 fleet a long-overdue cabin update, adding larger overhead bins, entertainment screens at every seat, and power throughout the cabin. These aircraft have needed attention for years and were always included in the United Next refresh plan, though I am somewhat surprised to see United keep these workhorses in the fleet.

United Airlines 757-300 aircraft will be modified in accordance with the United’s “United Next” strategy, which includes installation of new Boeing Space Bins, Panasonic Audio Video On Demand (AVOD), In Flight Entertainment at every seat location, full cabin In-Seat Power Supply System (ISPS), new class dividers and cabin headers, and new UAL branding elements. Additionally, all seats and monuments will be refreshed throughout the cabin.

United:“United Airlines 757-300 aircraft will be modified in accordance with the United's "United Next" strategy, which includes installation of new Boeing Space Bins, Panasonic Audio Video On Demand (AVOD), In Flight Entertainment at every seat location, full cabin In-Seat…

As I mentioned above, the surprise is not that United is refreshing its entire narrwobody fleet, which it has promised for years now, but that it is actually moving forward with the 757-300s rather than phasing them out. However, I also understand that an A321neo or 737 MAX is not necessarily a direct replacement for this workhorse.

My understanding is that one reason this project took longer to get moving was the lack of a certified larger-bin option for this particular aircraft. United had to work through that certification hurdle rather than simply order an existing installation, which puts the delay in context.

United listed just 21 Boeing 757-300s in its year-end 2025 fleet disclosure, each with 234 seats. Undertaking a specialized modification for a fleet that small is a more substantial commitment than fitting the same equipment across hundreds of aircraft. For passengers, however, the size of the subfleet is beside the point. If your flight is operated by a 757-300, the overhead storage and cabin condition are part of your United experience.

More useful bin space should make boarding less stressful: currently there are far too many bags that must be gate checked because the smaller overhead bins force larger (but standard) carry-on bags to be placed on their sides.

I will also be happy to see entertainment screens included throughout the aircraft. When traveling with my children, individual screens are especially useful.

JonNYC also mentions power and it will be great to have USB-C, but the aircraft already have universal A/C power outlets in every cabin.

But what JonNYC does not mention and I consider most important is that these aircraft will get Starlink. Currently, most 757-300s still have an ancient Panasonic Wi-Fi system that often does not work. I specifically avoid the 757-300 for this reason and have been burned almost every time I have flown it with non-operable Wi-Fi. Some 757-300s have been upgraded with Viasat, but I am unwilling to fly on the 753s unless absolutely necessary. The new cabins will be welcomed, but Starlink is the most important upgrade.

I do not object to an aircraft simply because it is older: Delta has shown that a 30-year-old aircraft with mood lighting, fast Wi-Fi, and seatback screens can feel just as comfortable as a more modern aircraft. Refreshed seating and better amenities can change that experience substantially, even when the aircraft itself has been flying for decades.

This investment suggests United sees a continuing role for the 757-300 for many years in the future.

The Boeing 757-300 is finally in line for the kind of cabin attention it has long needed. Larger bins, seatback entertainment, and Starlink Wi-Fi will make a noticeable difference. I figured these aircraft would just be retired, but it appears they will fly the “Friendly Skies” for many years to come.

#6265. New Credit Card Sets Annual Fee Dynamically, Based On Benefit Usage

Among savvy Redditors and credit card blogs, there’s a common thread with many recent credit card changes. “It feels like a coupon book” is often the consumer reaction, particularly as annual fees rise as justification for an increasing number of partner offer benefits, which if consumed in entirety could lead to more value.

Since many people simply won’t use all the benefits and partner offers being baked into the card, people increasingly feel like the annual fee rises are getting too steep. In a bold move, a new card launched today which offers a flexible annual fee, based only on the benefits you actually use.

Signed up for a card named after a precious or semi precious metal and shocked by the $450-$695 fee? You’re not alone.

To get your money back from such a fee, you’d need to take advantage of regular lounge access at airports, utilize your TSA PreCheck/Global Entry credit, maximize every monthly dining or entertainment credit and sign up for every other fee credit, which often requires a purchase.

To quell this issue, the new card is effectively a build your own card, card.

Despite the innovation, the card draws on the historical concept of the coupon book, where you only pay for the offers you tear out and redeem. The annual fee starts at zero, but as you actually redeem the cards benefits, you get billed accordingly. Your fee can be zero, or as high as $10,000 per year.

Done right, you can end up paying $650 in annual fees for about $800 worth of stuff, some of which you wanted and most of which, about $700 worth, you didn’t really want or need, but felt compelled to get, just because it’s there.

This model allows you to really dive into the classic coupon book, feeling like you’re really tearing offers out of the page, and simply leaving the ones you’re not using in the book. You’re only paying for the ones you rip out, but when there’s so many offers to choose from, the book just feels so compelling.

Obviously, it’s April 1st and no such card is coming to the market (yet, lol), but hopefully this light hearted amusement has been a helpful exercise in framing the true value you’re really extracting from your premium credit card, or conversely, the lack thereof.

Consider the things you’d actually purchase without the “offer” prompt and if that number still adds up to be more than the annual fee, you’re doing it right. If it doesn’t…

#6264. A350-1000ULR Sets New Distance Record

Airbus’ A350-1000ULR has been officially recognized for breaking the Guinness World Record for the longest flight by distance by a commercial aircraft.

The record-breaking flight from Melbourne to Toulouse, France, took place in July and was widely reported on, but was only recently confirmed by Guinness using data validated by the International Aeronautical Federation and flightradar24.

The nonstop journey covered 12,503 nautical miles and lasted 24 hours and 24 minutes. The -1000ULR flew over Sydney and the Pacific on a north-easterly routing toward Los Angeles, crossed North America and the Atlantic, and passed over London on its way to Toulouse. According to Airbus, the 13 people on board witnessed two sunsets and two sunrises.

The crew included three Airbus flight test pilots, two pilots from Qantas, and five Airbus flight test engineers. Also on board were two Airbus design engineers and a representative from the IAF.

Airbus is developing the -1000ULR for Qantas’ Project Sunrise, a yearslong effort to connect the east coast of Australia with far-flung destinations such as New York and London. The manufacturer expects to deliver the first of the type in April 2027. Qantas is aiming to operate the first Project Sunrise flight, from Sydney to London, later that year.

The Australian flag carrier has ordered 12 -1000ULRs.

“In responding to the challenge laid down by Qantas, our teams came together to extend the range of the A350-1000 in an efficient and economically viable way to undertake the world’s longest ever commercial flights,” Lars Wagner, CEO of commercial aircraft at Airbus, said in a news release. “Flying 12,503 nautical miles non-stop, we have fully proven the aircraft’s capability to fulfill its mission. And the world record was the icing on the cake.”

#6263. United Airlines CEO Talks Starlink In Veterans Day Message

United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby used his Veterans Day message to thank the 8,500 veterans who work at the airline. But before turning to their service, he spent a substantial part of the message discussing Starlink, winning customers from competitors, and his belief that United is the best airline in the world. The opening offers another glimpse into what Kirby sees as the opportunity ahead in 2027.

I typically share Kirby’s internal Veterans Day message each year (he also posted publicly on LinkedIN). His appreciation for military service and his affection for the United States are familiar themes. This year, though, he began with a thank-you for the summer operation and a look ahead at how better Wi-Fi might persuade passengers to switch airlines.

Happy Veterans Day everyone. Before I start on my Veterans Day message, I want to thank everyone for a really incredible summer. All the hard work you do. There was a lot of weather this summer, but the United team just did a great job so thank you. I also want to tell you how excited I am for 2027. In 2027 we’re going have a unique advantage in Starlink. And what that means is we’re gonna have a lot of customers who are loyal to other airlines today try us because of Starlink and I can already can hear this from customers. What’s going to happen is I hope they’re going to realize that United really is the best airline in the world when they come try United. We’re gonna be able to get those customers to come to United because of Starlink but to stay with United because everything else United is better. So thank you in advance for what you’re gonna do to win new brand loyal customers in 2027 for us at United.

But what I really wanted to do today is thank the 8,500 veterans that work here at United Airlines. I think all of you know that I am deeply patriotic. I love this country. I feel fortunate to have been born in this country and think it’s the greatest country in the history of the planet, but that wouldn’t be the case if it wasn’t for all the veterans who work at United but all the other veterans and the people that serve today. So to all the veterans not just at United, but around the world who have served to put their lives on the line to keep this country free and great, thank you for your service. Thank you for everything that you’ve done. And today when you’re out working and you see a veteran, and I’m sure you will because there’s so many United, give them a special thank you for their service. So to everyone at United, thank you for everything that you’ve done. And the veterans, a special thank you on Veteran’s Day and I look forward to seeing you in the friendly skies.

The commercial opening is an unusual preface to a Veterans Day tribute, though Kirby explicitly separates it from the message that follows. That makes sense considering he is addressing all employees and using the opportunity to discuss more than one subject. Still, his emphasis is revealing.

Kirby sees Starlink as a reason for passengers loyal to other airlines to give United a try, which is likely true. The more ambitious part is his expectation that the rest of the experience will persuade them to stay.

Reliable, fast internet can absolutely influence my booking decision. If I need to work during a flight, connectivity is more important than modest differences in the seat or meal and I’m hardly alone.

The second proposition is true, though certainly easier said than done. A passenger attracted by Starlink still has to navigate the airport, interact with the crew, and arrive at the destination. A great internet connection may get someone to book once. How United handles that journey, especially when something goes wrong, will help determine whether the passenger returns.

I remain unconvinced that there is one universally “best” airline. But Kirby is giving his employees a clear assignment: use the opportunity created by Starlink to earn repeat business. That is indeed a useful objective and to Untied’s credit, it improving operational performance and overall onboard product are giving front-line staff the means to deliver.

Turning to Veterans Day, Kirby’s message is direct. He credits those who have served with protecting the country he loves and asks employees to thank the veterans they encounter at work. I appreciate that practical request and will do the same today in my own interactions (I’m not flying, though).

Gratitude does not require agreement with every military deployment or government decision. We can (and should) scrutinize those decisions while appreciating the people asked to carry them out and the sacrifices their service entails.

Kirby’s Veterans Day message combines a familiar expression of patriotism with an enthusiastic commercial outlook for 2027. His expectation that Starlink will bring new passengers through the door does indeed create a golden opportunity for United. Whether United earns their loyalty will depend on what happens beyond the Wi-Fi connection.

But today’s central message deserves its own acknowledgment. To the veterans at United Airlines and elsewhere, thank you for your service.

Matthew is an avid traveler who calls Los Angeles home. Each year he travels more than 200,000 miles by air and has visited more than 135 countries. Working both in the aviation industry and as a travel consultant, Matthew has been featured in major media outlets around the world and uses his Live and Let's Fly blog to share the latest news in the airline industry, commentary on frequent flyer programs, and detailed reports of his worldwide travel.

Thank you for your service. Period, full stop.

Otherwise, as long as we’re just using this day as an opportunity for PR puffery (as Kirby clearly is), I thought the title of yesterday’s Nonstop Dan video was quite accurate: “No, United is not a premium airline.”

Most folks are beyond-exhausted with the era of the ‘imperial’/’celebrity’ CEO…

~38% of narrowbodies have Starlink at United. ~3% of widebodies have starlink at United. I’m sure United will speed up installation over the winter, but scott Kirby doesn’t seem to realize how little his product matches the expectation he’s setting up.

If you’re on a 737-800/900 NG, A321, or MAX9 you’ve got a great chance of having starlink, if you’re on a 319, 320, MAX8, 757, or 73G, your odds are awful but… you’ll have, at best, internet that matches AA and DL but more likely you’ll have internet that barely works.

I’ve flown UA a lot lately and only ever had it on my regional jets. United really is going all out to advertise a product that isn’t ready for roll out.

“Isn’t ready for rollout?” Its on like almost 700 aircraft dude? That sentence doesn’t make sense – what about Starlink is not ready? Your complaint is that its not on every aircraft yet – it’s on 54% of United operated flights today and they are the fastest installer of Starlink in the world installing about 2-3 aircraft a day on average now.

They have been very clear that its not on every aircraft yet but coming to every aircraft with AVOD – they literally run an ad on every flight sayings its coming but not everywhere yet. I flew UA over the weekend and saw it.

Not really sure what else you want them to do. I would say bringing up Starlink in a veteran’s day message is a bit tone deaf though – thank people for their services, thank the those who have sacrificed everything and the families that have lost loved ones but no one cares about United’s product advantage in a Veteran’s day message…

try googling “United fleet site”, I’m not calling it the gospel, but it reinforces that there are entire major fleet types with no starlink, whatsoever. Not even a start on the installation.

And no, when only 38% of your narrowbodies have starlink and ~3% of United widebodies have Starlink, I don’t think anyone would realistically call that “ready for rollout”. It’s quite similar to Delta proclaiming “free wifi” for years when they didn’t have it.

I’m aware the regional fleet got it first which is how your “54% of United flights have it” stat comes about — an interesting stat, but simple aircraft seat awareness would also make it highly obvious that United is NOWHERE Close to 54% of United passengers having Starlink on their flight.

I’m not saying United won’t meet their stated timeline for the end of 2027. But Today? No. It’s absent from the vast majority of the mainline fleet and it’s an odd thing to market so heavily when nearly ALL united customers on an international longhaul flight will not have Starlink on their flight and while significantly less than half of United passengers on a United mainline plane will have Starlink.

Most companies think about the ability to produce a product they’re marketing before presenting it as omnipresent. I do, however, appreciate that you’re one of the few reading the small print in the United ads that it isn’t on every plane yet — I think we both know that isn’t the gist of the United Starlink advertisement messaging at the moment. The ads are “we have starlink, fly United for better wifi”. Presently, United still has the worst internet of the US3. That will rapidly change but numbers don’t lie. United is still below 1/3 of their mainline fleet having starlink.

“Not really sure what else you want them to do”

to be blunt, I don’t really care what they do, I’m just noting it’s odd how much united is advertising Starlink as a reason to immediately try United Airlines, when the majority of their mainline fleet isn’t close to having it. I fly United quite a bit and I have yet to see it on a mainline plane but, like I said, they have it installed on about 30% of their mainline fleet.

“as a reason to immediately try United Airlines, when the majority of their mainline fleet isn’t close to having it.”

bit overdramatic of a statement by me. *when the majority of their mainline fleet does not have it” is the better way to say that.

UA has accelerated Starlink installations in an attempt to finish before next summer. 33 aircraft at a time are now being modified. #6262. Global Airlines Is “Fyre Festival”, Not Virgin Atlantic

Yesterday, a Hi-Fly charter airplane took off from Glasgow bound for New York, with Hi-Fly crews and pilots. If you read the papers, it was purportedly ‘Global Airlines’ maiden flight, even though there’s no regularly scheduled service, the pilots and crew weren’t theirs, they couldn’t legally sell airline tickets on their own website and they don’t have a license to operate.

In 2025, crazy things are par for the course, so that didn’t stop all sorts of promising headlines of a revolution in the skies. This is the airline that promised stunning innovation and joy in the air, and the press gave Global Airlines an early gift, by comparing the story to Richard Branson and Virgin Atlantic. That’s just insane, as you’ll soon read.

In reality, anyone can charter a plane and have Hi-Fly operate it, and anyone foolish enough can pay extra for a custom paint job with their logo, or more financially insane — buy a scrapyard A380 and be on the hook for its maintenance, while paying a third party to fly it.

The whole ‘Global’ pitch was that people love the Airbus A380, hate all the current global airline experiences ( really?) and airline services — and a revolution in the skies, can happen again. It sounded exciting. We all like to dream. Global’s first flight would be the testament to what air travel can be and something passengers love. So, how’d they do?

When Virgin Atlantic launched in 1984, the airline industry had been in a massively “beige” management consultant style, joy killer phase for a decade.

The fun “golden era” aircraft spaces and frills of the 60’s had largely been stripped out and bus travel comparisons were totally fair. Richard Branson’s light hearted approach to service and differentiated selling could shift dollars and votes — and measurably did.

Let me be very clear: that simplicity in differentiation is no longer the case. You cannot shift wallets and put butts in seats just by saying you have a cool airplane alone, or a bar on board (particularly when it’s just a beverage cart that says pub).

From leading (actually real) global airlines, passengers expect, at minimum, the following…

When “Global”, and by Global I really do legally, technically mean Hi-Fly the jet charter company which actually flew the scrapyard plane that “Global” bought, they did NOT have…

Travel blogger Noel Phillips shared some of the trip with his following. The following screen grabs are…. cute?

The truth is, Virgin Atlantic didn’t have nearly as gargantuan of a task in the 80’s as any airline coming to market does today. In the 80’s many airlines were stuck, did lack innovation and had a pool of largely uninspired talent, with no experience outside of the airline vertical. There also wasn’t this whole technology thing, as standard expectation.

That’s all so far from the case these days and most that are specialized in the airline world are wickedly sharp. Most new people I know at airlines now also come from major tech companies, other travel verticals or impactful innovation firms.

Airlines are getting pretty good at this ole’ air travel thing.

A differentiated approach to smiles on board and a little bit of extra focus on fun, food and drinks could really shift minds and mentalities in the 1980’s, but now you gotta back it up, baby.

Everyone likes to feel special and Virgin, forever, has made people feel special at a time without tech. I’d argue Virgin has taught Delta a lot about that, and it’s a contributing factor to Delta’s rise as a premium airline. It didn’t happen overnight, and what looks easy never is.

Getting people to fly with you is now about safety, reliability, excellence in mobile technology, schedule and personalization. Then fine, we can care about which champagne; or caterer or lounge style or airport, and which celebs like it. Yes, these legacy airlines can appear stuffy at times, but my god, can you not marvel at the technology revolution making air travel journeys excellent?

On real airlines, before I even arrive at the airport, I can use the NFC chip in my passport pressed against my phone to validate my document and bypass human interaction. I board a United, or any serious airline flight nowadays and see a notification that my bag is loaded onto a cart to be loaded on the plane, then again when it’s loaded onto the plane!

I hit the wifi and I’m connected sitting at the gate. If for some reason the flight is at all delayed, or connection in jeopardy, I can instantly rebook onto any other service at no charge, without talking to a soul, with just a tap on the app.

Their seag back screens have blockbuster movies, boxsets and everything else you could want for a one hour, or 15 hour journey. It’s all just standard now, not innovative.

The app navigates me through the airport and even tells me when my zone is boarding. AKA – stand the “f” back. The food is at least solid, the beverages are getting better because of their scale (buying power) and there are fewer poor customer service interactions because of how tech forward and seamless journeys are.

All the great, big airlines do this. This is like… baseline for a real player.

Tell me, or ask the Global Airlines CEO, James Asquith, where in the roadmap all of these essentials are? I want to make it clear that their priority for the last three years was a Soho House press conference about serving champagne in economy, maybe, “if they could get the economics right” rather than any of these basic things.

And in the end, they didn’t even deliver on the silly things they prioritized. The first Global flight wasn’t a remotely differentiated take on economy, business or first, as promised. It was 12 year old seats from another lackluster airline, without real refurb and even the long haul dignity of any seat back entertainment, which that airline which scrapped the plane offered.

If Richard Branson was at the helm, they never would’ve let that flight take off. Making a splash means at least doing one thing differently, right? An airline promising total innovation, A380 experience and differentiation cannot launch a flight which does not even meet the basic standards of budget carriers like Norse. You just can’t take off. You innovative something!

Let’s not forget that when Richard Branson formed Virgin Atlantic, he’d already founded a notable brand and number of businesses in the UK, was quite famous, and filed records and company books in a place where they are scrutinized. He was “real”, even if some was bluster. The public could and did use his businesses.

James Asquith’s only claim to fame, other than from the Instagram account he bought followers for, to fake fame — yes, factually — is that he was the “CEO” of Holiday Swap. Omg, so big time!

The business purports to be a home swap company, though there are no financial records of any legal merit in the West, and despite my damndest multi-year attempts, no record of actual customers. Simple use of Similar Web or review sites will help your own conclusions. You can read old blog posts for more musings. The rumors of what laundered through are scary. Maybe a real journalist can find out for us?

I actually think it’s dangerous to the public to compare these two people.

I’ve had the good fortune of meeting Richard Branson many times throughout the years and he’s always been wildly impressive. Wickedly sharp, analytical, funny and personable. It’s easy to put in a good shift for PR purposes, but I’ve observed levels of deep dive knowledge that no setup encounter can protect for — and genuine interest too. He cares about his people and he worries about the details.

I also have many people in my personal life connected to the Virgin Atlantic founder and I know of nothing but admiration and respect for the man, his company ethos and family. Business in the front, party in the back.

My only encounter with James Asquith was when he was fuming that he wasn’t invited on an airlines press trip, slid into my Instagram DM’s wanting me to blast them – and for us to be best buds as we roast a major (actual) global airline. That airline later confidentially told me he was banned from flying, due to his antics. I politely declined and he unfollowed me. It was soooo cool.

I guess if you can’t fly other airlines, you start your own?

So yeah, if you ever feel like putting your life in the hands of an airline without functioning entertainment screens, or WiFi, or regularly scheduled service, or new seats, or a mobile app, or an actual license to fly planes, definitely fly with Global. Oh, and no viable loyalty program either. Forget about earning points from daily spending and turning them into upgrades.

Those other “boring” airlines with all the bells and whistles above are clearly not ready to make travel great, with a new golden age, again.

Gilbert Ott is an ever curious traveler and one of the world's leading travel experts. His adventures take him all over the globe, often spanning over 200,000 miles a year and his travel exploits are regularly... More by Gilbert Ott

His intrusion and snide comment ab0ut Simon Calder was entirely unnecessary. I have little respect for Asquith as it is, he doesn’t seem to actually “do” anything other than post Insta’s of slamming Champagne, and buying an Instagram account for the new venture is downright deceptive. Prove me wrong, I’m all for new carriers, but part of me wants it to fail just because of the insufferable “CEO”.

‘Global Airlines’ reminds me of the line from ‘The Producers’: “Under the right circumstances, a [person] could make more money with a flop than he could with a hit.”

This is why many say “hire for personality and train for skill.” James Asquith has failed this test with his attitude and stands little chance of building a culture within his company that can grow to compete with the likes of Virgin. I was always concerned that this airline was launching without any unique selling points at all. Now to read that what little was brought in from China Southern does not even work: it’s for me very sad to read. Substantial funding was needed to get this far and there seems to have been very little planning around the customer experience. I raised 350k externally to launch my last business, and that was not easy for me to do. So to imagine the capital sums that will be wasted here for all the unforced errors made, it’s so disheartening given it was foreseeable! There are so many case studies, even from Virgin with Virgin Nigeria and Virgin America to review! James Asquith seems to be very lazy and entitled. A great opportunity not afforded to many better qualified people (not me), has been thrown away!

While I agree with everything in this article, I also feel like immediately criticizing new entrants and disrupters is not fair. There is not a single person in aviation that wants to see less A380’s, that want les competition transatlantic, or fewer carriers. I appreciate Global, I appreciate BOOM, and I think it is just as sensational to criticize Global as it is for them to put on a metaphorical Fyre Fest in the sky. This is responsible reporting, but let’s also at some recognize the feat that getting this particular plane in the sky, with people, to NY was. Aviation was built on the backs of visionaries and risk-takers, I hope we will continue to celebrate that spirit.

I’m genuinely surprised that yours seems to the the only objectively credible take on this fiasco. I’ve watched a couple of the first flight review videos and the aircraft and service are laughable, yet the internet is still awash with “great to see!” and “Go Global!”, all blindly ignoring the current capabilities of the competition summarised above as if they don’t matter.

At least it’s given us a good laugh over the last few years but someone is losing money (hard to call anything sunk into this shambles an “investment”) and I imagine the flag carriers will be delighted as it makes them look stellar by comparison. Got to seriously question the judgement of anyone that wanted to get involved with Global. It’s all been smoke and mirrors from day one.

#6261. Lufthansa Takes Delivery of Its First A350-1000

Lufthansa this week took delivery of its first Airbus A350-1000, a type it says will offer a better customer experience while reducing operating costs.

The aircraft was formally handed over to the carrier on Tuesday in the presence of Lufthansa Group CEO Carsten Spohr and Lars Wagner, CEO of commercial aircraft at Airbus. Nicknamed “Deutschland,” the jet is Lufthansa’s 700th Airbus airplane, and the seventh in a special commemorative fleet bearing 100th anniversary liveries.

The white and dark blue designs feature an oversized crane, a symbol first used by predecessor Deutsche Luft Hansa.

Lufthansa Group has ordered a total of 15 A350-1000s. The first 10 will operate for the Lufthansa core brand, and will be based at its Munich hub.

“Deutschland” will fly to Munich on Wednesday, officials said, and operate its inaugural flight, to Tokyo-Haneda, on Dec. 3. The aircraft will also be Lufthansa’s first long-haul airplane equipped with Starlink satellite internet service.

“The fact that, as the world’s largest Airbus customer, we are taking delivery of our 700th Airbus aircraft exactly 50 years after the first Airbus delivery to Lufthansa, and in the year of our 100th anniversary, makes this a very special moment for us,” Spohr said in a statement. “Our partnership is a prime example of what Europe can achieve when it works together.”

Lufthansa’s -1000s will seat 300 passengers in four cabins – First, Business, Premium Economy, and Economy.

#6260. These 9 Hotels for Broadway Lovers Put You in the Heart of NYC’s Theater District

As a Californian who discovered the wonderful world of Broadway by borrowing CDs from my local library, it was only fitting that the first trip I ever planned by myself was to New York City—and the entire itinerary revolved around collecting Playbills. Now, after living in the area for more than two decades, I’m that unlikely New Yorker who still claims Times Square as her favorite and most-frequented neighborhood. I just love the Theater District—where else can you find 41 venues featuring the world's best live theater all within a single mile?

In this age of event tourism, Broadway has remained a constant. And seeing a show is about more than just the storyline of a play or the numbers in a musical—it’s an experience that you’re a part of. Over my 20 years as an entertainment editor and journalist, I’ve interviewed numerous Broadway stars, and they always say they feed off of, and are fueled by, audience reactions. You’re not just a passive viewer; your presence drives the show. It's something special to take part in.

If you've got a Broadway trip in your future, chances are you're going to need a hotel that will help you maximize your experience. The list below features properties with themed suites, theater lore, and locations just steps from the Great White Way. Read on for the best places to stay in NYC for a show-stopping Broadway getaway.

Closest theaters: 1-minute walk to Palace Theatre, 3-minute walk to James Earl Jones Theatre and Lunt-Fontanne TheatreWhy we love it: Right across from Palace Theatre, pre- and post-show prix-fixe menus, Studio 54 history

These days, Studio 54 is one of Broadway’s most popular stages (currently home to The Rocky Horror Show ), but back in 1977, Ian Schrager opened it as a nightclub, and it has since come to epitomize celebrity culture for a generation. Schrager brought that same visionary spirit when he opened the 452-room Times Square Edition in 2019, just across the street from the Palace Theatre. One of my favorite spots in Times Square is the hotel's Terrace and Outdoor Garden, a lush dining oasis that offers three-course Broadway Express prix-fixe menus both pre- and post-show. For those looking for an upgraded theater experience, the Edition's Showstopping Stay package—which can be booked up to 10 days in advance—includes two premium tickets to select shows, dinner with Champagne, theater-themed amenities, and house-made snacks.

Closest theaters: 9-minute walk to Studio 54, 10-minute walk to Vivian Beaumont Theater, 11-minute walk to Broadway TheatreWhy we love it: Central Park views, Broadway VIP Experience

Though a few blocks north of the Theater District thrills, the Mandarin Oriental is still less than a 15-minute walk to most theaters—yet it feels a world apart. It overlooks Central Park in one direction, and its 75-foot lap pool has views of the Hudson River. Guests are pampered with a true five-star experience every step of the way, whether it’s raising a glass at The Bar speakeasy or lounging around at celeb-favorite MO Lounge. You can also rub shoulders with the stars via the hotel's Broadway VIP Experience package, which includes an hour-long meet-and-greet with a Broadway cast member over bites and Champagne at the lounge. Also included are orchestra tickets (choose from 13 shows, including Hamilton and Harry Potter and the Cursed Child) and show merch, as well as add-ons like a theater transfer in a Mercedes, a 90-minute guided tour of the Museum of Broadway, or even acting lessons or a private concert with a stage star.

Closest theaters: 3-minute walk to Belasco Theatre, 4-minute walk to Hudson Theatre, 5-minute walk to Stephen Sondheim TheatreWhy we love it: Official partner of the Tony Awards, recently refreshed, early check-in option

If hotels could earn Tonys, the Sofitel New York would be a clear winner. As a longtime partner of Broadway’s iconic awards show, many a theater star has walked through its doors. That includes George Clooney during his Broadway debut in Good Night, and Good Luck, Jonathan Groff during his turn as Bobby Darin in Just in Time, and Mia Farrow while she was in The Roommate. Just last year, the property underwent a full makeover, reimagining its 398 rooms and suites (some with Empire State Building views), as well as its lobby, fitness center, and dining options (including Social 45 Bar & Bistro), drawing on the Art Deco glamour of Paris and New York. While an exclusive Broadway package is currently in the works, the Sofitel does currently offer The Ultimate Manhattan Luxury Staycation experience, which includes a welcome drink, dining credit, signature pastries, and early check-in at noon, perfect for squeezing in an extra Wednesday or weekend matinee.

Closest theaters: 2-minute walk to Eugene O’Neill Theatre, Walter Kerr, and Longacre TheatreWhy we love it: Quiet, designed by a Tony-winning scenic designer, curated theater mementos

Despite being footsteps away from several Broadway theaters, Civilian Hotel manages to create a cozy boutique experience, starting with an entrance just around the corner from Eighth Avenue. One step inside, and you feel like you’ve earned a backstage pass— hotelier Jason Pomeranc teamed up with scenic designer David Rockwell (Hairspray, Legally Blonde, Elf) on a classic theater theme featuring everything from marquee-inspired lighting to dramatic curtains. Even its 203 guest rooms channel vintage dressing room vibes. Rockwell's goal was to create a space for NYC’s creatives—performers, designers, directors, producers, and writers—that paid homage to classic Broadway. Stop by the Blue Vault tasting room and lounge to spot some theater relics, and the Olio Collection rooftop bar for more than 250 pieces of theater-inspired art.

Closest theaters: 1-minute walk to Palace Theatre, 3-minute walk to Marquis TheatreWhy we love it: Location across from TKTS booth, buzzy Sky Lobby

When it comes to Theater District locations, you can't find much better than the 661-room Tempo by Hilton New York Times Square. Making its debut in the dense area in August 2023, it snagged a prime spot right across from Duffy Square’s TKTS booth, the bright red discount ticket outlet that sells last-minute show tickets for up to 50% off (psst, check here for today’s offers). Even closer is the Palace Theatre, currently home to the musical The Lost Boys, which the property has partnered with on a themed suite, bookable through September 14, 2027. Inside the suite, you'll find an ’80s seaside feel mimicking the musical’s world of Santa Carla.

Closest theaters: 2-minute walk to Eugene O’Neill Theatre, Walter Kerr, and Ambassador Theatre; half a dozen more a 3-minute walk awayWhy we love it: Vacation vibes at its Bar Sprezzatura, daily complimentary wine in the Living Room Lobby during Evening Social Hour, Roundabout Theatre Company partnership

The first time I stepped off the elevator into Kimpton Theta New York’s Bar Sprezzatura, I immediately craved an Aperol spritz. That’s how much I was transported to the Italian Riviera. The contrast between the lively Midtown streets below (the bar sits on the 15th floor) and the laid-back rooftop bar made me fall in love with the 364-key property instantly, and with multiple two- and three-bedroom suites, it's perfect for families and groups looking to book a foodie-friendly Broadway bonding trip. This November, the hotel launched the Roundabout Theatre Co. x Kimpton Theta package, giving guests 20% off tickets to Roundabout Theatre Co. shows (currently The Rocky Horror Show and Imaginary Invalid) plus pre- or post-show drinks at the bar.

Closest theaters: Attached to Marquis Theatre, 1-minute walk to Minskoff Theatre, 2-minute walk to Richard Rodgers TheatreWhy we love it: Ideal for Marquis Theatre shows, home to NYC’s only rotating restaurant, Broadway Bound Dining Package

For a mega-sized hotel smack dab in the middle of Times Square, the Marriott Marquis still has a sense of character. When I first moved to the area 23 years ago, I used to frequent its eight-floor Broadway Lounge, looking out at Times Square and marveling that I had finally “made it." Nowadays, I still pop in for a dose of nostalgia, gazing up at the 36-floor atrium’s elevators leading to the hotel's 1,900 rooms—a constant in a world that’s changed so much since it opened in 1985. But that throwback feel comes with a new spring in its step, most notably at its 48th-floor spinning restaurant, The View, reimagined by Danny Meyer in 2024. (Note: TodayTix members get free bubbly and bar snacks here, depending on their tier.) But what makes the property so unique for theater fans is that it’s the only hotel ever built with a Broadway theater inside—yes, the Marquis Theatre is literally on the third floor. Also special: The Broadway Bound Dining Package includes the chance to mingle with a theater star!

Closest theaters: 2-minute walk to the Nederlander Theatre, New Amsterdam Theatre, and Lyric TheatreWhy we love it: Themed rooms, located on 42nd Street, close to other attractions

Now here’s a hotel that reflects both “A Whole New World” and “The Circle of Life.” Through its partnership with Disney’s two long-running musicals, Hilton New York Times Square guests can go all in with themed rooms curated by Broadway designer Devin Sparkles Design. Aladdin's Times Square Palace Suite is decked out just like Agrabah, down to a genie lamp, Moroccan magic carpets, and Jasmine-inspired silks. Over in The Lion King’s Royal Suite, it’s all about the wonders of the Serengeti Pridelands, with hand-painted Rafiki-like patterns and bird puppets flying from the ceiling. Both include wake-up calls from each musical’s most iconic characters—the Genie and Rafiki—as well as themed drinks. But perhaps the most valuable part of the package, especially for those driving in? Parking in Times Square.

Closest theaters: 1-minute walk to Hudson Theatre, Belasco Theatre, and Lyceum Theatre

Why we love it: Passageway running between Hudson Theatre’s entrance and stage door, June 2026 refresh

Ever since my first Broadway trip to NYC in 2002, I’ve been stage-dooring shows. The Hudson Theatre shows can be tricky for this, as the theater’s entrance is on 44th Street, but its stage door is on 45th. It wasn’t until I discovered that the Millennium Hotel had a secret passageway—which is also the entrance to the hotel—that I started snagging spots close enough to get autographs (including from Daniel Radcliffe during Merrily We Roll Along). That said, I've always been jealous of those actually staying at the 751-room property, with a trio of theaters literally at their doorstep. Those eager to dive even deeper into the Theater District's history will love that the property is just across the street from the Museum of Broadway.

Is it expensive to see a show on Broadway?

Yes, price tags can be high—the year-to-date average per ticket for 2026 is $122.67. But there are also plenty of ways to find discounts through lotteries, TodayTix, Theatr, and the TKTS Booth. I’ve only paid more than $100 five times in my life—and never more than $200. (That’s why I haven’t been to a movie in nearly a decade, but have seen nearly 40 shows in the last year!)

What show should I see on Broadway this winter?

For last-minute trips, hot tickets right now include Bowen Yang’s record-breaking run in Cole Escola’s Oh, Mary! (Lyceum Theatre), plus A Few Good Men (Vivian Beaumont Theatre), Much Ado About Nothing (Winter Garden), Other Desert Cities (Hudson Theatre), and School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play (Samuel J. Friedman). And of course there are long-running hits like Wicked (Gershwin Theatre), Hamilton (Richard Rodgers Theatre), Harry Potter and the Cursed Child (Lyric Theatre), The Great Gatsby (Broadway Theatre), and Disney’s The Lion King (Minskoff Theatre).

Are there any shows I should plan a 2027 trip around?

As we’re standing on the precipice of one of the most anticipated Broadway seasons, there’s no better time to plan a theater getaway. Coming soon are Dolly: A True Original Musical (opening December 7 at St. James Theatre), the Julia Roberts and Paul Rudd–led Small Mouth Sounds (February 10 at Ethel Barrymore Theatre), Jonathan Groff’s The Amish Project (February 10 at Broadhurst Theatre), Dirty Dancing (February 12 at Lena Thorne Theatre), Evita on Broadway (February 27 at Winter Garden Theatre), Lin-Manuel Miranda’s Warriors (March 9 at Lunt-Fontanne Theatre), Purple Rain (March 12 at Majestic Theatre), The Sound of Music (March 23 at Vivian Beaumont Theatre), Damn Yankees (March 24 at Marquis Theatre), and the one I’m most thrilled about, the West End transfer Paddington: The Musical (March 30 at Al Hirschfield Theatre)—I already have my ticket for the first preview!

#6259. I Gambled Our Business Class Flight Home On A 65-Minute Connection And Separate Tickets

In the interest of maximizing our time on the ground (it was a short trip after all) and avoiding an early morning and long drive to Zürich, I booked a separate ticket from Basel to Copenhagen on Norwegian with a rather tight 65-minute connection to catch our SAS flight to Chicago…

When I booked my tickets for this trip, there was no award space on SAS from Zurich to Copenhagen. I figured it would open (intra-Europe space reliably opens a day or two before travel) and it certainly did, but I wasn’t thrilled about getting up before dawn to drive to Zürich in order to make the flight.

The change fee on a SAS EuroBonus award ticket is about 75USD as well, which caused me to look for options out of Basel, which is 15 minutes away from my in-laws house instead of an hour. I knew easyJet operates service on this route, but I was pleased to see Norwegian Air is now operating and the fares were cheap…cheaper than the change fee on SAS.

It was 177EUR for all four tickets on Norwegian from BSL-CPH, which I found compelling, though it was not without risk. Connecting on separate tickets is always a risk and the connection here was only 1 hour, 5 minutes, which would include walking from the Schengen area to the non-Schengen area (where lines can be very long).

Nevertheless, we opted to take the risk, knowing that if the flight was delayed we would miss our connection and might be stuck in Copenhagen another day or forced to fly back to the U.S. in economy class.

There was another wrinkle. My kids and I are U.S. citizens, but my wife sill is not…she travels to the USA on a Green Card and I figured we would be unable to check her in because the Green Card would need to be verified. That turned out to be an issue…I could not compete her check-in, though I was able to for the kids and me.

Long story short: the gamble worked…but it was very close.

We took off early from Basel and the captain announced we would arrive 15 minutes early into Denmark.

But the weather was poor and we ended up circling and pulled up to the gate late…we know we had less than an hour to go to the transfer counter, collect my wife’s boarding pass, pass through passport control, and board our flight.

We landed at the furthest possible gate and had a long walk ahead of us.

My biggest concern was that even though I had initiated check-in on the SAS app, we might be too late to check-in for Heidi. Thankfully, although we did not reach the transfer desk until 40 minutes before departure, an agent was able to complete check-in and issue the boarding pass.

We saw immigration lines were very long for non-Schengen citizens, but short for us so we ducked into the SAS Lounge for Kanelbullar (Swedish cinnamon rolls) and then headed to the gate. I know, I really do push it.

We reached the gate 26 minutes before departure…the gamble worked. Barely.

I love reading your posts, but you are NUTS doing this!

Hahaha nice gamble! If you have a backup plan and or flexibility for one more day in Copenhagen it’s worth the risk I reckon.

If you’d stayed in Copenhagen it would have been a treat for the kids and you wouldn’t have regretted it either so all good.

I’m surprised by how inadequate the immigration processing staff and gates are at CPH, even for EU citizens.

I’m confused by the line “We saw immigration lines were very long for non-Schengen citizens, but short for us …” You had indicated that you and the kids are US citizens which presumably meant you needed to use the non-Schengen lines. Were you allowed to use the Schengen lines?

They are dual citizens (but my wife is no a dual citizen).

Have the kids been to Tivoli Gardens yet? I bet they loved/would love it! Plus, there is Wagamama for a “fun” meal.

If thing hadn’t worked out you would have had to fly – Le Gasp – coach!?! Kidding mostly. Glad you pulled it off but I wouldn’t have stopped in the lounge.

#6258. Virgin Atlantic Ups The Ante In India, As The World Dials In

This week, Virgin Atlantic celebrates 25 years of flying to India. In Virgin fashion, it’s doing so in style, with a joint announcement among partners Delta Airlines, Air France-KLM, and a new strategic partner IndiGo.

On the sidelines of the IATA Annual General Meeting, basically the UN General Assembly of airlines, the new strategic partnership for India was announced with very interesting nods to the future.

IndiGo carries more passengers in India than anyone else and will connect US and UK/European customers flying Virgin, Delta and Air France KLM onward in India, while also helping fill seats for these European and North American partners, as their own customers head West.

That’s probably a good thing, because with recent service additions, Virgin now flies a million seats a year to India and it sounds like others are piling on more flights too. It’s now one of the largest operators to India.

I’ve been bullish on India as the next great center of the world for a while now. It’s not necessarily that I’m at all intelligent, it’s just based on the fact that India is the world’s largest population. But, when Ed Bastian, Delta’s formidable CEO says it, people tend to listen. Bastian mentioned India being the most important aviation market globally now and signaled a return of direct services for the carrier as well.

Virgin has been a small step ahead, adding service regularly on their Delhi, Mumbai and Bangalore routes. IndiGo chose this alliance over formidable competition and this will certainly be a space to watch as more global airlines and alliances focus on India.

Geo-political activity points to India becoming a new manufacturing super power, in addition to its prolific work in tech, IT and customer service, not to mention blossoming tourism. These kind of globally connected businesses are big business, huge in fact, for corporate contracts and easy onward connectivity to regional sites is essential. The partnership makes sense.

In a somewhat rare and impressive signal of unity and seriousness towards India, Virgin Atlantic made their India crews part of the core Virgin family, rather than as contractors through a third party local company, known in aviation world as a GSA. This means Virgin’s India crews are a part of the full team, with benefits too.

When asked about loyalty implications of the new alliance, Virgin Atlantic CEO, Shai Weiss, noted a mutual passion for using loyalty to enhance guest experience far beyond just the earn and burn of points and miles. For future iterations, they’ve offered the following…

The MoU (memorandum of understanding) also creates a framework for deeper collaboration between the carriers on a bilateral and multilateral basis; contemplates commercial collaboration including network, loyalty, cargo and sales, subject to regulatory approvals; explores areas of non-commercial cooperation including aircraft maintenance, sustainability, training, ground handling; and acknowledges the need to develop advanced collaboration through use of technology to efficiently service joint customers.

IndiGo will provide onward connectivity for Virgin and the other strategic partners to 32 destinations, making it easier than ever to see Udaipur, Jaipur, Mumbai, Kashmir and delights further south in Bangalore and Goa.

I just returned from the lovely Leela Palace in Delhi, as I watched the news happen live.

To me, India is a country of joy. Even people with truly nothing seem to find positivity and it’s generally a way of life here. Hospitality is as warm and steeped in tradition as it comes, too. It’s hot, it’s humid, but it’s an experience unlike any other and that’s something that’s harder to say these days than I’d like.

The food, ugh. I adore. Sure, I’ll take a dosa from the South over a heavy curry from the North most days, but I love both and if you don’t love a good black daahl there’s something wrong with you.

In short, it’s already fairly easy to get to India but it’s about to get a whole lot easier and not just to hub cities too. More seats means more chances to use points, by the way!
