#6257. 15 Best Grand Canyon Hotels, Rentals, and Glampsites for Sleeping in Style Under the Stars

A mile deep and 277 miles long, the Grand Canyon is a jaw-droppingly majestic chasm in Arizona’s rust-red desert that’s speckled with pinyon pines. Standing on its edge, one can’t help but feel small, watching the mighty Colorado River churn vigorously along the ravine’s bottom. Whether you’re hoping for a challenging all-day hike to the canyon’s floor, a soul-stirring overlook near the visitor center, or a multi-day rafting expedition, this national park has all that (and more) in spades. It’s hardly a surprise that it drew more than 4.4 million visitors in 2025 alone, so you know you'll have some competition when it comes to finding the best place to stay nearby.

Personally, I like to stay as close as possible to the park, to make the most of dreamy desert sunrises and maximize my time on the trails. Grand Canyon is famous for its historic lodges and quirky Route 66 nostalgia, which can make picking the perfect spot for your crew a little overwhelming. Cozy cabin or fancy, family-sized rental? Canvas glamping tent under the stars or a fun getaway that’s in the heart of the action? I’ve sorted through the hundreds of options so you don’t have to. Here are my favorite Grand Canyon hotels, glamping sites, vacation rentals, and cabins for a memorable stay in and around this utterly striking national park.

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Full kitchen, colorful decor, telescope

Location: Valle, ArizonaThings to do nearby: Kaibab National Forest, Grand Canyon Village, Rim Trail

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Telescope, soaking tub, firepit, secluded location

This fantastic two-bedroom wilderness retreat is situated on two private acres filled with fragrant juniper trees in the arid Arizona desert. Though it’s full of modern creature comforts (like high-speed Wi-Fi, a smart TV, two plush queen beds, and stainless steel kitchen appliances), this guesthouse is also fit for nature lovers, with amenities like an outdoor firepit, comfy front porch, and even a telescope for late-night stargazing. The home also boasts a coveted location that’s right between the city of Williams and the South Rim entrance gates near Tusayan.

Location: Williams, ArizonaThings to do nearby: Grand Canyon Railroad, Pete's Route 66 Gas Station Museum

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: Studio, 1 bathWhy we love it: Open kitchen, fenced backyard, washer and dryer

Prepare to enjoy lofted ceilings and an airy, open floor plan at this home in Flagstaff. When the weather’s nice, light up the gas-powered grill, sit by the firepit, and enjoy alfresco dining in the property’s fully fenced backyard. Inside, guests can unwind with a 65-inch flat-screen TV, a king and queen bed (on the main floor and in the loft, respectively), a full kitchen, and split air-conditioning that keeps the space comfortable no matter the season. Best of all, the house is located smack dab in the heart of the city, near funky bars and fabulous restaurants.

Location: Flagstaff, ArizonaThings to do nearby: Foxglenn Park, Elden Pueblo Heritage Site, Picture Canyon Natural and Cultural Preserve

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathTop amenities: Outdoor patio, desert vistas, eat-in kitchen

Bright whites, natural light, and pops of blue bring fun character to this modern desert casita, situated right off Route 66 in Williams. At 529 square feet, this cute, pet-friendly cabin epitomizes indoor-outdoor living, with 12 private acres of serene desert surrounding it, plus a gorgeous patio for post-park cocktails with friends. Enjoy fast Wi-Fi, smart TVs, and a Keurig coffee maker, all while sleeping just 20 minutes from the park’s South Rim.

Location: Williams, ArizonaThings to do nearby: Kaibab National Forest, Grand Canyon Village

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Skylight, solar power, desert views

Calling all adventurous couples: this light-soaked tiny home is a dreamy, romantic escape. A mere 30-minute drive from the Grand Canyon, this off-grid spot is the perfect place to sip a glass of wine and stare at the stars after a day of hiking through craggy red rocks. Take in the sunrise from the enclosed outdoor shower, or sip coffee in the airy kitchen. After dark, snuggle up by the firepit and test your astronomy knowledge while you point out constellations from the outdoor seating area. With so much open space, you’ll feel like you’re a million miles from anywhere.

Location: Valle, ArizonaThings to do nearby: Mather Point, Yavapai Geology Museum

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Off-grid solar power, log cabin vibes, spacious kitchen

Boasting three bedrooms with plush bedding (the rooms have a king, a queen, and two trundles, respectively) and two bathrooms, this off-grid, solar-powered cabin is the perfect home base for your entire crew after a day exploring the Grand Canyon’s South Rim. Situated 30 minutes from the park’s entrance station, this home offers sweeping views of the San Francisco Peaks, a full kitchen with gas appliances, and an indoor fireplace—all set on an ultra-secluded piece of land in the desert.

Location: Valle, ArizonaThings to do nearby: Grand Canyon Village, Yaki Point, South Rim Visitor Center

Number of guests: VariesBed and bath: VariesWhy we love it: Roomy canvas tents, private decks, organic bath products

Over the last few years, Under Canvas has earned itself a sparkling reputation as a top purveyor of luxurious glamping experiences. From organic bath products and morning yoga to nightly s’mores around the fire, it has comfortable camping dialed in—so much so that even the choosiest hotel snob will feel right at home. Pro tip: Splurge on a stargazer tent for dreamy Milky Way views without ever leaving your bed.

Location: Valle, ArizonaThings to do nearby: Grand Canyon IMAX, Mather Point

Number of guests: VariesBed and bath: VariesWhy we love it: On-site dining, desert-themed decor, Navajo canyon guides

Perched at the edge of the Vermillion Cliffs about five miles from Lees Ferry (the launch point for multi-day rafting trips on the Colorado River), Marble Canyon Lodge is a new base camp for travelers looking to explore this less-touristed side of the Grand Canyon. Here, adventure seekers have their pick of colorful, refreshed motel digs, from two-bedroom cottages to no-frills king bedrooms with tea kettles and gear storage areas. Start your morning on the porch with a cup of Lucky Foot coffee as the canyon walls turn amber with the first light, then fuel up at the Lonely Jackrabbit Restaurant, the only real eatery for many miles, which serves up Southwestern fare, like cactus burritos and epic burgers, seven days a week.

Location: Marble Canyon, ArizonaThings to do nearby: Colorado River rafting, Antelope Canyon, Horseshoe Bend

Number of guests: VariesBed and bath: VariesWhy we love it: Ultra-private, on-site wellness program, private plunge pools

This dreamy Aman property is one of a kind. Set in remote Canyon Point, Utah, Amangiri is a rare breed of luxury hotel because it truly blends in with the natural landscape that surrounds it. From canvas-lined pavilions with private plunge pools to a four-bedroom mesa home, guests here get to mingle with high sandstone bluffs and rose-hued cliffs, no matter which room they pick. Plus, with an on-site via ferrata and in-house guides at the ready to help book national park outings, experiencing the best of canyon country is a cinch. (Of note, this is the farthest hotel from the Grand Canyon on my list, at two and a half hours away.)

Location: Canyon Point, UtahThings to do nearby: Lake Powell, Skylight Arch, North Rim trails

Number of guests: VariesBed and bath: VariesWhy we love it: Excellent spa, daily activities, fine dining

Why not pair a luxe spa vacation with your Grand Canyon adventure? L’Auberge de Sedona offers elegant creekside cottages and lodge rooms with verdant garden views, ideal for the discerning traveler who likes their hikes with a side of Swedish massage. Open year-round in the high-desert mecca of Sedona, two hours from the park, the lodge boasts a bevy of daily activities (think Qigong meditation and chakra-balancing yoga) as well as a mindful fine-dining menu at Cress on Oak Creek, the on-site restaurant.

Location: SedonaThings to do nearby: Cathedral Rock, Devil’s Bridge Trail, Slide Rock State Park

Number of guests: VariesBed and bath: VariesWhy we love it: Magical views, private decks, world-class wellness at Mii Amo

Soak up the magic of red rock country by immersing yourself in the hip, Southwestern flair of Sedona. Enchantment Resort is set in the heart of the Vermillion Bluffs of Boynton Canyon, with adorable casitas and roomy suites for groups of up to 10. This pet-friendly hotel oozes with thoughtful architectural details, like log ceiling beams, gas fireplaces, and sienna-tinted adobe clay, with elevated American cuisine at its restaurant, Che Ah Chi.

Location: SedonaThings to do nearby: Boynton Canyon hikes and mountain biking, Seven Sacred Pools

When is the best time to visit Grand Canyon National Park?

With an elevation spanning 2,000 feet to 8,000 feet, Grand Canyon experiences a wide range of temperatures on any given day. Thus, the best season to visit greatly depends on what your adventure priorities are.

If you’re planning to raft “the big ditch” with a guide, go between April and October for warm, sunny days that perfectly contrast the 50-degree Colorado River. Hoping to hike to the bottom and camp at Bright Angel? Don your favorite traction devices atop the canyon to crunch through seasonal ice and book a backcountry permit for late fall, winter, or early spring. Auto tourists who want to explore the canyon’s south rim by car can travel in virtually any season—just be prepared for crowds in summer months and occasional snow closures at the height of winter.

Lastly, a good rule of thumb for intrepid travelers hiking down into the canyon is that you’ll gain roughly 5 degrees for every 1,000 feet you descend. Plan on it being 20 degrees warmer at the bottom of the canyon than it is at the rim. The National Park Service (NPS) does not recommend hiking to the bottom of the canyon during summer months, as temperatures at Phantom Ranch often surpass 100 degrees.

How do you get to Grand Canyon National Park?

If you’re planning to fly in, the closest major airports are Sky Harbor International in Phoenix and Harry Reid International in Las Vegas, but both are at least a three-hour drive away, so you’ll want to rent a car and crank up the tunes to brave the journey. Regional airports are scattered around the area, most notably in small-but-commercial Flagstaff, Sedona, and Tusayan. There’s also a vintage train service that runs daily from Williams, Arizona.

Notably, Grand Canyon National Park is a stone’s throw away from one of the most iconic road trips the US has to offer–historic Route 66. Running from Chicago all the way to the Pacific Coast in Santa Monica, California, this legendary trip ventures across northern Arizona on Interstate 40.

What are the best things to do in Grand Canyon National Park?

Spanning 23 breathtaking miles between Grand Canyon Village and the Desert View area, Desert View Drive is the only scenic byway in the park that’s open year-round to private vehicles. Enjoy Mary Colter’s iconic Desert View Watchtower, which was inspired by ancestral Puebloan architecture and features murals by Hopi artist Fred Kabotie, at the park’s far eastern edge.

Another popular drive along the South Rim is the winding Hermit Road, which ends at the historic stone structure of Hermit’s Rest that date back to 1914. The drive is only open to private vehicles in December, January, and February; in all other months, travelers must use the park’s free shuttle system, hopping on and off at popular sites.

Though the hiking distance between the canyon’s north and south rims is a scant 21 miles, the drive to get between the two is a circuitous 220 miles. As a result, only 10% of the national park’s visitors set foot on the just-as-striking North Rim. This high-elevation outpost (over 8,000 feet) and log cabin-style lodge have a shorter visitation season than the South Rim (you’ll have to travel there between May 15 and October 15 most years), but adventurous drivers desperate to escape the crowds should make a beeline for the pinyon and ponderosa pine–studded views of crumbling crimson sandstone along Cape Royal Road. Plus, you’ll be within easy driving distance of Zion, if you’d like to extend your journey.

If you’re into hiking past dramatic vermillion outcroppings, secret waterfalls, and hanging gardens, you’re in the right place. The Grand Canyon also boasts some of the most stunning wheelchair-accessible paths in the country (check out the 13-mile, mostly-paved Rim Trail), as well as hamstring-busting overnight treks into the belly of the ravine.

For an epic out-and-back excursion with much of the expansive red rock scenery you’d find on a longer jaunt, head to South Kaibab Trailhead and venture just under a mile downhill to the aptly named Ooh Aah Point. Want a little more bang for your buck? Continue down to Skeleton Point for a sweeping panorama of the Colorado River (six miles round trip). Bright Angel Trailhead is another iconic starting point for a day hike or overnight trek into the canyon. Lace up your boots for a three-mile round-trip stroll to the shade structure at Mile-and-a-Half Resthouse or, if you’re an experienced hiker looking to sweat, start early for an all-day 12-mile journey to jaw-dropping views of Plateau Point.

Trekking to the bottom of the Grand Canyon and back is the stuff hiking bucket lists are made of. But due to midday heat and the extremely strenuous nature of these hikes, the National Park Service does not recommend aiming to complete such a journey in a single day. It’s highly recommended to nab a backcountry permit and camp overnight at one of the many below-the-rim sites (like Bright Angel Campground or Havasupai Gardens). Pro tip: Use the free park shuttle and create a loop starting at South Kaibab and ending at the Bright Angel Trailhead. Heading for the quieter North Rim? Tramp down the North Kaibab Trail for two miles (one-way) to Supai Tunnel.

Find our full list of the best Grand Canyon hikes here.

It’s rare that a national park offers a designated bike path along its most iconic sights, but at the Grand Canyon, visitors can spin for roughly 13 miles along the park’s dreamy South Rim vistas. BYO-bike or rent one at Canyon Adventures in the village, then steer onto the paved Greenway Trail to South Kaibab. Or, utilize the free shuttle system (yes, they’ve got bike racks) and ride the bus to Monument Creek Vista, then cruise along the South Rim to Hermits Rest.

North Rim visitors hoping to escape that South Rim fervor can enjoy loads of rugged mountain biking. A 12-mile swath of the enormous, 800-mile Arizona Trail runs right through the park.

Are there guided tours at Grand Canyon National Park?

There are dozens of phenomenal guided tours available for guests who aren’t comfortable backpacking alone or want a unique type of experience. Mule rides are a storied part of the canyon’s past and how many early tourists ventured into the canyon (sometimes in full Victorian regalia). Though it might seem like a rough place for a working animal, mules are much better equipped to handle heat and steep, rocky terrain than their horse counterparts. Plus, these rides offer below-the-rim access for visitors with mobility concerns. Today, both short day trips and extended overnight ventures to Phantom Ranch on muleback are available for those looking to pay homage to a bygone era.

For a brag-worthy addition to your hiking checklist, seek out Wildland Trekking’s guided rim-to-rim backpacking journeys (or, in winter, go big and test your skills on a rim-to-rim-to-rim hike). Craving something off the beaten path? The remote, five-day Hermit Loop offers miles of fire-red sandstone plateaus.

I’d be remiss if I didn’t mention the second-to-none river rafting to be had at Grand Canyon National Park. Grand Canyon Expeditions and Western River Expeditions have been guiding for decades and both offer first-class service for intrepid travelers looking to go the distance on the mighty Colorado.

#6255. This Is The Summer To Tick Santorini Off The Bucket List

It’s June, and for perhaps the first time in modern history, Santorini isn’t crowded. Those earthquakes a good few months ago? Not even a flower pot was tipped over, yet incessant clickbait headlines managed to have a lasting impact.

And that’s a shame, because there’s been a lovely tourism revolution brewing there, where local hoteliers are bringing back the kind of experience and hospitality that you want to come back for over and over again.

As someone who goes at least once or twice a year, and will again very shortly, I can only advocate to tick it off the bucket list this summer, because you’ll never find prices, availability or an experience quite like it again for a while.

In the last 20 years, Santorini got totally overrun. Cruise tourism and day trip mania somewhat ruined a once idyllic, low-key fishing island and then Instagram and TikTok lit the match.

But now the TikTok crowd is in Mykonos and Santorini, as unequalled in beauty as ever, is lovely again. Hotels like The Vasilicos and Santorini Sky bring wildly different, delightfully luxurious and hospitality driven experiences to the island.

Beach clubs, yes Santorini’s beaches are underrated, have made a nice little mark on quieter coasts with great effect too. Assyrtiko, the local grape has hit the world stage as a darling of sommeliers in top restaurants and vineyards like Vassaltis offer stunning tasting experiences.

And the food? There’s no Nobu, or Scorpios here, so there are plenty of places to feel the benefit of European pricing, including a personal favorite at Kantouni.

The trouble with Santorini has historically been that many of the best hotels are small, they fill up quickly, and as they do, they charge a fortune. For the best, like the ones mentioned above, it’s still worth it. But this season, all across the board, prices are lower and even if you don’t care about price, many of the best which might typically be sold out for the season have rooms.

As an additional tailwind for travelers, flights between the US and Europe are quieter this summer, which means there’s deals to be had with both points and cash from major markets to Santorini. If you don’t see cheap flights to Santorini, try a major hub and booking an onward ticket separately.

Naturally, precaution is a good thing in life. But fear mongering for the sake of clicks is another beast and I can’t help but be fairly appalled by the many weeks and months of coverage and follow up coverage, reiterating a narrative of fear… despite no damage to anything, anywhere.

If you do bag a great deal this summer and visit one of my very favorite places, and use this great Santorini guide to make the most of your time, you can thank the media.

#6254. Aer Lingus Pilots Wanted A Safer Place To Land After Bomb Threat, Now Face Criminal Investigation

Aer Lingus pilots responding to a bomb threat were directed to land at a French military airfield. According to their unions, they lacked the charts and operational information needed to land safely and requested another airport. They ultimately landed at the base, but then faced questioning and now a criminal investigation over their initial response. I find that troubling, particularly if their supposed failure to cooperate was an attempt to protect the people onboard.

As One Mile At A Time highlights, the handling of a recent Aer Lingus diversion has prompted a pointed warning from European pilot unions.

The incident occurred on November 5, 2026, aboard Aer Lingus flight EI402 from Dublin (DUB) to Rome (FCO). Following a bomb threat, the Airbus A320 diverted to Évreux-Fauville Air Base in Normandy under a French fighter escort. No explosives were found, and the aircraft eventually returned to Dublin.

But the dispute over how it reached that airfield deserves a closer look.

In a November 10 joint statement, the European Cockpit Association, Irish Air Line Pilots’ Association, and French pilot union SNPL said the crew did not have the necessary aeronautical charts and operational information for the military airfield. According to the unions, the pilots requested a more suitable alternative, but that request was refused.

The organizations also expressed concern that the pilots subsequently faced possible criminal prosecution over decisions they say were intended to protect those onboard. ECA Vice-President Captain Paul Reuter put it succinctly:

“The pilots must not find themselves treated as a threat by the very authorities whose assistance they require.”

That strikes me as a very reasonable starting point.

French authorities described the initial exchange differently. The prime minister’s office said fighter aircraft were dispatched because the pilot had not cooperated as expected.

Évreux public prosecutor Rémi Coutin told The Irish Times that investigators were examining whether the pilot initially refused the landing instruction and whether that conduct could constitute a criminal offense. Both pilots were questioned and permitted to leave France. The prosecutor said on November 6 that the investigation remained ongoing.

Aer Lingus has defended its crew, saying they “acted impeccably and were thoroughly professional.”

So we have competing descriptions of the same exchange. An investigation has been opened, but no criminal charges have been filed. I would be interested in what the cockpit recordings and communications with authorities actually reveal.

It is understandable why authorities might want an aircraft carrying a suspected explosive brought to a military installation rather than a busy passenger airport. There may have been very good reasons to choose Évreux.

But those reasons need to account for whether the crew can safely get the aircraft onto the ground there.

The objection described by the unions concerns missing operational information. That is a substantial concern, even if the runway itself can easily accommodate an A320. Pilots still need to understand the approach and assess the conditions for their particular aircraft (I realized this myself when trying to land at Madeira Airport in the United Airlines 737 flight simulator).

A fighter escort cannot make those calculations for them.

I would not expect a captain to continue toward Rome simply because diverting was inconvenient. But requesting an alternative airport because you lack information needed for a safe landing sounds like precisely the sort of judgment I want the person flying my aircraft to exercise!

If the authorities had a compelling reason why no alternative was acceptable, that should have been explained to the pilots and more precise guidance given for landing at the diversion airport. I have trouble seeing how the prospect of prosecution helps anyone land more safely.

I recently wrote about European pilots reporting fatigue and fearing the consequences of speaking up. This is a different situation, but it raises a similar concern: what happens when exercising professional judgment appears personally riskier than going along?

Of course pilots are accountable for their decisions. Their position does not place them above the law, and authorities should examine a disputed response during a security emergency. But there needs to be room for a captain to say that an instruction creates a safety problem. Otherwise, we tell pilots they bear responsibility for everyone onboard while discouraging them from exercising the judgment that responsibility requires.

I also would not dismiss the original threat simply because the search found nothing. I made the same point after the recent Austrian Airlines diversion under a MiG-29 escort. Crews and authorities must respond to the information available at the time and hindsight does not make a precaution foolish.

But taking a bomb threat seriously should include taking the pilots’ landing concerns seriously too.

I cannot resolve this dispute without knowing what was actually communicated between the aircraft and French authorities. Reviewing those communications is appropriate and I hope they are released soon.

Nevertheless, if the union account is accurate, I am firmly sympathetic to the pilots. Asking for an airport where they could conduct a properly informed landing was a responsible response to an already difficult situation.

The bomb threat required a security response. The concern now is whether that response gave enough weight to the safety judgment of the people actually flying the airplane. Those pilots deserve a substantive answer…not prosecution.

#6252. Aeromexico Adds New U.S. Routes, Flights

Aeromexico is again expanding its footprint in the U.S. with assistance from longtime partner Delta.

The carrier announced Monday that it will connect Mexico City with Nashville, Tennessee, New Orleans, and San Juan, Puerto Rico. None of the three cities currently has nonstop service to the Mexican capital.

All three connections will operate four times weekly. Service to Nashville will launch first, on June 13, 2027, followed by New Orleans on June 17 and San Juan on June 24.

Flights to Nashville and New Orleans will use Embraer E190 aircraft with 99 seats. For the route to San Juan, the airline will operate Boeing 737 MAX 8s with 166 seats.

Aeromexico will also launch a second daily service between Mexico City and Austin, Texas, on June 3.

“The addition of Nashville, New Orleans, and San Juan to our network will allow us to provide more connectivity options, bringing our customers closer to destinations known for their unique identity and remarkable attractions,” Giancarlo Mulinelli, senior vice president of global sales at Aeromexico, said in a news release. “Together with Delta, we continue to open markets and create more opportunities that strengthen tourism and ties between Mexico and the United States.”

Last month, the partners announced new routes from Mexico City to Orange County, California, Fort Lauderdale, Florida, and Portland, Oregon.

#6251. Wander.com: Best Luxury Take On Airbnb (With Real Value Too?)

At first, the big hotel chains of the world laughed off Airbnb and vacation rentals. No seriously, they did. Now, they all compete in the vacation rental business and act like it was always the plan.

The problem for the traveler, is that almost all of the newer entrants just plug into a massive pipeline of already existing vacation homes and apartments and pop them on their own branded website with no added luxury, differentiation, amenity or expertise in curation.

There’s no huge unlock of new places or highly curated places that you could virtually always stamp as worth recommending to a friend, the way you’d rate an Aman, St. Regis, or Four Seasons hotel.

This is precisely where Wander.com comes in, and it’s by far my favorite luxe vacation rental platform to date. The fact that it’s boutique and limited is what makes it, at least for me. And, the $350 off Wander promo code doesn’t hurt either.

Wander is a vacation rental company which truly hand picks every property that it lists, and has the exclusive listing on. Crucially, each of the vacation properties undergoes a sort of ‘Wander’ transformation to conform with brand standards for wifi, amenity, style and vibe.

It’s above my pay-grade as a blogger on this topic, but it seems like Wander co-invests in the real estate portfolio’s, or partners with owners in a unique way that’s far more integrated than others.

Where are they? Most Wander.com properties are scattered across the US, from the shores of Malibu to the great National Parks in Wyoming and all along the Eastern seaboard too. Hawaii is also a recent addition. New destinations keep popping up!

Each of their properties feels uniquely wonderful and aspirational, and I’d say all have a very modern and contemporary slant to luxury. Grandma’s cabinets are not in any of these homes, but Tesla chargers are. One nice touch: each Wander offers a dedicated workspace with desk, chair, monitors and lightning fast wifi.

I completely respect that all tastes are individual, but the interiors and setups of these homes much more reflect my personal tastes, more minimalist chic, than many less curated vacation rental options.

Most Wander properties are around $1000 a night. Some will be half that, some will be double. On its face, that’s intimidating to many, but when you factor in the number of bedrooms and features it’s really reasonable. Families, or multi-family get togethers… amazing.

All Wander.com properties are at least two bedrooms and many are four, five or even twelve. One is an entire island with multiple residential complexes. For me, I love these sort of getaways for catching up with family or friends, and I never mind when other people are contributing too.

We’ve had some of our best ever vacations renting a house in Palm Springs for weeks or months at a time. Often, family or friends want in too, so we split the house and end up with two bedrooms each for under $500 per night.

We’ve used these bonus rooms and features to socialize or catch up with people in the serenity of the home, not annoyed by service, crowded pools or tight room setups. For a longer stay, I absolutely hate having to rely on a hotel kitchen for every meal. I love to hit a local market and grill with family or guests.

Wander is offering $350 off first bookings, which is a great way to get started. To browse the homes, you simply download the Wander app and start doom scrolling. When you find one you’re ready to book, the process is very self explanatory and easy to share with others.

I’m personally a fan of virtually California vacation and the properties offered on the platform cover everything from Palm Springs to Napa and all in between in stunning form. The $350 off is a solid discount and combined with new property discounts, which are frequent, there is a lot to love. You can browse Wander and download the app here.

#6250. United Airlines Bans AI Booking Agents, But Who Is It Really Protecting?

In a November 11 announcement, United said it is restricting unauthorized third-party personal AI agents across its digital platforms and through travel agencies and aggregators.

The airline warns that sharing credentials with these tools could expose sensitive information or lead to unwanted purchases and account changes. It also raises regulatory concerns, pointing to the acknowledgment passengers must make concerning hazardous materials during check-in.

Those concerns deserve consideration. But they do not adequately explain why an assistant should be prohibited from making a change that I understand, authorize, and could make myself.

United has added the following to its prohibited ticketing practices:

“The use of AI Agents to make, modify or service a Ticket, and/or to purchase any service or product.”

The definition encompasses autonomous and semi-autonomous assistants, including those whose actions a passenger supervises or approves.

We already have tools that monitor airfare and notify us when prices change. I use fare alerts myself. But receiving an alert still leaves me with work to do. I must examine the offer, check the restrictions, and determine whether changing the ticket actually leaves me better off.

Imagine an assistant doing that work continuously, then completing an authorized change whenever the savings justify it based on the parameters I input at the start of the process…something I would happily use.

Consider a hypothetical $800 ticket whose rules allow you to rebook at a lower fare and retain the difference as a future flight credit, with no change fee.

The price drops to $650. Your AI assistant identifies the same flight and fare conditions, completes the permitted change, and secures a $150 credit.

Later, the price drops to $575. It does the calculation again and captures another $75.

You still take the flight you intended to take, but now have $225 available toward future travel.

That is not a cash refund on a nonrefundable ticket, and the actual opportunity depends on the fare rules. But evaluating those complications is precisely what would make the technology useful. Tell it what you want to preserve and when it may act. Let it calculate whether the lower price represents actual savings.

Airline revenue management benefits from passengers behaving differently. Some book early, some wait, and some keep checking after buying. Many understandably consider the transaction finished once the confirmation email arrives.

An assistant that keeps shopping changes that calculation.

A brief fare reduction that I would otherwise miss becomes an opportunity and a small saving that would not justify 20 minutes of my time may become worthwhile when software handles the work. Multiply that across millions of reservations and you can understand why an airline might become uncomfortable.

It would put serious pressure on the ability to retain a higher fare from someone whose ticket permits a lower-price exchange. The airline could still set its prices and restrictions, but fewer customers would leave available savings unclaimed merely because they were busy living their lives.

I suspect United understands this very well. This strikes me as a preemptive move to control who can manage a reservation before automated consumer tools become an ordinary part of travel.

These new rules do not suggest that United intends to eliminate every fare alert: the more consequential restriction is preventing the assistant from acting on what it finds.

I would not hand any application unrestricted control of my MileagePlus account and yes, I do not want software canceling an important trip because it misunderstood an instruction. But those are reasons to establish permissions and accountability.

United’s hazardous-materials example is particularly weak as a justification for prohibiting reservation management. The federal passenger-notification rule requires disclosures and passenger acknowledgment in specified circumstances. Reading that requirement, I do not see why an assistant could not stop and ask the traveler to complete the necessary acknowledgment personally.

More to the point, checking whether my ticket can be exchanged for a lower fare does not require an assistant to make a declaration about what is inside my suitcase. A responsible system should require approval where needed and limit what software can do. United’s restriction still encompasses an assistant whose actions I supervise and approve.

So no, I do not accept the customer-protection explanation.

Scott Kirby offered a more revealing observation at a Chicago event, according to The Wall Street Journal:

“To be honest, I don’t want to create another middleman.”

I understand why United would prefer to control the customer relationship, but my interests are not identical to United’s. I may want someone working for me, comparing the options and continuing to look after my reservation once United has collected payment.

I recently examined Kirby’s argument that technology helps make United the best airline in the world. I agree that its app is excellent. Better technology has made my United travel easier. But I also want technology that helps me spend less. An assistant that understands my preferences and captures an eligible fare reduction would be doing exactly that.

United should explain what secure, authorized access would require. Simply blocking an AI assistant carte blanche protects the airline’s control much more clearly than it protects my interests.

United says its restrictions on third-party AI agents protect customers. I think they also–and primarily–protect United from a future in which passengers can monitor and manage reservations far more effectively than they do today.

Just as airlines use complex algorithms to extract the highest fare fro Mme, I want to use technology to help capture savings without having to babysit every reservation.

To me, this looks like a cheap shot dressed up as customer protection. United is entitled to secure its systems, but I am far less sympathetic to using that explanation to block an authorized assistant from helping me obtain a better deal.

Especially given the rise in fares and the destruction of loyalty.

“Someone” can be held accountable when something goes wrong. Technology that tracks and alerts you of fare changes has existed for a while. AI agents are a whole other can of worms.

Forgive me for anthropomorphizing the technology, but my point is that I want to use technology to my advantage just as UA uses technology to its advantage.

My point is that you use AI agents at your own peril. You may see it as using a tool to fight a big and mighty corporation, but you are doing so by throwing in your lot with an even bigger and more mercurial corporation that is not your friend and certainly won’t take responsibility for the actions of their unaccountable by design agents.

Personally I wouldn’t use an agent for this as I enjoy the thrill of the chase but the general public it gives, as you note, a massive leg up in the value wars. The cat is out of the bag and they won’t be able to regulate it effectively even with their own technology–and they shouldn’t to begin with. They’re trying to keep the public in the 1990s while they race ahead for a profit advantage.

I think you’re reducing the argument to “airline wants to prevent customers from saving $50 on fare drops,” and ignoring the much broader implications of unauthorized redistribution, cost of sale, corporate fare integrity, transactional accountability, etc. etc. etc. Something tells me United cares more about that stuff than they do you letting your lil AI agent monitor pricing.

Alaska Airlines is rolling out a new invite-only status level called Atmos Global Concierge. Like the other major U.S. airlines that have such a tier, Alaska is not publicly disclosing what it takes to earn an invitation — though you can be sure it will require a lot of spending.

News of Alaska's new invite-only tier began spreading across aviation blogs Tuesday, and the company confirmed the move to TPG.

"Atmos Global Concierge is a new, invitation-only program," said Alaska in a statement, " ...  that, in addition to all the award-winning benefits of Atmos Rewards membership, provides personalized travel support when you need it the most."

For now, this is a beta program rollout, so it's likely to change over time.

In addition to published top tiers, like American Airlines' AAdvantage Executive Platinum, Delta's Diamond Medallion and United Airlines' Premier 1K, all three major U.S. carriers offer an even higher level of status generally saved for the elites who spend the most with the airline (and some travel providers and C-level executives and celebrities).

American Airlines has ConciergeKey, Delta Air Lines has 360, and United Airlines has Global Services. And now Alaska has Atmos Global Concierge.

None of these airlines publicly disclose the exact qualification requirements for their invitation-only programs, which makes pontificating about what it takes to qualify something of an unofficial pastime for loyalty die-hards.

Among the theories: Invites are tied not only to flight spending, but also to credit card spending and even to your home airport. For example, an American Airlines frequent flyer based at the carrier's Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) hub might have a harder time securing an invitation than a similarly high-spending traveler based in a more competitive market.

Alaska isn't revealing the full list of benefits that come with its new status, but it did share some details with TPG.

"Members are supported by a dedicated Concierge team throughout their journey, including proactive trip monitoring and travel assistance, along with exclusive benefits and curated experiences," Alaska said.

That means help with travel disruptions, such as a next-flight guarantee and dedicated, specialized assistance.

Reports suggest other benefits include the ability to gift Gold status, a free Clear+ membership and Avis Chairman's Club status. Those invited are also reportedly being given Atmos Titanium status, even if they haven't already qualified organically this year.

If Alaska follows the lead of its larger competitors, additional perks could include VIP airport transfers, higher upgrade priority and expanded lounge access. However, Alaska has not confirmed those benefits.

As for what it might take to get invited to this special club, it will likely require spending tens of thousands of dollars on tickets. Some reports suggest the invitations appear to be targeted at potential customers for Alaska's new international routes with lie-flat business class. On the flip side, some Titanium-level Alaska flyers haven't been invited even after earning as many as 250,000 Alaska Atmos status points and buying international business-class tickets.

"Through this beta program, we’re creating new ways to recognize some of our most loyal members as our global network grows," Alaska told TPG.

While this won't mean much for most of us, it's still exciting to see a new layer of potential perks for some of Alaska's most loyal flyers. Alaska has been one of the most innovative U.S. airlines when it comes to loyalty, so it's an interesting development to see the carrier recognize its highest-value customers with an invite-only tier that matches what the other big global U.S. airlines have done.

Alaska is also now the only major U.S. airline that lets you earn elite status from actual flight miles (though you can choose to earn status by spending). A new top-tier status level is another way the airline is differentiating itself.

#6247. My First “New” Chase Sapphire Reserve Travel Redemption Blew My Mind

There’s… a lot… of coverage surrounding the revamped Chase Sapphire Reserve Card. As per usual these days, the hot takes are plentiful and people are fired up. It’s either the apocalypse or the beginning of something great, depending on which attention seeker you read. As a long time cardholder, I’m really intrigued by the new changes.

The changes really fit my profile and sure, the card will cost more, but I won’t have to introduce any behavior change to get more, unlike some other cards. I’ll do most of my spending on this card. I’m a keeper just from the fee credit and earning multipliers.

Well, if my first Chase Sapphire Reserve redemption is any indicator, this card may single handedly change the redemption game and just about everyone should take note — including airline and hotel transfer partners. It’s already a huge win.

Chase Travel’s ‘The Edit’ is a curated selection of nice hotels, which offer benefits similar to those provided by a travel agent or other luxury credit card booking platform. When booking a ‘The Edit’ property, you can expect breakfast for two, a $100 F&B credit, late check out and an upgrade subject to availability.

Which leads me to the important bit! With the revamped Sapphire Reserve Card, there’s a new “Points Boost” feature, which offers up to two cents per point (25,000 points would cover $500, etc) for some flight or hotel purchases.

This can be amazing value, with flights of $3,000 being grabbed for just 150,000 points, with no taxes and fees and the ability to still earn frequent flyer miles and elite status points, since the airline treats it like a cash ticket.

Previously, the Sapphire Reserve card offered a steady point redemption opportunity directly on Chase Travel at 1.5 cents per point (100,000 points would cover $1500, etc). But with the new version, some travel purchases you want to redeem for will either offer less value than before, the same, or more, with this new ‘Points Boost’ at 2 cents per point. We like more!

I am in New York and wanted to do a little staycation, so I fired up Chase Travel and found one of my more reliable upper mid-scale hotels, The Thompson Central Park was on as part of ‘The Edit’. My two options became a very clear singular, third option.

Typically, I’d consider paying cash or transferring my points from Chase to Hyatt to pay for a stay like this. Hyatt has “fixed” points rates, meaning the points price is largely irrespective of the cash price and only changes by seasonal dates. For this season, it was 25,000 points per night for the Thompson Central Park.

If I were to transfer my points, I’d get a free night (the cash rate was around $500) and have a really solid points redemption at exactly two cents per point. I’m not loyal to any hotel chain really, so I wouldn’t get any breakfast or “elite” benefits, but a free night is a free night.

BUT — Chase Travel had a ‘Points Boost’ option to book the hotel directly on their platform and not transfer points to Hyatt. Chase Travel was offering this property for circa 25,000 points and that would cover the $500 cash rate, but unlike transferring points to Hyatt, because I was redeeming a ‘The Edit’ property on Chase Travel, I’d receive…

Yep, by NOT transferring my points (and dealing with the fractured transfer journey) I was able to get myself basically $200 in additional value added to my stay with the breakfast and $100 property credit, not factoring in the value of late check out or a category room upgrade. In addition, I’ll be able to earn elite nights and Hyatt Points on the stay.

A mere 25,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards Points got me a “free” $500 hotel night, breakfast for two, and $100 to spend at the hotel. That’s a pretty stunning redemption, giving more than two cents per point of value and still allowing me to earn on the stay, unlike when you transfer your points to a loyalty program. I wish I could’ve stayed longer.

For the first time I can remember, transferring points to Hyatt was not the best option here and that’s something to stand up and take notice of.

If Chase can keep up this Points Boost game, it can really send ripples through rewards. For the first time, people can easily receive tremendous value for their points through a credit card portal while still earning elite status and points with the hotel or airline of their choosing.

You can check out the new 100,000 point + 500 travel credit offer for the Sapphire Reserve. It’s 200,000 points for Sapphire Reserve Business Cards.

#6246. A Thief Grabbed His Backpack From A Delta Carousel At JFK, But A Friend Tracked Him Down In Washington, DC

A stolen backpack at New York JFK could have been the start of a miserable few weeks for travel writer JT Genter. Instead, it became an interstate detective story involving a luggage tracker, a bus number, and fellow travel writer Jamie Larounis riding in a Washington, D.C. police car. This one has a happy ending…and Jamie deserves a huge round of applause.

JT, who writes about points and miles and nomadically travels full-time with his wife Katie, reported that his checked bag had been stolen from Delta’s baggage claim belt at JFK Terminal 4. Before leaving the terminal, he filed a missing-baggage claim with Delta and a police report.

Ugh. Checked baggage stolen off of @Delta baggage claim belt in JFK Terminal 4.

Delta missing baggage claim and police report filed before leaving the terminal.

Never had this happen before. Happy for any tips on what to do next.

— JT Genter (@JTGenter) November 11, 2026

He subsequently explained that the backpack contained his clothing, medication, toiletries, and irreplaceable mementos. He was also decidedly unimpressed by the response from Delta employees.

For someone who lives on the road, that is considerably more than losing a suitcase of vacation clothes. Understandably, his bag contains much of his daily life. Replacing the contents becomes another job, and some things cannot simply be purchased again.

But there was something JT had deliberately left out of his initial account.

People understandably suggested that he should have put a tracker inside. In a subsequent update, JT revealed that he already had one. He had kept that information private while police were tracking the man.

And to be precise, this was a Tile tracker, rather than an Apple AirTag.

I appreciate the restraint. When something like this happens, the temptation is to post every development, especially when people are offering advice (and condemnation) about the precaution you already took.

But the more useful audience for those location updates was the people who could actually help recover the bag.

According to Jamie’s account, the man took the stolen backpack from New York to Washington, DC on Amtrak.

Using the Tile location, Jamie found a man with the bag at a bus station. Then the man boarded a bus.

That could have been the end of the opportunity, but Jamie caught the bus number and found two police officers willing to help. The officers located the suspect a few blocks away and apprehended him.

They then asked Jamie to ride in the police car to identify the man. Afterward, they went to the station to retrieve the items.

Jamie summed up his unexpected afternoon rather nicely:

“Gotta say, I didn’t have being in a Metropolitan Police cop car on my bingo card today”

https://twitter.com/TheForwardCabin/status/2120615885626835334?a=hFcZDL9PoGdHYVjUzks&s=20

Usually when someone ends up in a police car, the story has taken a less encouraging turn. This was a very welcome exception!

I also love that the bus number became such a useful detail. The tracker got Jamie close enough to spot the bag, but paying attention when the man boarded gave the officers something concrete to work with.

I know Jamie, and I am delighted to see him get credit for this.

There is a considerable difference between feeling sorry for someone who has lost a bag and going out to help find it. Jamie gave his time and followed through when the situation became more complicated than simply spotting a backpack.

The police officers deserve credit too. A location on a tracking app is useful, but recovering stolen property still requires someone to act on that information and I don’t consider it very smart to confront a thief directly. In this case, Jamie found officers who helped turn a promising lead into an actual recovery.

JT’s response to Jamie was understandably enthusiastic:

He also expressed amazement at how much had been recovered. A great story involving two people I consider friends.

A backpack stolen from a JFK baggage carousel ended up in Washington, where a tracker and a determined friend helped police catch the suspect and recover belongings.

What a satisfying ending. So many missing-bag stories conclude with a claim number and a disappointing reimbursement discussion. This one concluded with Jamie doing some excellent detective work and JT getting back possessions he thought he might never see again.

Well done, Jamie. That is friendship in action!

#6244. JetBlue is Launching a New Domestic First Class—and We Got a First Look

Flying domestic with JetBlue just got an upgrade. On Wednesday, November 11, the airline introduced BlueFirst, a brand-new domestic first class product, ahead of its debut flight on December 8. The cabin is a dedicated section in the first three rows, arranged two-by-two (read: no middle seats). It will be installed across the airline's fleet on planes that do not already have a Mint business class cabin, bringing a domestic first class to the shorter routes for which JetBlue is more commonly known. As Stephanie Evans Greene, the airline’s senior vice president of marketing and brand, tells Condé Nast Traveler, the idea is "premium, but not pretentious."

BlueFirst will begin rolling out across JetBlue’s fleet in early December, beginning with the carrier’s daily Boston–Fort Lauderdale flight and soon followed by its popular Fort Lauderdale–New York LaGuardia route.

The new cabin is a big shift for JetBlue, an airline that for most of its 26 years in business flew economy seats only. The one exception is Mint, a lie-flat business class available on the airline's transcontinental and transatlantic routes, like New York to Los Angeles and London. To be clear: BlueFirst is not a version of Mint, and the two will never appear on the same plane. Mint planes keep Mint, and BlueFirst goes on every other aircraft. Where Mint is a bed, BlueFirst is a recliner, built for the shorter leisure routes that make up most of JetBlue's network.

To test out the BlueFirst product, we checked out the first aircraft with the new cabins installed on the ground at New York—JFK. Here's everything travelers should know before booking.

The first three rows of the plane will be dedicated to BlueFirst, with 12 seats in total.

As for the seat itself, the first thing that will stand out to travelers is just how much more space there is. BlueFirst has only three rows—12 seats total—and each seat is about three inches wider than a standard economy seat, with room to spare in every direction. The seat is spacious enough to hold a passenger and a laptop bag next to them (or a large purse, in my case), and the space in front is just as generous, with up to seven extra inches of legroom compared with JetBlue's regular Main seats. It reclines five inches too, though the recline takes a bit of pressure (hold the button and push back on the seat firmly). Press the button again, and the seat pops right back up. In true JetBlue fashion—this is, after all, the airline that built its name on being the un-stuffy one—there's no curtain cutting the BlueFirst cabin off from the rest of the plane.

Mattress company Tuft & Needle designed the seat cushion using T&N Flex foam.

The seat cushion is made with Tuft & Needle's T&N Flex foam (yes, the mattress company), developed just for JetBlue. It's squishy enough to comfortably sink into, and it responds as you shift, in both the bottom cushion and the backrest. The adjustable headrest also has wings that fold in to cradle your head. "I'll go on record and say I think they're some of the most comfortable recline seats that are out there in domestic first class," Greene says.

BlueFirst passengers receive a blanket and an amenity kit with socks, earbuds, mouthwash, and OSEA Malibu skincare products.

Aside from the bigger, more comfortable seat, BlueFirst gives travelers a slew of other perks. At every seat, there's a 13.3-inch screen with Bluetooth for personal earbuds, USB-A, USB-C, and a regular outlet, plus JetBlue's free Wi-Fi. The overhead bins above the cabin are reserved for BlueFirst passengers, so boarding doesn't come with the usual scramble for space, and each large bifold tray table has a stand for your phone or tablet. Travelers also get a blanket and an amenity kit with socks, earbuds, mouthwash, and OSEA Malibu skincare products, including a lip balm, hand cream, and the fan-favorite calming pulse point oil.

What's more, the perks start before passengers even get on the plane: BlueFirst comes with priority check-in, a faster security lane at more than 30 airports, and Group 1 boarding. Most BlueFirst fares come with two free checked bags—even BlueFirst Base, the cheapest of the three, includes one checked bag.

The dining options in BlueFirst depend on how long your flight is. A bento-inspired box is served on flights of 899 miles or more, with an entrée, a side, and a dessert. The exact menu changes based on the route. Dinner might be a tortellini pasta salad with marinated green olives, a pastrami sandwich with a citrusy cabbage salad, or sesame noodles with crispy wontons and a Szechuan dip. The desserts are a highlight: the pasta comes with a carrot cake with a caramel icing top that's deliciously moist (my personal favorite), and there are colorful macarons and a pistachio chocolate cake on other menus. Breakfast runs from hazelnut-ricotta crêpes to a sweet potato and bean bowl with guacamole and hot sauce, a poached pear, and blueberry chia pudding. There are also kosher, vegan, and gluten-free versions of the boxes.

Drinks in this section of the cabin deserve their own mention, because BlueFirst's come with a twist you won't find on other US airlines. Everything is ordered right from the seatback screen in Mixologist Mode, which lets you build your own cocktail (or mocktail) instead of choosing from a list. You start with a base—a spirit, a soft drink, coffee, a mixer—and add up to four items in total from the full drink menu. The crew then brings the ingredients right to your separate pop-out cocktail tray, and you mix it yourself. There's a limit of two drinks per order, but once the first round lands, you can start the next. The drinks come in real glassware from Fable, on handmade watercolor coasters by New York-based illustrator Danielle Rose Fisher. For anyone not playing bartender, there's also wine from Parcelle, coffee from Cometeer and Joe Coffee, and Smith Teamaker teas.

The new cabin will first roll out on JetBlue flights from Fort Lauderdale to and New York LaGuardia and Boston.

The retrofit should be nearly done by the end of 2027, covering every JetBlue plane that doesn't have Mint.

BlueFirst tickets are currently on sale for travel dates beginning in December. The cabins will be added to more than 30 routes throughout 2026; you'll start seeing the new seats on flights from JFK to Cancún, Liberia, and San Juan beginning in January. However, even on those inaugural routes, not every flight will have BlueFirst right away (it depends on whether a fitted plane is operating that flight). Just over a dozen planes will have the cabin by the end of this year, with the rest of the fleet following through 2027.

By the end of next year, the retrofit should be nearly done, covering every JetBlue plane that doesn't have Mint. Until then, it's worth double-checking before booking since JetBlue notes BlueFirst may only be available on select flights or dates, and planes can be swapped at a moment’s notice depending on equipment needs and maintenance.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

If you fly United Airlines regularly, you've probably considered adding one of its cobranded credit cards to your wallet. But with several options offering everything from complimentary checked bags to United Club lounge access, figuring out which one is worth the annual fee isn't always easy.

I carry the (see rates and fees) myself, and between its annual travel credit, award flight discounts and the boost it's given me toward Premier status, I've found plenty of reasons to keep it in my wallet. But that doesn't necessarily mean it's the right United card for everyone.

And with United's recent MileagePlus changes making cobranded cards more rewarding, it's worth taking a closer look at what each one offers.

Here's how the Explorer, Quest, Club and Business cards compare — and how to decide which is the best fit for your travel habits.

Here’s a quick look at four of the United cards:

Best for: Occasional United flyers who want the core travel perks without a premium price tag

The covers the basics that matter most on a typical trip, such as a free bag, priority boarding and a couple of lounge passes, without asking you to pay a premium fee for perks you'd rarely use. It's the right fit for someone who flies United a handful of times a year and wants the card to pay for itself without overthinking it.

TPG credit cards editor Olivia Mittak says the two United Club passes alone tend to make the card worth it for her: "A day pass into a United Club costs $59, so if I use both of my passes, I've almost entirely covered my annual fee." She adds that the 9-miles-per-dollar-spent rate on standard United fares booked with the card is the other reason it's stayed in her wallet (earning rate may vary for those with United MileagePlus status and for those flying basic economy or with a base option ticket).

Compared to the United Quest Card, the Explorer is the more accessible option for less frequent flyers, while the Quest makes more sense once you're checking bags and chasing status often enough to justify the higher fee.

Best for: Regular United flyers who check bags often and want a real head start toward Premier status

The is built for travelers who fly United often enough to want more than the free bag and priority boarding the Explorer offers — and who want a card that actively pushes them toward Premier status.

Between the $200 credit and the two free checked bags, much of the $350 annual fee can be offset for anyone flying United a few times a year, especially if you prefer to check a bag rather than tow a carry-on. For example, United charges $45 for a first checked bag and $55 for a second on domestic flights (when you prepay), so checking two bags on a round-trip flight could otherwise cost $200. Take a few similar trips each year, and those savings can quickly add up.

Clint Henderson, a principal spokesperson at TPG, says the $200 trip credit and elevated earning on United flights initially won him over, with "free checked bags and priority boarding" giving him reason enough to keep the card long-term.

One major shortcoming of the Quest, especially compared to the lower-fee Explorer, is its lack of lounge access — as a reminder, the Explorer offers two, one-time United Club passes per year. Best for: Frequent United flyers who want lounge access

The Club Card is for travelers who treat lounge access as a need rather than a nice-to-have. The unlimited visits for two can outweigh the $695 annual fee on their own for anyone who flies regularly with a plus-one, before factoring in the checked bags, Premier Access or partner credits.

Christine Gallipeau, a senior loyalty program editor at TPG, says the card’s "fantastic benefits," including its complimentary United Club membership, discounted United awards and up to $150 in annual ride-hailing credits (yearly activation required), "have justified keeping the card in my wallet, especially as a frequent traveler based near United's Washington, D.C., hub."

Against the Quest, the Club costs nearly double, but that gap effectively replaces what would otherwise be a separate United Club membership. The Club only pulls ahead once lounge access becomes a habit rather than an occasional treat.

Best for: Small-business owners and frequent United flyers who want lounge passes and perks without a premium annual fee

The packs a surprising amount of value into a moderate $150 annual fee, pairing a travel credit and lounge passes with a PQP boost that can meaningfully nudge business travelers toward Premier status.

It carries the same annual fee as the Explorer (after the first year; the Explorer has a $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150), but is built for business travelers who can turn everyday business expenses into progress toward Premier status.

Unlike the United Club Card, it offers just two one-time passes a year, which should be enough for someone who only wants occasional lounge access.

That's part of the appeal for Carly Helfand, TPG's director of site content strategy. She says the card works particularly well alongside the United Quest Card: "That card doesn't include any lounge access, so the United Business Card fills a gap with its two United Club one-time passes per year." She also appreciates the 5,000 bonus miles she gets each anniversary for holding both cards: "It's not a ton of miles, but it's a nice reward for keeping a card combo I was going to carry anyway!"

#6242. Singapore Airlines CEO May Rethink New Business Class Colors, And He Should

Singapore Airlines has made a mistake with the colors of its new business class cabin. The gray and black surfaces with bright yellow accents look more like a cheap hybrid of Spirit Airlines and Scoot than the premium airline whose name is on the aircraft. Now CEO Goh Choon Phong has left the door open to changes. I hope Singapore Airlines takes that opportunity.

When I covered the new Singapore Airlines business class seat, I welcomed several functional improvements, particularly the redesigned footwell. Singapore has addressed complaints about sleeping comfort and added features passengers increasingly expect.

I keep looking at the photographs and wondering how this particular color scheme made it through the approval process. Singapore Airlines has spent decades cultivating an identity associated with understated luxury. Its warmer, muted cabin colors help communicate that identity before a “Singapore Girl” even shows up to offer a welcome drink.

The new business class looks disconnected from it. The yellow accents against the gray and dark surfaces suggest a budget airline or a gaming chair. Neither association strikes me as particularly useful for Singapore Airlines.

During the launch Q&A, executives defended the decision to move in a different visual direction.

A post shared by Brandon · The Points Wanderer (@thepointswanderer)

Vice President of Product Experience Ong Wah Li said customer research had identified a desire for a more contemporary appearance. She described the resulting palette as “modern and refreshed, yet elegant and refined.”

Chief Commercial Officer Lee Lik Hsin emphasized that the Singapore Airlines experience extends beyond cabin colors. He defended the different palette, saying:

“We do not feel that a different colour palette creates any kind of inconsistency.”

Of course the Singapore Airlines experience involves more than colors. Service and comfort are far more consequential over a long flight. But the airline does not invest in cabin design because appearance is irrelevant. It understands that the surroundings help establish what passengers think they are buying.

Asking for something “modern” does not mean asking for this. Singapore Airlines could refresh its interiors while preserving the warmth and restraint that make them recognizable. I simply do not understand why contemporary design should require such a sharp departure from the brand. Plenty of modern interiors feel inviting and expensive without a bright yellow accent running through the seat.

At a November 11 employee town hall, Goh acknowledged the negative reaction. According to The Business Times, he said:

“We’ll look at it, we’ll see what is feasible.”

He also expressed confidence that passengers would appreciate the seats once they experienced their comfort and practical features.

They may well do so. I hope I do too. But enjoying the seat would not make the color choice better. I can appreciate a more comfortable bed while wishing the cabin looked like Singapore Airlines…and the fact that I say that underscores what a brand Singapore has built and should be careful not to fritter away over idiotic consultants who are out of touch with Singapore’s customer base.

Goh has not promised a redesign, and I would not describe this as a reversal. Still, his willingness to consider what can be changed is welcome. We all make mistakes. There is considerably more dignity in acknowledging one and correcting it than spending years defending it.

The contrast with the new Singapore Airlines first class suite makes the business class decision even stranger.

PriestmanGoode designed first class, while Designworks, a BMW Group company, designed business class. Factorydesign handled premium economy and economy.

First class looks like a natural evolution of Singapore Airlines. The warmer finishes and batik details give the new suite a connection to the airline without making it look old. It demonstrates that you can introduce a substantially different product while retaining a recognizable identity.

I worked closely with PriestmanGoode during my time at Star Alliance and have a great appreciation for its work. Looking at these two cabins, I would ask the firm to help bring the business class finishes into the same visual family.

Designworks does have aviation experience, including work with STARLUX and EVA Air. Nevertheless, I think it has badly misjudged this assignment. The BMW association does not automatically make the result luxurious, and this particular result does not look worthy of Singapore Airlines.

I am not particularly impressed with the new premium economy aesthetic either, though that is a different firm’s work. Ultimately, Singapore Airlines approved all these designs. The responsibility for how they fit together belongs to the airline.

There is nothing inherently wrong with yellow. It works for Scoot because Scoot has a different identity and sells a different proposition. It worked for Spirit Airlines (until it didn’t…).

But Singapore Airlines has little reason to make its premium cabin evoke its own budget subsidiary. Nor does the comparison with Spirit help communicate the experience it wants passengers to pay for, right?

That is particularly strange in Southeast Asia, where travelers have plenty of experience distinguishing a full-service premium carrier from a budget airline. Singapore Airlines should reinforce what makes it different.

The yellow stripe will not suddenly send loyal passengers to another carrier: I don’t think people will book away from Singapore because they don’t like the seat color. But why should that be even a consideration? Singapore Airlines has the resources to deliver both comfort and an interior that reflects its reputation.

The earthy, muted colors have worked because they convey quality. This new palette feels like a needless attempt to be different, with too little consideration for what is being lost.

I welcome the functional improvements in the new Singapore Airlines business class seat and look forward to trying it. But the color scheme is a mistake. Sorry, it is. To my eyes, it cheapens the appearance of a product intended to command a premium.

Goh has indicated that the airline will consider what is feasible. My suggestion is straightforward: retain the improvements to comfort, ask PriestmanGoode to help reconsider the finishes, and give business class an appearance consistent with the airline passengers have chosen. Dark brown would work well.

Singapore Airlines does not need to spend the next decade explaining why a cabin that reminds people of Scoot actually represents luxury. It has time to reconsider. I hope it does.

Matthew is an avid traveler who calls Los Angeles home. Each year he travels more than 200,000 miles by air and has visited more than 135 countries. Working both in the aviation industry and as a travel consultant, Matthew has been featured in major media outlets around the world and uses his Live and Let's Fly blog to share the latest news in the airline industry, commentary on frequent flyer programs, and detailed reports of his worldwide travel.

Customers are fickle. Prestige and premium are an ever changing thing. Why be thought of in any capacity as cheap, bland and muted? Why be thought of in any capacity as budget?

Branding matters. This is a small city-state with an outsized reputation and results in finance and aviation. But nothing is finite, things can change quickly. Anyone have Nvidia’s CEO being ousted on their 2026 bingo cards?

Is the seat an improvement? Probably – will await the reviews – I don’t mind the fold down seat, others feel strongly. Are people suddenly booking away from SQ because of a seat that isn’t even flying yet? No. But these new seats will likely be around for ~20 years, and I can’t tell you what the Singapore of 2045 looks like at all as compared to its regional neighbors.

I can say that playing chicken with a well respected and identifiable upscale brand is madness. Whomever was responsible for this simply should not have a job anymore.

I couldn’t agree more, timeless beats modern any day of the week. What is modern today won’t be tomorrow but timeless holds its appeal no matter what. Singapore is a timeless airline their brand is flawless they should fix what’s broken which the seat itself seems to address without abandoning what make Singapore Airlines well Singapore Airlines.

I agree wholeheartedly. That pallet, and in fact all the other aesthetic choices on Singapore’s new business suite, are truly awful. Looks like a second-rate hotel in a third-tier Asian city. I don’t know why some airlines insist on using fast cars as design inspiration. Commercial air travel is about relaxation not speed. It’s a design mismatch and a fundamental misunderstanding of the aesthetic language of their own brand. I suspect this will become a cautionary case study for design students.

Either the J seats are a mistake, or the photos that represent them are ill-taken (or, I suppose, both things could be true). Judging from what SQ has shared, the finishes look plasticky and harsh. Color affects how people feel, and I at least feel more comfortable in a palette that doesn’t look like a nice subway car. But even more important to me is the armrests: it’s bizarre that SQ seems to have overlooked that most people have two arms and need a place to put both. I’ve appreciated SQ for decades, but I’m not feeling like 19 hours in a sterile booth with one armrest is a very compelling proposition.

The missing armrest is a big deal. Hard to believe they decided it wasn’t needed.

This has been more hyped than that ‘controversy’ at Aman in Cabo…

Please comment on Malaysia Airlines’ narrow bodied aircraft. The blue & white seats scream of low cost yet this seat design is the economy AND business class seats of a full service airline. The 737-800s & 737-8 aircrafts can fly over 4 hours and even after 2 hours my bum hurts. Ergonomics were not on their minds. Neither was functionality. Airline redesigns would try to use IFE for video presentations of cabin safety. Malaysia Airlines went back in time, at least for the narrow bodied fleet to bring back manual safety demonstrations. Singapore Airlines’ narrow bodied business class seats define what a full service airline should be. Sadly it’s northern neighbour has no clue.

Who cares what color they are? I want a seat that is comfortable and private, with good food, good IFE and cool cabin temperatures. The seats can be pink and purple for all I care.

The color scheme looks crap. They could have asked a 100 of their PPS and Solitaire customers to pick from a few option and they would have had a pretty good clue of how things are supposed to look like.

This has a cheap plastic feel that one would expect on Batik, Lion or Ryan Air.

A yellow strip. A color palette. My god, seriously? Do you all stand there and stare at the seat for hours to gain some sort of energy transference? Personally, I sit down on it, eat the food, sleep and arrive somewhere I need to be. It’s a tiny cocoon of transport. Not a hotel room. Yes, I want comfort and decent things to pass the time. But anyone who obsesses over feeling less comfortable given a yellow stripe needs to seriously assess priorities.

#6241. Alaska, Hawaiian Pilot MECs Approve Tentative Joint Contract

Pilots at Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines are one step closer to a deal that will bring both work groups together under a single labor contract.

ALPA announced Wednesday that its Alaska and Hawaiian master executive councils unanimously approved a tentative agreement on a joint collective bargaining compact. The two councils had been negotiating since February 2025.

The proposed agreement will now go before the combined membership for a ratification vote.

Details of the agreement were not immediately available to the public.

Union officials said they worked to address the priorities of both work groups and have established a “contractual foundation for their future as a combined workforce.”

“This TA is the result of more than 600 days of challenging negotiations, countless hours of work by our volunteers, and an unwavering commitment to the pilots we represent,” Drew Coyle, the Alaska MEC chair, said in a statement. “Our Joint Negotiating Committee remained focused on the priorities of both pilot groups while working through some of the most complex issues facing our combined membership. Nothing about this process was easy. Now it’s our pilots’ turn to review the agreement, ask the tough questions, and decide whether it meets their expectations.”

Ratification voting starts Dec. 1 and closes Dec. 22.

Alaska and Hawaiian merged in 2024 and received a single operating certificate from the FAA in 2025. This effectively transformed Hawaiian from an independent airline to a brand under Alaska Air Group. Alaska has pledged to maintain Hawaiian’s brand identity, and Hawaiian retains a separate corporate leadership based in Honolulu.

The two brands have continued to integrate however, with Alaska now making use of long-haul aircraft originally owned by Hawaiian. Earlier this year, Alaska implemented a single passenger service system.
