#6216. GOP governor and prominent Dems congratulate senator-elect on flipping Mississippi seat blue

Democrat Scott Colom speaks in Jackson, Mississippi, after winning the U.S. Senate race. Colom defeated Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith in an upset, becoming the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction.

Mississippi's Republican Gov. Tate Reeves, former President Bill Clinton and former Vice President Kamala Harris were among those to congratulate Democrat Sen.-elect Scott Colom on his victory in the Magnolia State's U.S. Senate contest.

More than a week after Election Day, The Associated Press on Wednesday called the race for Colom, the district attorney for Mississippi Circuit Court District 16 who defeated President Donald Trump-backed incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.

"We may have had to count One Mississippi, Two Mississippi, but Blue Mississippi sure has a nice ring to it! Scott, you put your heart and soul into this race because you believe in the promise of your state’s people. And they believed in you right back. I’m honored to have stood alongside you. Congratulations!" Clinton said in a Wednesday post on X.

DEMS PROJECTED TO SCORE HISTORIC UPSET IN DEEP-RED MISSISSIPPI, TOPPLE TRUMP ALLY HYDE-SMITH

Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom, wearing an "I Voted" sticker, walks across the campus of Jackson State University on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026, in Jackson, Miss. (Aron Smith/Jackson State University via Getty Images)

Colom is the first Democrat to win election to a Mississippi U.S. Senate seat since 1982; the late Sen. John Stennis, who served in the U.S. Senate from late 1947 until early 1989, was the last Democrat to serve as a U.S. Senator in the state.

"Congratulations to Senator-Elect @scott_colom. I hope to collaborate as we continue our very important work to support Mississippi families, grow jobs and wages for our people, and improve educational outcomes for our kids!" Gov. Reeves wrote in a post on X.

Colom shared the governor's post and wrote, "Thank you for the congratulations @tatereeves. I also look forward to working with you on the issues that matter to our state. Together, there’s nothing our beautiful state can’t accomplish." He added the hashtag, "#MississippiMatters."

KAMALA HARRIS URGES DEMS TO 'BE RUTHLESS' WITH POWER AFTER MIDTERMS, DEMANDS TRUMP ACCOUNTABILITY

Then-Vice President Kamala Harris and former President Bill Clinton mark the 30th anniversary of the Family and Medical Leave Act during an event in the East Room of the White House on Feb. 2, 2023, in Washington, D.C. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

Colom will be the third Black person ever to serve as a U.S. senator in Mississippi, the state's first Black senator since the 1800s and the first Black person popularly elected to serve as a senator from the state, since the prior two men were selected by the state legislature prior to the adoption of the 17th Amendment in the 20th century.

"The power is with the people, and the people of Mississippi are with Scott. @scott_colom makes history today as the first Black senator elected in Mississippi since Reconstruction. I saw firsthand when campaigning with him in his hometown that he is a brilliant leader and dedicated public servant who will work tirelessly to serve every Mississippian with pride. Congratulations, Scott," Harris wrote in a post on X.

SOROS NETWORK TARGETS DEEP-RED MISSISSIPPI IN BID TO FLIP SENATE SEAT

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., said in a post, "Congratulations to Scott Colom on winning his election and making history as Mississippi's first Black senator since Reconstruction. Scott ran on a bold agenda — taking on Big Tech, the billionaire class and corruption in Washington — and WON. Scott: Welcome to the Senate."

Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

#6215. Philippine Airlines Launches New U.S. Route

Philippine Airlines has landed in the U.S. Midwest.

The carrier on Monday operated its inaugural flight between Manila and Chicago O’Hare. The nonstop connection is the first ever between the Philippines and the Midwest.

“For Philippine Airlines, this is a strategic addition to our North American network,” PAL Executive Vice President and COO Carlos Luis Fernandez said in a news release. “It expands our presence to the Midwest and provides more convenient access to one of the largest regional economies in the United States. We know that many Filipinos and Filipino-Americans in Chicago, Illinois, and neighboring states have long looked forward to a direct and more convenient connection to the Philippines. We are proud to finally make this possible.”

Manila-Chicago service will operate three times weekly going forward.

PAL’s other U.S. destinations are New York-JFK, Los Angeles, San Francisco, Seattle, and Honolulu. It also serves Toronto and Vancouver in Canada.

‘Tis the season … when frequent flyers scramble for eleventh-hour ways to qualify for airline elite status they haven’t quite reached yet.

If Southwest is your airline of choice, the end of 2026 is particularly important to hit status milestones, as Southwest’s Rapid Rewards program is about to change in major ways in early 2027.

With fewer international flight options and no premium cabins for upgrades, chasing Southwest status might not seem as necessary as it does with larger competitors like United Airlines or Delta Air Lines.

But if you fly Southwest a lot and are close to hitting a status goal, it’s wise to explore easy and inexpensive ways to get over that hump.

What you need to do to earn status depends on what part of Southwest’s program you are targeting. Southwest technically has two official status tiers in 2026. Plus, members who fly (or spend) the most can unlock its popular Companion Pass.

Coming next year: Commonly asked questions about Southwest's recent Rapid Rewards reboot and Companion Pass changes

You can check how close you are to status by logging into your Rapid Rewards account where there are easy-to-read status bars for each goal.

There are very different methods for earning the Companion Pass than there are for earning A-List and A-List Preferred status. If the Companion Pass is your only goal, you need to act quickly. The “easy” way to do that with credit card bonuses effectively ends forever no later than Dec. 2, 2026.

This year also marks the last that many partner points count towards Companion Pass, from credit card refer-a-friend bonuses to completing hotel stays booked on the Southwest Hotels portal.

More: Last chance to earn a Southwest Companion Pass the easy way with card bonuses as high as 90,000 points

If traditional A-List or A-List Preferred status is your goal, however, here are 5 ways you can get the flights or points you might still need.

Note that beginning in 2027, Southwest will rename those tiers as part of a broader overhaul (more on that below), but that will not affect how you qualify in 2026 for 2027.

If you are only a few flights away from qualifying for Southwest status, one of the easiest ways to get to the finish line is by taking a trip or two before year’s end.

The amount of money spent doesn’t matter at all if you qualify purely by counting up the number of one-way flights flown, so book and fly the cheapest nonstop Basic fares you can find.

Use Southwest’s Low Fare Calendar to search quickly for the least expensive days to fly to various destinations. The best deals are usually midweek. Early and mid-December (between peak Thanksgiving and Christmas holiday travel) will likely offer lower prices and reduced chances of travel disruptions.

If you can’t hit a status goal by counting one-way flights and need to earn status via tier qualifying points instead, you should take the opposite approach. Instead of booking inexpensive Basic fares, book and fly Southwest’s most expensive fare option: Choice Extra.

This fare earns a whopping 14 TQPs per dollar spent in 2026. If you spend $500 on Choice Extra fares for a November or December mileage run, for example, you will add a quick 7000 TQPs to your Rapid Rewards account balance—one fifth of the way to A-List status.

Those same points are also worth about $90 when redeemed for award travel, so consider the rebate in your cost-benefit calculation.

If actually flying the airline before the year is up isn’t a realistic option, another way to earn tier qualifying points is by spending on a Southwest credit card.

The different cobranded cards earn TQPs differently in 2026. Holders of the lower annual fee (see rates and fees) are out of luck; that card doesn’t earn TQPs at all.

The higher fee cards each earn incrementally higher TQPs, as follows:

(Note, however, that all cards earn Companion Pass qualifying points at a different rate—1 point per $1 spent.)

One critical detail: TQPs earned from credit card spending only count towards 2026 status if the points post to your account before year’s end. That means it is essential to complete all spending before the closing date of your December credit card statement, meaning many travelers may only have a few weeks left.

A reminder, though: Credit card spending will count differently beginning next year for customers trying to qualify for status for 2028.

*The information for the Southwest Rapid Rewards Premier Credit Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

If you have a card (see rates and fees) and already spend heavily on it, there is a quick and easy shortcut to Southwest A-List status (but not A-List Preferred). If you spend $75,000 on that card annually, you'll be rewarded with complimentary A-List status for the remainder of the year and the following year (activation required).

You'll also earn a $500 annual credit towards booking Southwest flights in the Chase Ultimate Rewards portal. That same spending level unlocks other perks from a variety of travel brands like Hyatt and IHG, so there are more benefits than just the Southwest ones to consider.

This method doesn’t require fussing with flight counts or TQPs or even hopping on an airplane before 2026 is up, but it’s only a viable option for a smaller subset of Southwest customers who carry the card and are capable of meeting a significant spending minimum.

Like many airlines, Southwest offers a status match promotion and challenge where you can leverage your elite status on another airline into temporary status on Southwest. If you hold status elsewhere, consider taking advantage.

The current promotion is open for registration through Dec. 30, 2026. As soon as you register, Southwest confers automatic status for a 120-day trial period. You can extend this status for another 12 months if you complete additional flights or earn additional TQPs in the promotion period.

If you plan to fly several trips on Southwest at the end of 2026 or in early 2027, this promotion might make sense. The requirements to meet the status challenge extension are substantially lower than the ones for achieving status the standard way.

Just be aware that only flights booked after registering for the status match count. If you have future Southwest travel already booked, you’ll need to cancel and rebook, potentially at higher prices.

Before committing to any of these strategies, be certain that you understand how Southwest counts Rapid Rewards points in 2026.

Southwest currently counts points three different ways. There are points redeemable only for award travel, and there are two other types that count towards status. Only tier qualifying points, earned primarily through flying or credit card spending, count towards A-List and A-List Preferred Status.

A broader collection of companion pass qualifying points (including credit card welcome bonuses) still count towards earning the Companion Pass for 2026 only.

A lot will soon change when the calendar page turns to 2027.

A-List members will become Silver, and A-List Preferred members will become Gold. Members who have earned a Companion Pass due to points activity in 2026 will continue to be able to use those benefits until the end of 2027.

If you want to earn a Companion Pass anew in 2027 or later, however, you’ll have to aim for a new status tier: Platinum. And if you want to achieve Silver or Gold in subsequent years, be aware that that benchmarks will change. The way TQPs are calculated for several Southwest fare types and for credit card spending will be different as well.

#6213. End Of An Era: Hong Kong’s Iconic “Symphony Of Lights” Show Ending

Hong Kong is one of my favorite cities in the world. When I think of Hong Kong, the beautiful waterfront and skyline on both sides of Victoria Harbour come to mind. Along those lines, a nightly staple of the waterfront is coming to an end, and I’m sad about it…

Since 2004, Hong Kong has had the “Symphony of Lights” show every single night at 8PM, lasting for around 10 minutes. It holds the Guinness World Record for being the world’s largest permanent light and sound show, as it involves dozens of buildings.

It’s one of the things that contributes to Hong Kong’s electric energy, as you have a sea of people lining up on the waterfront (typically on the Tsim Sha Tsui side, though sometimes also on the Central side) every night to watch it.

Well, after 22 years, the Symphony of Lights will be coming to an end. The last show is expected to take place on Wednesday, November 18, 2026. To mark the end of the era, the final show will feature special pyrotechnics and fireworks.

Why has Hong Kong decided to end the nightly Symphony of Lights show? Officially, it’s a strategic shift in the city’s tourism and event strategy, described as being driven by shifting visitor habits, diminishing appeal, high maintenance costs, and a pivot to seasonal attractions. We’re told that we can expect “something new” in the future, but it doesn’t sound like it’ll be a full replacement for the Symphony of Lights.

I must admit, I’m sad to see this change in Hong Kong. No matter how often I visited Hong Kong, I always made a point of watching the Symphony of Lights, and always found it to be so enjoyable. Hong Kong has one of the world’s most gorgeous skylines, and the nightly show just took that to the next level.

I am curious what the backstory here is. Was the cost of operating this really so high, in the scheme of things? While I can in theory appreciate the concept of diminishing appeal, the nightly show always had a crowd in the thousands waiting to enjoy it — that was true 20 years ago when I first visited Hong Kong, and it was also true when I visited earlier this year.

Hong Kongers will soon have to bid farewell to the Symphony of Lights, the iconic nightly show that has been lighting up the city’s skyline since 2004. Officially, this change is described as being due to shifting visitor habits, diminishing appeal, high maintenance costs, and a pivot to seasonal attractions.

I’ve enjoyed this show every time I visited Hong Kong, so I’m sad to see this development. The skyline is still incredible and leaves me in awe every time, but there’s no denying that the nightly show added just a little bit of extra sparkle.

What do you make of Hong Kong’s nightly Symphony of Lights ending?

#6212. 8 Things Frequent Flyers Do Differently To Survive Long-Haul Flights

Long-haul flying can be taxing at the best of times. Prolonged exposure to reduced air pressure and low humidity in cabins, as well as lengthy periods of immobility and sleep disruption, all take their toll on the body. Even if one factor can be prevented by flying on a premium fare, chances are the effects of another will catch up to passengers.

But there are things travelers can do to mitigate the impacts of spending so long in such conditions. A long-haul flight does not have to be completely unbearable, of course. Preparation ahead of time is key. Here, we highlight some of the tricks frequent flyers use to survive long-haul flights.

Although it may sound obvious, getting a seat reservation in sooner rather than later ensures a desired spot and, most importantly, reduces the chance of being stuck in a dreaded middle seat. The majority of airlines let their passengers pick a specific seat or seats well before their flight departs. The caveat is, doing so may come at an additional cost.

Airlines on the whole have increasingly taken to charging passengers extra for seat selection as a means to generate additional revenue. The alternative in many cases is to wait until check-in opens, the timing of which can depend on fare class and type, and be assigned a seat by the airline or choose from what is left at no additional cost. Bear in mind, policies vary carrier to carrier, so it is always worth checking how the specific airline treats booking and seat selection ahead of time.

That said, generally speaking, travelers get the option of either saving money and losing out on being able to pick their own spot onboard, or forking out a bit extra for the choice. On long-haul flights, the question to ask is how important sitting in the right area is. If possible in the cabin attached to a fare, sitting forward of the engines can mean a quieter journey, for instance. Similarly, being next to a window allows that bit of extra space, while direct aisle access means the choice of standing up and moving about the cabin if and when one pleases.

Once onboard, having easy access to anything that may be needed during the flight is vital. An easy way to ensure this is by separating such essentials into a smaller bag or kit that can be removed from carry-on luggage and kept handy at the seat. That, in turn, means the carry-on can remain in overhead storage and free up legroom.

As to what to pack in this kit, everyone will have their preferences. Generally speaking, though, device chargers, an eye mask, and toiletries all come in useful. Tod Covich, travel director at tour company Trafalgar, also previously flagged the likes of a reusable water bottle, lip balm, toothbrush, snacks, and compression socks as among his own essentials.

Long-haul flight essentials, from Trafalgar’s Tod Covich:

*Some airlines restrict the use of portable chargers onboard

Any means of staying and feeling cleansed during long-haul journeys can go a long way to adding to one's sense of wellbeing. Bringing snacks, too, means some choice over when to eat rather than meal times being fully determined by the airline.

Although somewhat encompassed within the kit of essentials to keep handy on a flight, noise-canceling headphones deserve their own honorable mention. Constant background noise is proven to drain energy and contribute to fatigue during long-haul journeys, so any means of drowning it out is worth considering.

Where airlines offer in-flight entertainment, complimentary headphones are usually included. Anyone who has traveled long-haul will tell you that the quality of these can leave much to be desired. Although some airlines may surprise in this sense, the risk is arguably not one worth taking.

For reference, Singapore Airlines, British Airways, Delta Air Lines, and All Nippon Airways (ANA) are among a score of carriers that do in fact supply noise-canceling headphones. This tends to be the case for premium passengers, though, meaning the chances of being offered the technology in economy are incredibly low, regardless of carrier.

Flying in the present day can be a stressful experience, but using certain tips and tricks can ease potential annoyance.

Headphones and inflight entertainment go hand in hand. There is no point in trying to watch a movie or listen to music if a headset does nothing to drown out the noise of a plane’s engines or enclosed cabin environment, of course. Alternatively, having a suitable means to hear the likes of movies or music is pointless if the entertainment itself is not suited to your tastes.

The solution: Bring backup entertainment. Anything from a book to songs, movies, or a series downloaded on a personal device can stave off boredom once and for all. Boredom itself is part and parcel of flying long-haul, particularly among younger travelers.

According to 2017 research undertaken on behalf of Emirates, under-12s took just 49 minutes and 47 seconds to show signs of boredom on flights. In other words, parents could expect to hear “are we nearly there yet” incredibly early into an hours-long journey. Adults could not be blamed for admitting they had had similar thoughts too. All of that goes to say, everyone has a pastime, and when better to get into it?

Preparing in advance does not solely relate to a flight alone; it also relates to the destination. By definition, long-haul routes extend across multiple time zones, so chances are the body will be out of sync upon arrival in a new part of the world.

One way to mitigate that is by adjusting your own body clock to fit the time at the destination before arriving there. Doing so can be as simple as adjusting a watch upon boarding the aircraft. It can also involve adapting well before the flight even takes off.

That could mean syncing meal times, caffeine intake, and sleep to fit the destination’s time at the departure airport or beforehand, and then staying in that rhythm through the duration of the flight. Upon arrival, exposure to daylight or making the most of the night to sleep can then help the body adapt and stave off jet lag.

Aircraft cabins can be drier than deserts, particularly aboard traditional designs built from metals like aluminum where corrosion has to be avoided. Those onboard can easily become dehydrated as a result, leading to dried-out nasal passages and cracked skin, for instance.

Quite simply, the primary way to battle dehydration is to drink lots of water. Recommendations for staying properly hydrated on long-haul flights call for 6.8 to 8.5 ounces (200 to 250 ml) of water per hour. In order to keep skin moisture levels up, the likes of sprayable hydrating mists and petroleum-based lip balms can also help to soothe dryness.

But it is not just drinking water and tending to skin that can help. Going easy on alcohol consumption is another clear way of staving off dehydration and fatigue during long journeys. Not only does alcohol contribute to dehydration, but it can also impact sleep quality. In other words, alcohol can add a touch of luxury to a flight, but the trade-off is a more restless experience and possibly even worse jet lag upon arrival.

Which items are most important to take as carry-on luggage?

Another simple yet effective way to survive a long-haul flight is to dress comfortably. Once upon a time, when flying was a novelty few could afford, aircraft cabins were a scene of glamour where men sported suits and ties, and women wore dresses. Luckily, those days are long since over, and no one is expecting anyone to dress to impress.

That goes to say, wearing clothes that are comfortable and will remain that way for the duration of a day spent traveling is vital. A flight alone may span six hours, but transfers and waiting could mean the time from door to door is double that, of course. Much of that will be spent sitting down too, so wearing jeans that dig in at the waist is never going to be pleasant.

Similarly, keeping several layers at hand is important. Plane cabins can be cold, an issue that is only worsened as core body temperature drops prior to and during sleep. Always think: It is better to be too warm and able to remove a layer than be too cold without anything else to put on.

Ultimately, for the majority of travelers, preparing for a long-haul flight is about getting mentally and physically ready to spend hours on end in a seated position. Such inactivity can lead to swelling of the feet, slowed kidney function, and a general sense of fatigue, among other things.

Mitigating those effects is easy, though, and takes being as mobile as possible to keep blood flowing as normal. That includes before the flight, where something as simple as a walk around the terminal coupled with some stretches can help with relaxation and prevent tension once seated onboard, according to Qantas-cited physiotherapist Emma Readman-Thorley. Add in a good night's rest prior, and the chance of being floored by a long-haul trip is only going to be reduced.

During the flight, in Readman-Thorley’s words, “move your limbs for about three to four minutes every hour and regularly travel about the cabin to help make your journey – and your post-flight wellbeing – more pleasant”.

#6211. Report: Google Accepts Privacy Safeguards for Spirit Data

The Wall Street Journal reported Monday that the proposed sale will exclude personnel records, including medical files, results of drug and alcohol tests, performance reviews, payroll information, and grievance and arbitration filings.

Unions representing former Spirit pilots and flight attendants had objected to the inclusion of that data, noting Google’s plans to use the information to train its artificial intelligence models. The agreement reached this week resolves the unions’ concerns, the Journal said.

Google and Spirit initially planned to have an outside company “deidentify” the airline’s records. That process will still take place, though at a higher standard than Spirit intended to use, and Google will be prohibited from attempting to “reidentify” the data.

Spirit went out of business in May following a dramatic rise in jet fuel prices. The decision to auction off its internal records for use by AI was a first for the airline industry and opened up a new realm of contestation for workers and employers.

#6210. Buy Wyndham Rewards Points With Best-Ever 100% Bonus (0.65 Cents Each): Worth It?

Wyndham Rewards has launched its latest promotion on purchased points, which is potentially in line with the best-ever offers that we’ve seen from the program. This could be a great value for unlocking discounted award stays, as the program is offering up to a 100% bonus, which is an opportunity to acquire points for 0.65 cents each.

Link: Buy Wyndham Rewards points with a bonus

Between 12:01AM ET on November 11 and 11:59PM on December 31, 2026, Wyndham Rewards is offering a bonus on purchased points. The best offer appears to be for up to a 100% bonus, though you’ll have to log into your account to see what you’re eligible for.

With this offer, you can unlock the highest bonus if you purchase at least 3,000 points in one transaction. If you purchase 1,000 or 2,000 points, you don’t receive any bonus. If you purchase points, they’ll post to your account within 72 hours, and purchases are non-refundable. Purchased points don’t count toward Wyndham Rewards elite status.

Ordinarily you can buy Wyndham Rewards points for 1.3 cents each, before any discounts or bonuses, and that includes all taxes and fees.

If you maxed out the promotion and were eligible for a 100% bonus, you could purchase 400,000 points (including 200,000 bonus points) for $2,600, which is a rate of 0.65 cents per point.

This is the best bonus offer I ever recall seeing from Wyndham Rewards, so if there has ever been a time to buy points, this is it.

Wyndham Rewards ordinarily lets members purchase up to 100,000 points per account per calendar year, before any bonuses. However, during this promotion, that cap has been doubled, to 200,000 points.

When Wyndham offers a promotion on purchased points, it’s most commonly an 80-100% bonus. So this 100% bonus is at the very top end of that scale. However, personally I’d decide on whether to make a purchase more based on if I had an immediate use in mind, rather than the exact cost per point.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from Wyndham Rewards on buying points, before this one, with the highest bonus amounts offered.

Wyndham Rewards points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as a hotel purchase for the purposes of credit card spending.

I’d recommend using a card with which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. When in doubt, review which credit cards are best for buying points and miles.

Generally speaking, I only recommend buying points when you have a specific, short-term use in mind. In the case of Wyndham Rewards points:

More generally, there are definitely some properties where there’s value in outright buying points for the purposes of a redemption. Let me actually give a direct example, as I recently purchased some Wyndham points for a hotel stay, rather than booking with cash. I needed to be in Colorado Springs, and I booked The Mining Exchange Hotel, part of Wyndham Registry Collection (the hotel even has a Michelin key!)

The cash rate for a base room at the hotel would’ve been $307.57, inclusive of taxes & fees.

Meanwhile the hotel was charging just 30,000 points. At a rate of 0.65 cents per point, that’s like paying $195 for the stay, inclusive of taxes & fees. Not bad, eh?

Well, it gets better than that. Wyndham Rewards often lets you book premium rooms at no extra cost when redeeming points, so I was able to book a club room for the same 30,000 points.

If paying cash, that would’ve cost $438.54, inclusive of taxes & fees.

Now, the club rooms absolutely aren’t worth it, since you just get access to a pantry with some packaged snacks. But hey, if the cost is the same, I’ll take it. 😉

Wyndham Rewards has a four tier award chart, so free night redemptions will cost one of the following amounts:

While I wouldn’t say there’s widespread appeal to buying Wyndham Rewards points for these kinds of redemptions, there are some situations where the numbers will work out. Perhaps the best value would come in situations where you just need to buy a few thousand points to have enough for an award stay.

Wyndham Rewards has more than 9,000 hotels across 20 brands in 80+ countries. Some of the most popular Wyndham Rewards brands include Registry Collection, Wyndham Grand, Dolce, Wyndham, La Quinta, Wingate, Wyndham Garden, Ramada, Days Inn, Super 8, Howard Johnson, and Travelodge.

Everyone will value points differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Wyndham Rewards points to be worth 0.6 cents each. Admittedly that’s a very conservative valuation, and there should be opportunities to get way more value than that.

Wyndham Rewards has one of the most complicated points expiration policies of any hotel loyalty program:

Wyndham Rewards partners with a variety of transferable points currencies, including Bilt Rewards, Capital One, Chase Ultimate Rewards, and Citi ThankYou. The catch is that transfers are at a 1:1 ratio, so I wouldn’t at all consider that to be a good redemption value.

That’s because you could be getting way more value from your transferable points than moving them to a program where points can be purchased for well under a penny each.

Wyndham Rewards also has a portfolio of credit cards issued in the United States, which are potentially quite lucrative if you frequent the brand.

Wyndham Rewards is offering up to a 100% bonus on purchased points, which is an opportunity to buy points for as little as 0.65 cents each. While I most definitely wouldn’t speculatively buy Wyndham Rewards points at this cost, there are some situations where the math works out, so everyone should crunch the numbers for themselves.

#6209. The Boeing 737 NG Still Has Years Of Flying Left, But Its Largest Operator Doesn't Want It Anymore

vesperstock | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

The symbiotic relationship between Southwest Airlines and the Boeing 737 Next Generation family has defined the very essence of low-cost domestic travel. Operating hundreds of Boeing 737-700 and Boeing 737-800 aircraft, the carrier built its legendary point-to-point network around the reliability, commonality, and rugged versatility of Boeing’s popular narrowbody workhorse. These airframes logged millions of flight hours, connecting passengers across thousands of city pairs while fostering an operational culture deeply rooted in single-type fleet efficiency.

During its September 2024 Investor Day, Southwest made a decision that stunned industry observers: a firm commitment to retire all 571 Next Generation aircraft by the end of 2031 in favor of an all-MAX fleet. This decision comes even though many of these airframes retain substantial structural and calendar life and can fly for years to come. The move is part of a profound evolution in modern airline fleet planning, where superior fuel efficiency, reduced emissions, and higher seating capacity outweigh the mechanical longevity of mature narrowbody types.

It cannot be overstated how significant Southwest's pivot is, especially given the sheer scale of the fleet involved in this generational transition. Operating 450 Next Generation aircraft consisting of 262 737-700s and 188 737-800s in active service, according to ch-aviation. Southwest is the largest operator of the type in global aviation, by some distance. These aircraft have been the fundamental building blocks of the airline's dense domestic schedules, operating multiple short-to-medium-haul legs daily with exceptional dispatch reliability.

The cornerstone of the 2031 roadmap is a dramatic rejuvenation of the carrier's asset profile, designed to bring down the average age of its operating fleet from approximately 11.5 years to just 5 years, as reported by Airline Geeks. By replacing older NG variants with new Boeing 737 MAX 8 and upcoming MAX 7 airframes, Southwest aims to modernize its operational footprint while enhancing environmental performance.

Completing a retirement campaign of this scale will not come without its challenges, especially in managing manufacturer delivery schedules, regulatory certifications, and network capacity demands. While the end-of-2031 target provides a clear strategic horizon, executive leadership has acknowledged that the exact pace remains tethered to Boeing's delivery cadence and certification timelines for smaller variant types. Consequently, while the ultimate destination is an all-MAX operational model, the winding down of the Next Generation era will be a methodical, multi-year process.

The underlying justification for moving away from the 737 Next Generation family centers entirely on modern thermodynamic efficiency and seating economics. When Southwest introduced the 737 MAX 8 into active service, manufacturer projections indicated a fuel burn reduction of approximately 14% compared to the NG airframes. In operational practice, Southwest annual reports have consistently credited fleet-wide fuel savings to the strategic integration of MAX aircraft alongside the systematic retirement of older 737-700s, turning environmental efficiency into a powerful bottom-line advantage.

A standard Southwest 737-700 accommodates 143 passengers in a single-class configuration, whereas the larger MAX 8 expands capacity to 175 passengers. This density gain allows the carrier to generate significantly higher revenue per departure on high-demand trunk routes without increasing aircraft count or slot footprint at congested airports. Ultimately, the economic performance gap between NG and MAX equipment becomes insurmountable for long-term fleet planning because of the higher passenger counts with lower fuel burn per seat.

Transitioning away from legacy NGs enables Southwest to compress its average fleet age, with benefits that may not seem obvious at first. Operating a substantially younger aircraft family slashes unscheduled maintenance events, reduces component replacement costs, and enhances schedule reliability across thousands of daily departures. The airframes of the older generation are still airworthy, but the sheer financial velocity of MAX-generation operating margins makes retaining the older fleet commercially unjustifiable.

The carrier is hyperfocused on fleet simplicity and fuel efficiency for now.

Embarking on a fleet transition of this magnitude, however, is heavily constrained by external aerospace supply chains and manufacturer delivery cadences. Southwest originally outlined an ambitious target to phase out all Next Generation aircraft by the end of 2031, but the pace of this retirement campaign is intrinsically tied to Boeing's ability to roll out new single-aisle jets from its assembly lines. Supply chain issues, regulatory scrutiny, and production-rate adjustments have repeatedly pushed carriers worldwide to recalibrate their fleet retirement horizons.

Recent operational cadences illustrate the delicate equilibrium needed between retirements and incoming deliveries. For instance, the airline retired 55 Next Generation aircraft in 2025, comprising 48 737-700s and 7 737-800s, while taking delivery of 55 new MAX 8 airframes, followed by planned schedules for roughly 66 MAX deliveries and 60 retirements in subsequent operating cycles, as per data from Cranky Flier. Annual delivery volumes fluctuate based on OEM manufacturing stability, so matching retirements one-to-one with new arrivals is a complex logistical challenge for fleet planners.

Consequently, executive leadership has adopted a pragmatic stance regarding the timeline's rigidity. Chief Financial Officer Tom Doxey noted that Southwest still maintains more than 450 Next Generation airframes that will be phased out gradually for years to come, well into the next decade, according to Aviation Week. Of course, the 2031 target is the ultimate strategic horizon, but aircraft production backlogs will likely extend the twilight of the 737 NG era beyond initial projections.

Southwest Airlines is aggressively shedding its Next Generation fleet to the point that the existing fleet seems far too outdated, though these airframes are far from obsolete and still have robust demand across the secondary global market. Regional carriers, leasing companies, and growing airlines eagerly queue for surplus 737-700 and 737-800 units, allowing Southwest to capitalize on strong secondhand asset valuations. Southwest is focused on monetizing select airframes and surplus spare engines while market conditions remain highly favorable.

The cargo sector is a particularly lucrative second life for the larger 737-800 variants. Passenger-to-freighter (P2F) conversion programs have taken on substantial inventory from major operators looking to upgrade their fleets. According to market data compiled by aviation analytics firm IBA, operators completed 265 737-800 freighter conversions between January 2020 and August 2026. These numbers show that the airframe's structural integrity and engine reliability easily outlast its primary passenger utility for carriers chasing ultra-high-density MAX efficiencies.

Consequently, the retirement of the Next Generation family is driven entirely by strategic single-fleet standardization rather than mechanical fatigue or structural exhaustion. Airframes leaving Southwest's active roster find immediate new leases on life hauling express freight or serving secondary passenger routes worldwide. It means that the 737 NG legacy will endure across global aviation networks long after Southwest completes its transition to an all-MAX operating model.

Managing a multi-year transition away from a massive fleet of aircraft takes careful coordination to maintain a consistent, competitive passenger experience on legacy airframes. The phase-out timeline extends well into the next decade, so Southwest cannot afford to let its remaining Next Generation cabins deteriorate while waiting for new deliveries. Passengers flying on older aircraft still need to enjoy a modern, comfortable onboard environment that aligns with the airline's brand standards.

Southwest has therefore invested in targeted cabin refurbishments for select 737-700s slated for extended service during the twilight of the NG era. These interior refreshes include updated seating materials, modernized cabin lighting aesthetics, and refreshed bulkheads that mirror the interior ambiance of incoming MAX jets. By revitalizing passenger touchpoints on mature airframes, the airline is ensuring there is no perceptible drop in onboard quality for travelers during the multi-year handover period.

The meticulous approach to the NG twilight highlights the operational pragmatism needed in modern fleet management. Even as executive leadership targets an all-future-generation fleet, maintaining the operational integrity and customer appeal of the existing inventory protects the carrier's reputation. The 737 Next Generation may no longer align with Southwest's long-term efficiency vision, but its final years in service are being treated with the same disciplined attention to detail that built the airline's success, and that is truly impressive.

The retirement trajectory of the 737 Next Generation fleet illustrates a profound reality in modern commercial aviation: economic obsolescence frequently arrives long before structural exhaustion. Airframes like the 737-700 and 737-800 have decades of potential calendar and cycle life, as evidenced by booming passenger-to-freighter conversions and robust secondary market demand, but the rapid gains in fuel efficiency and seating capacity offered by newer generations make holding onto older assets financially unviable for major network operators. Decarbonization goals, emissions standards, and operating margin pressures dictate that remaining useful life is superseded by the immediate return on investment delivered by modern engine and wing architectures.

Southwest is now well on its delivery-dependent path toward an all-MAX operating model over the coming decade, and once this transition is complete, the airline will likely permanently reshape North American single-aisle operations. Phasing out hundreds of airframes to establish a uniform, ultra-young fleet profile sets a new benchmark for low-cost carrier fleet strategy, showing that even a legendary aircraft family must eventually yield to the relentless march of technological progress.

IHG One Rewards is currently offering a limited time 100% bonus on purchased points. With this, IHG One Rewards members can purchase points for as little as 0.5 cents each. Is this a good deal?

While I wouldn’t recommend buying points without a specific use in mind, there are absolutely ways to get outsized value, and this is in line with the best offers that we see from the program. With the right strategy, this could be an opportunity to get a significant discount on an IHG hotel stay, and I’ll show exactly how.

Link: Buy IHG One Rewards points with this promotion with a 100% bonus

Between 12:01AM ET on November 11 and 11:59PM ET on November 15, 2026, IHG One Rewards is offering a bonus on purchased points. Points can be purchased in increments of 1,000 points, and the bonus is structured as follows:

Note that the purchase of IHG points doesn’t count toward elite status, and purchased points will post within 72 hours of an eligible purchase (though usually much faster than that).

Ordinarily you can buy IHG One Rewards points for as little as one cent each (the pricing isn’t linear), before any discounts or bonuses, and that’s inclusive of all taxes and fees.

With that in mind, if you were eligible for a 100% bonus and purchased 200,000 IHG One Rewards points pre-bonus, you’d receive a total of 400,000 points at a cost of $2,000, which is a rate of 0.5 cents per IHG point.

While The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Credit Card (learn more), and The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more), offer a 30% discount on purchased points, that benefit only applies when buying points at the normal cost, and wouldn’t be applicable here.

When IHG One Rewards does offer a promotion on purchased points, the 100% bonus or 50% discount is the most common offer. A 100% bonus and 50% discount give you the same price per point, so you’ll typically pay 0.5 cents per point during a promotion.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from the program, before this one.

IHG One Rewards points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as a hotel purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. That means if you pay with an IHG credit card, you wouldn’t earn any bonus rewards, so it’s not treated as if it’s IHG spending.

Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. See this post for more on which credit cards are best for buying points.

IHG One Rewards has dynamic award pricing, which means there’s no minimum or maximum number of points a hotel stay can cost. Rather, the cost of an award stay generally correlates somewhat to the cost of a revenue stay.

However, that doesn’t necessarily mean you’ll get the same value with all hotel stays. There are many situations where you can get outsized value by buying points and then redeeming them. Let me just give a few examples, using stays I pulled up for random dates (again, pricing is dynamic, so this won’t reflect what you see every day).

For example, the Six Senses Kyoto is bookable for 165,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $825.

That represents massive savings over the cash cost, which is $1,493.

On the other end of the spectrum, the Holiday Inn Express & Suites Tampa is bookable for 33,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $165.

That represents massive savings over the cash cost, which is $230.

However, this won’t always be a good deal. For example, take the Kimpton Tres Rios in Playa del Carmen is bookable for 104,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $520.

That’s not a good deal compared to the cash cost, which is $429, so there you’d be better off just paying cash directly.

Another thing to keep in mind is that select IHG co-branded credit cards offer free night awards, and those are worth up to a certain number of points. What’s great is that these free night awards can typically be topped off with points, so there could be merit to buying IHG points so that you have points with which to top off these certificates.

You’ll get the most value from your IHG points if you have The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card (learn more), and The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more).

That’s because the cards offer a fourth night free benefit, meaning that you can book a four night award stay for the cost of three nights. This is essentially the equivalent of 25% off in increments of four nights, since you can use this benefit an unlimited number of times.

Just to use the Six Senses Kyoto example above, if you earned 495,000 points (worth $2,475 at 0.5 cents per point), that would be enough for four nights with the fourth night free. That represents an absolutely massive discount.

IHG has over 15 hotel brands, so there are lots of options for redeeming your IHG One Rewards points. IHG points can be redeemed at the following properties, among others:

Everyone will value points differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider IHG points to be worth 0.5 cents each, and I tend to value points pretty conservatively. So the purchase price is around what I value these points.

For non-elite members, IHG One Rewards points expire after 12 months of inactivity. However, any sort of points earning or redemption activity would reset the expiration of your points. Furthermore, IHG One Rewards points don’t expire for elite members in the program.

Keep in mind that IHG elite status is quite easy to earn. Just for having The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more) or The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more), you receive Platinum status, without any sort of a spending requirement.

IHG One Rewards doesn’t have blackout dates on award nights, but the program does have capacity controls. What this means is that some number of standard rooms will be made available for award redemptions every night, but that doesn’t mean that all standard rooms are available for award redemptions.

IHG One Rewards is offering a sale on purchased points. Through November 15, 2026, IHG One Rewards is offering a promotion, and members seem to be eligible for a 100% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy points for 0.5 cents each.

There are instances where buying points can save you over 50% on the cost of a luxury hotel stay. I also think there’s value in having a “reserve” of IHG points, given the brand’s global footprint. You can get even more value out of buying IHG points in conjunction with a premium IHG credit card, so you can get a fourth night free on award redemptions.

Jeffries replied "certainly" when asked during a "PBS NewsHour" interview whether he would support bringing deported DACA recipients back to the U.S. He also said those he believes were treated unfairly by the Trump administration should receive "remedial assistance."

"Anyone, whether they are a citizen, whether they were here lawfully, whether they're DACA recipients, who've been treated unfairly and unjustly by the administration, we need to provide remedial assistance to them and undo the damage that's been done to the country, to law-abiding immigrant families and to the American people over this last 20 months or so," Jeffries told PBS News.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) speaks at a press conference on Department of Homeland Security (DHS) funding at the U.S. Capitol on February 4, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

DACA offers eligible immigrants brought to the country illegally as children temporary protection from deportation and the ability to apply for work authorization, but does not grant legal immigration status, according to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

#6206. Why Boeing 787-9 Airlines Face Different Maintenance Costs With Rolls-Royce & GE Engines

Craig Russell | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

Selecting a powerplant for a widebody fleet is one of the most consequential financial commitments an airline executive can make, locking the carrier into a multi-decade maintenance relationship that is quite tough to get out of. During the years where Boeing developed the Boeing 787 family, it made the decision to offer two distinct engine options, with the General Electric GEnx-1B and the Rolls-Royce Trent 1000. The dual-engine strategy successfully distributed supply chain risk and gave network planners purchasing leverage, but it also exposed airlines to vastly divergent operating economics and maintenance profiles.

Over the past decade, the operational histories of these two powerplants have gone on their own individual paths, driven by unexpected durability hurdles, time-on-wing variances, and costly fleet modifications. As a result, maintenance expenses can differ by millions of dollars per aircraft because of the engineering differences, repair liabilities, and long-term financial structures tied to each manufacturer.

Boeing's decision to engineer the 787 to accept two mutually exclusive engine types was rooted in lessons learned from earlier widebody programs. Offering both the General Electric GEnx-1B and the Rolls-Royce Trent 1000, Boeing wanted to show airlines that they no longer needed to be locked into a single supplier monopoly, but also to protect the airframer from production problems if one manufacturer faced factory delays. The flexibility allowed carriers to match engine performance characteristics to their specific route networks, balancing fuel burn against operating weights and thrust ratings.

The General Electric GEnx-1B is built on a twin-spool design featuring a carbon fiber composite fan and Twin Annular Pre-Swirl (TAPS) combustors, sharing operational lineage with engines powering larger Boeing aircraft. In contrast, the Rolls-Royce Trent 1000 is built on a signature three-shaft (triple-spool) configuration with intermediate-pressure stages and hollow titanium fan blades, designed exclusively for the Dreamliner family. These fundamental engineering differences meant that maintenance tooling, spare parts inventories, and overhaul procedures were entirely unique to each fleet type.

Over at the airlines, the choice initially came down to commercial inducements, leasing structures, and projected aircraft utilization. Airlines with heavy historical ties to Rolls-Royce naturally gravitated toward the Trent 1000 to maintain cross-fleet maintenance familiarity, while operators favoring General Electric chose the GEnx-1B for its established high-bypass efficiency. However, as aircraft accumulated operational flight hours, the underlying maintenance realities of each powerplant began to drift off in ways that reshaped global fleet orders.

The divergence in maintenance costs accelerated rapidly as early iterations of the Rolls-Royce Trent 1000 encountered intense, unforeseen durability hurdles. As noted by AirInsight, the powerplant's initial years in service were plagued by fatigue and corrosion issues within its intermediate-pressure turbine (IPT) blades, leading to accelerated wear and premature component failures. Although Rolls-Royce introduced the upgraded Trent 1000 TEN standard to resolve these issues, subsequent engineering evaluations showed that high-pressure turbine (HPT) blades were also wearing out significantly faster than projected design models anticipated.

What came was tough operational fallout for airlines flying Trent 1000-powered Dreamliners. It was immediate and severe, characterized by unexpected engine groundings, plummeting dispatch reliability, and soaring maintenance expenses. Major international operators such as Air New Zealand and British Airways were forced to ground aircraft for lengthy inspections and unscheduled overhauls, as reported by Aviation Week. To stick to already published flight schedules during these mandatory groundings, several affected carriers had to lease older, less fuel-efficient backup aircraft from the open market, incurring millions of dollars in supplementary operational expenses.

Airlines and their respective maintenance departments became reactionary, where engineers had to manage aggressive removal schedules and emergency component replacements well ahead of standard lifecycle intervals. While safety was rigorously maintained through constant borescope inspections and regulatory airworthiness directives, the financial toll of keeping these aircraft operational strained airline engineering budgets and disrupted long-term route planning.

While around 34% of the Dreamliners flying today have RR engines, only around 8% of the known engine option orders are for RR engines.

The mechanical difficulties encountered by the Trent 1000 triggered profound financial consequences for Rolls-Royce and caused a noticeable shift in global widebody purchasing patterns. Industry reports from Aviation Week indicate that the cumulative cost of retrofits, customer compensation, and engine modifications surpassed $3 billion for Rolls-Royce, with aviation analysts estimating that up to 500 engines across the worldwide fleet needed remediation. The massive financial liability prompted corporate restructuring and an intensified engineering focus on redesigning hot-section components to restore customer confidence.

Concurrently, the maintenance disparity heavily influenced subsequent airline procurement decisions. Fleet data compiled by Simple Flying highlights a pronounced market shift: roughly 35% of the active Dreamliner fleet operates on Trent 1000 powerplants, while 65% relies on General Electric GEnx engines. In recent sales campaigns, widebody customers overwhelmingly selected GE, ordering 677 GEnx-powered aircraft compared to just 71 for the Trent 1000. Rolls-Royce's leadership, including engineering chief Simon Burr, candidly acknowledged that the company had surrendered market share because earlier iterations of the engine were simply not sufficiently durable.

That market contraction demonstrated how crucial predictable maintenance performance is to an aircraft's commercial success. Even though airlines frequently put pen to paper on aggressive initial acquisition discounts when finalizing engine selections, the long-term cost of unreliability and frequent shop visits quickly outweighs upfront savings, making durability the primary metric for fleet evaluation.

At the heart of widebody maintenance economics is the concept of time-on-wing, or the operational duration an engine can complete commercial flights before needing a major workshop overhaul. A General Electric GEnx-1B engine stays in the wing three times longer and can frequently achieve more than 20,000 operating hours before its first major shop visit, maintaining consistent fuel efficiency and low thermal stress. This extended durability significantly reduces the frequency with which an airline must unhang heavy powerplants from the wing and transport them to certified overhaul facilities.

In contrast, the early generations of the Trent 1000 suffered from time-on-wing intervals that were a fraction of their competitor's benchmark, leading to repeated, premature shop visits. When an engine suffers an unplanned removal, the financial impact extends far beyond the repair bill. Transport logistics, spare engine leasing fees, and teardown labor mean that a single unscheduled shop visit can easily exceed $5 million in direct and indirect costs, severely impacting an airline's quarterly profitability.

Predictability is paramount for airline finance departments trying to stick to fixed operating budgets. While GEnx operators benefit from stable, linear maintenance amortization schedules, Trent 1000 operators historically faced fluctuating maintenance reserves and unexpected capital outlays to cover recurring shop visits. As a result, the reliability gap created a clear economic divide between the two subfleets, influencing how asset managers value leased 787-9 aircraft depending on which engine hangs beneath the wing.

Each engine can run into millions of dollars.

Determined to reverse its competitive disadvantage, Rolls-Royce instituted a comprehensive technical turnaround centered on its newest engine standard, the Trent 1000 XE. Designed to triple the time-on-wing performance of the older TEN variants, the XE incorporates advanced thermal barrier coatings and redesigned turbine geometry. Leadership at Rolls-Royce, including CEO Tufan Erginbilgic, noted that targeted operators could see up to six years between major shop visits, as per Reuters. Following initial certification milestones in June 2025, rollout programs are actively modernizing in-service units across global fleets through late 2027.

On the operator risk side, many Rolls-Royce airlines rely on TotalCare agreements, comprehensive power-by-the-hour maintenance contracts where the carrier pays a fixed rate per flight hour, effectively transferring the financial liability of shop visits back to the manufacturer. Rolls-Royce committed to upgrading existing Trent 1000 engines to the improved durability standard at no additional charge to airlines. However, industry analysts at Aircraft Monitor point out an enduring secondary cost: because the Trent 1000 fleet now spans multiple engineering build standards and retrofit configurations, airlines and maintenance hubs must manage complex parts inventories and tooling for varying sub-generations.

With the parts fragmentation comes an administrative and logistical overhead that can complicate line maintenance. TotalCare agreements protect airlines from direct overhaul bills, but the operational friction of supporting a mixed-standard engine fleet is still a distinct and important consideration for engineering planners comparing the streamlined configuration of the GEnx-1B ecosystem.

The divergence in maintenance costs between 787-9 aircraft powered by General Electric GEnx engines and those equipped with Rolls-Royce Trent 1000s is a case study in the unforgiving economics of modern propulsion engineering. In the beginning, the Trent 1000's early durability struggles and subsequent retrofit campaigns cost manufacturers billions and reshaped market share, but now, with ongoing technical enhancements like the XE standard, reliability is now firmly under control at Rolls-Royce.

Ultimately, choosing between these two powerplants is a choice between initial acquisition incentives and long-term lifecycle risk. The lessons learned from the Dreamliner's dual-engine experiment will continue to guide how airlines evaluate maintenance predictability across all future widebody acquisitions. Many airlines still have the 787 on order, and many others are likely to add new orders over the coming years, so it will be interesting to see if that split between both engines becomes far more even.

#6205. Etihad Slashes Flights, Pulls Airbus A380 Off Two Routes (Including Toronto)

Etihad Airways has just filed a major schedule update for early 2027, impacting a couple of dozen routes. In isolation, you might not think much of this, as the first several weeks of the year have weaker demand in many markets. However, in light of what’s going on in Etihad’s commercial division, I can’t help but be curious if there’s a bit more to this, and wonder how things will evolve.

AeroRoutes reports on how Abu Dhabi-based Etihad has filed a schedule change for the first quarter of 2027, with most of the changes taking place for flights as of January 11, 2027. For the most part, the reductions are for around a couple of months, through March 2027. There are two ways to look at this:

The frequency reductions we’re seeing are pretty significant. Just to look at service to North America:

Specific to the A380, it seems that Etihad is taking the jet off the Toronto and Singapore (SIN) routes over that period, and it doesn’t seem like the super jumbo will be flying any other routes in place of that, at least based on current schedule filings. During that period, Etihad will only be flying the A380 to four destinations — Bangkok (BKK), London (LHR), Paris (CDG), and Tokyo Narita (NRT).

It’s a fascinating time for Etihad. Obviously Gulf carriers are having a rather difficult time with everything going on in the region at the moment, and it comes at a unique time for Etihad, as the carrier has been going through a massive expansion.

Now, I’ve been a bit skeptical about the claimed economics of this expansion, but Etihad management has insisted everything couldn’t be better… until Etihad Chief Commercial Officer Arik De recently “departed” the airline.

The can of worms that this departure opened is truly unlike anything I’ve seen at any airline before… and I’ve been following this industry for a long time. Seriously, check out the 520+ comments on my post about his departure, because employees have a lot to say. It’s so salacious that it has gotten OMAAT blocked in the UAE.

The point is, if even a quarter of the things are to be believed — and I’ve had some very interesting conversations with some formerly very high up people at the airline — then the carrier’s entire commercial strategy has been a bit questionable, to put it politely, and more about serving a certain someone’s LinkedIn profile ego, rather than actually developing a commercial strategy.

So with him no longer there, I’m curious to see how this all evolves. Let me emphasize that this is of course in no way a knock on all the hardworking employees at Etihad who have had to endure this “leadership” for too long. It seems like they now have quite the web to untangle, especially given the toxic people who are reportedly still there.

Etihad Airways has just filed a pretty big schedule change for early 2027, whereby a couple of dozen routes are seeing significant capacity reductions. Most notably, the Airbus A380 is being taken off of both the Toronto and Singapore routes.

In isolation, you might not think much of this, as demand is often a little lighter earlier in the year. But what I find interesting is that this follows a period of very rapid expansion, along with the carrier’s head of commercial strategy getting the boot.

Based on what I’ve heard from a countless number of current and former Etihad management employees, the strategy of the past couple of years hasn’t been as sound as a certain someone has tried to make it appear. We’ll see how this all unravels.

What do you make of this Etihad schedule change, and how do you see things playing out?

#6204. Alaska Adds Service to Four New U.S. Cities

Alaska Airlines will bring four new destinations into its domestic network next summer.

The carrier announced Thursday that it will serve Charlotte, North Carolina, Jacksonville, Florida, Norfolk, Virginia, and Des Moines, Iowa, from Seattle. Three of the four cities – Jacksonville, Norfolk, and Des Moines – have never had nonstop flights to Seattle.

Currently, only American Airlines connects Charlotte and Seattle.

The Des Moines service will also mark Alaska’s debut in Iowa.

All four connections will operate daily, year-round. Flights to Charlotte and Norfolk will begin June 10, 2027, with Jacksonville and Des Moines launching later that month, on June 24.

Alaska will also offer seasonal service from Seattle to Guadalajara, Mexico, from March 18, 2027, to Aug. 9. Flights will operate three times weekly, using Boeing 737 aircraft.

#6203. Cathay Pacific Orders 41 Airbus A330-900neos, As New Regional Workhorse

In August 2024, Cathay Pacific placed an order for 30 Airbus A330neos. There’s now an update, as the airline has just bumped this order by 11 more planes, meaning that there are now a total of 41 of these aircraft on order. Let’s take a look at all the details, and discuss what this means for fleet modernization at the Hong Kong based oneworld carrier.

Cathay Pacific now has a firm order for 41 Airbus A330-900neo aircraft, which are expected to be delivered between 2028 and 2035.

This follows an evaluation of the carrier’s mid-size wide body fleet renewal program, and it will enable Cathay Pacific to modernize its earlier generation A330-300 fleet, and expand its operations on high capacity regional routes. However, the airline is leaving plans for this plane open, and also emphasizes how the jet offers the flexibility to serve longer range destinations.

For those not familiar, the A330neo is the updated version of the A330, featuring improved range and fuel efficiency. The A330-900neo is the larger of the two new variants (with the other being the A330-800neo). The plane has a range of 7,200 nautical miles, plus a capacity for 287 passengers in a standard three cabin configuration.

I think it’s safe to assume that at least most of these A330neos will be equipped with the new Aria Studio business class product, which is expected to be retrofitted on select existing A330s in the coming months. This will finally see the carrier introduce a dedicated regional product with flat beds, which is exciting, though it’s not quite to the level of the long haul Aria Suite business class.

Here’s how Cathay Pacific CEO Ronald Lam described how the A330neo fits into the carrier’s fleet, back when the first 30 frames were ordered:

“The A330 is an aircraft type that has been serving Cathay Pacific well for nearly 30 years. These new aircraft will principally serve our regional destinations in Asia, while also providing the flexibility to serve longer-haul destinations as required. The improved fuel efficiency of these A330neos, together with their high standards of comfort, will enable us to further elevate the experience we provide for our customers while also contributing towards our goal of net-zero carbon emissions by 2050.”

Cathay Pacific refreshing its short and medium haul fleet with the Airbus A330-900neo makes perfect sense, and is just about the safest, most expected aircraft order that Cathay Pacific could place. For context on Cathay Pacific’s fleet, the airline has:

Now Cathay Pacific’s fleet renewal plans are becoming a bit clearer, as the airline has:

So a decade down the road, you can expect that Cathay Pacific will primarily be flying A321neos, A330-900neos, A350s (-900s and -1000s), and 777-9s. That seems like a pretty logical fleet development plan to me.

Cathay Pacific now has an order for 41 Airbus A330-900neos, which the airline will primarily use to modernize and grow its regional fleet. The carrier already flies A330-300s, some of which are nearly 25 years old, so it’s logical that the airline would slowly be looking to replace these jets.

Cathay Pacific now has a pretty impressive (but not overly ambitious) order book, with A321neos, A330-900neos, and 777-9s, used for fleet renewal.

What do you make of Cathay Pacific’s Airbus A330-900neo order?

#6202. Alaska Airlines Grows More With 4 New US Cities From Seattle & 1 Seasonal Route To Mexico In 2027

Alaska Airlines is pressing ahead with its ambitious expansion at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA), announcing five additional nonstop routes for 2027 despite a challenging third quarter that saw profits fall sharply. The carrier will introduce year-round services to Charlotte, Norfolk, Jacksonville and Des Moines, alongside seasonal flights to Guadalajara, Mexico.

The new additions will bring Alaska's Seattle network to 119 nonstop destinations, nearly double the reach of arch-rival Delta Air Lines, which has also been expanding aggressively at its Pacific Northwest hub. However, the announcement also comes as Alaska Air Group faces mounting pressure to translate network growth into stronger earnings.

Alaska confirmed the expansion on Thursday, reinforcing its commitment to growing its largest hub. The five routes will launch between March and June 2027, with Guadalajara receiving three weekly flights, and all four domestic destinations served daily. Jacksonville, Norfolk and Des Moines will gain their first nonstop links to Seattle, while Des Moines will become Alaska's first destination in Iowa.

Charlotte Douglas International Airport (CLT) represents a different competitive proposition from the other domestic additions where Alaska will face no competition. American Airlines, Alaska's oneworld partner, already operates approximately 20 weekly nonstop flights between Charlotte and Seattle. Guadalajara also has established competition from Mexican carriers Volaris and Aeromexico.

The expansion follows other investments in the Pacific Northwest, including a substantial increase in service at nearby Paine Field (PAE). But these latest additions are aimed squarely at supporting its broader strategy of building Seattle into a more comprehensive domestic and international connecting hub.

Ben Minicucci, Alaska Air Group CEO, emphasized the airline's growth strategy.

"Strengthening our Seattle operation means giving passengers more nonstop choices and additional opportunities to connect across our network. These are the things that earn guest loyalty, diversify our revenue, and ultimately drive stronger earnings."

The choice of Jacksonville International Airport (JAX) and Norfolk International Airport (ORF) appears particularly deliberate. Analysis of 2026 US Department of Transportation DB1C data identifies them as the two largest airport markets without existing Seattle nonstop service. Both currently depend on connecting itineraries, giving Alaska an opportunity to capture established demand and grow it further by offering shorter, nonstop journeys.

However, Des Moines International Airport (DSM) stands out. It ranks ninth among the unserved airport markets examined, behind six other destinations with greater existing demand. Its relatively modest local demand suggests that Alaska is either picking up incentives to fly there, or sees opportunities beyond just the passengers traveling directly between Iowa and Seattle, such as connecting on to Alaska's expanding international services from Seattle.

Late night Seattle departures connect to early morning arrivals in Guadalajara three times weekly aboard 737-800.

The route expansion comes as Alaska pursues its ambitious Alaska Accelerate transformation, targeting $1 billion in incremental annual profit by 2027, including $500 million in Hawaiian Airlines merger synergies. By September 2026, management reported capturing approximately two-thirds of that opportunity. Nevertheless, the airline continues investing in new routes, premium cabins and international operations, seeking to build a more diversified business despite difficult near-term conditions.

Alaska's latest results illustrate the challenge. Operating revenue increased 14% year over year to $4.31 billion, driven by its recent growth, but operating profit fell 45% to just $82 million. The airline also reported a $147 million net loss, compared with a $73 million profit a year earlier. This is directly attributable to fuel expenses, which surged 60%, as the carrier reported notable improvements in passenger yields and premium revenue.

Despite these pressures, Alaska is betting that broader network coverage, stronger connecting traffic and its increased ability to meet premium demand will eventually support higher earnings. Premium revenue rose 25% during the quarter, while corporate revenue increased 30%, and loyalty program cash remuneration increased 21%, reaching $721 million in Q3 2026.

However, management now expects a full-year adjusted loss of $5.00–$5.50 per share, reflecting substantial fuel-related headwinds. The new Seattle routes therefore represent another test of whether Alaska can convert ambitious network growth into sustainable profitability.
