#6201. Delta Platinum Amex Card Review: Big Benefits & Strong Welcome Offer

The Delta SkyMiles® Platinum American Express Card is the second most premium personal credit card in the Delta SkyMiles and Amex co-brand card portfolio.

If you fly Delta several times a year and want perks like a companion certificate and the ability to spend toward elite status qualification, the Delta Platinum Amex is worth a look, and can easily be worth more than the fee. This post is my in-depth Delta Platinum Card review, so let’s get into all the details.

Link: Learn more about the Delta SkyMiles® Platinum American Express Card

Before we get too deep into my Delta Platinum Amex review, let me give a quick overview of the card’s main features and fees:

I also put together my top pros and cons for the Delta Platinum SkyMiles Card:

Let’s cover the welcome bonus, eligibility details, and fees, of the Delta Platinum Card. After all, these are major factors that people consider when applying for cards.

The Delta Platinum Card currently has the following welcome offer: You may be eligible for as high as 90,000 Bonus Miles after you spend $3,000 in eligible purchases on your new Card in your first 6 months of Card Membership. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, SkyMiles are worth 1.1 cents each. That means to me, the welcome bonus is worth up to $990. While Delta SkyMiles is far from my favorite mileage currency, it does have quite a high floor value, so there are good ways to redeem Delta SkyMiles.

The welcome offer on the Delta Platinum Card is “once in a lifetime,” so it’s not available if you currently have the card, or if you’ve had the card in the past. You’re also not eligible for the welcome offer on this card if you have or have had the personal version of the Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card (learn more). However, you are eligible for this card if you’ve had any version of the business Delta Amex cards before.

One thing worth emphasizing is that if you’re going to apply for multiple personal Delta Amex cards, you’ll want to pick up the less premium cards first, and then work your way up. That way you’re potentially eligible for the welcome offers on each of the cards. Meanwhile if you start with the most premium card, you wouldn’t be eligible for the offers on the less premium cards.

You can read more about Amex’s general application restrictions here.

The Platinum Delta Amex has a $350 annual fee (Rates & Fees). You can add additional users to the card at no extra cost (Rates & Fees). As mentioned above, this is the second highest annual fee personal card in the Delta and Amex portfolio.

If you are going to put spending on the Delta Platinum Amex, the good news is that there are no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees), so you can use the card abroad without paying high fees.

When applying for a credit card, the rewards structure is obviously a major consideration for people. With airline credit cards, the question typically comes down to both the miles offered on spending, as well as the ability to qualify for elite status with spending. How does the Delta Platinum Card do on that front? Well, among airline cards, I’d say it’s pretty competitive, so let’s cover those details.

The Delta Platinum Amex offers the following miles earning opportunities for spending:

Since I value Delta miles at 1.1 cents, I think this card offers a 3.3% return on its 3x miles categories (purchases made directly with Delta and directly with hotels), a 2.2% return on its 2x miles categories (restaurants worldwide and U.S. supermarkets), and a 1.1% return on non-bonus spending.

The card has solid bonus categories for a co-branded airline card, but purely in terms of rewards for spending, I think there are still better cards out there for airfare purchases, hotel purchases, restaurant purchases, and grocery store purchases.

Nowadays, Delta SkyMiles Medallion elite status is earned exclusively based on how many Medallion Qualification Dollars (MQDs) you rack up. When it comes to earning MQDs through credit card spending, the Delta Platinum Amex can help you earn status:

For context, Delta SkyMiles Medallion elite status has the following annual MQD requirements:

If you’re serious about earning elite status with credit card spending, you’ll want to consider the more premium Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card (learn more) instead, since it earns MQDs twice as fast — you earn $1 MQD per $10 of eligible purchases, rather than $1 MQD per $20 of eligible purchases.

While Delta SkyMiles is far from my favorite mileage currency, it does have a high floor value, so there are good ways to redeem Delta SkyMiles. You can redeem SkyMiles for flights on Delta or SkyTeam partners, like Air France, China Airlines, and Korean Air. You can also redeem SkyMiles on airlines like LATAM and WestJet, which aren’t part of SkyTeam.

Partner award flights can be an especially good option if you focus on flights that don’t touch the United States, since flights that do are more expensive and get you less value for your miles. I’ve also seen some good award prices for Delta One (business class) awards, specifically for booking roundtrip rather than one way.

The Platinum Delta Credit Card has a nice welcome offer. In general, I’d say it could be worth putting spending on the card if you’re trying to earn Medallion elite status with Delta SkyMiles. For most people, the reason you’ll want to keep this card long term is because of the perks and benefits that it offers, which for many people will more than offset the annual fee. Let’s go over some of those benefits.

Every year upon renewal of your Delta Platinum Card, you can receive a Delta Main roundtrip companion certificate. You just have to pay the government-imposed taxes and fees for the companion. This is a great deal that can be worth significantly more than the annual fee in and of itself.

If redeeming the certificate there are some things to be aware of:

Just for having the Delta Platinum Card, you can receive up to $150 in Delta Stays credit annually. The way this works, you can receive $150 in statement credits per calendar year when you use your card to pay for a new Delta Stays prepaid hotel or vacation rental booking on the Delta Stays platform.

While I’m not usually a fan of using airline portals to book hotel stays and vacation rentals, this could prove worthwhile, as you can use it for a hotel stay costing right around $150, if you wanted to. If used right, there’s real value here.

Just for having the Delta Platinum Card, you receive up to $120 in rideshare credits annually (Enrollment required). The way this works, you can receive up to $10 in statement credits each month after using your card on U.S. rideshare purchases with select providers. This is super easy to unlock, though admittedly the increments as such are quite small.

Just for having the Delta Platinum Card, you receive up to $120 in Resy credits annually (Enrollment required). The way this works, you can receive up to $10 in statement credits each month after using your card on eligible purchases with U.S. Resy restaurants.

Just for having the Platinum Delta Card you get a first checked bag free. With the ever-increasing cost of a checked bag with Delta, this can really add up.

Depending on how many bags you’re checking, a single trip could pay for the card’s annual fee.

You receive priority boarding just for having the Delta Platinum Amex. This helps maximize your odds of finding space for your carry-on and getting to your seat sooner. To receive this benefit, you’ll need to ensure the primary cardmember’s SkyMiles number is linked to the reservation (though there’s no need to actually pay for the flight with the card).

This benefit is valid for a total of up to nine people traveling on the same reservation with the primary cardmember.

If you have the Delta Platinum Card, then you can save 20% in the form of a statement credit for eligible pre-purchased meals, and in-flight purchases of food, alcoholic beverages, and audio headsets, on Delta flights. Allow 8-12 weeks for the statement credit to post.

The Platinum Delta Amex offers a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck credit. This benefit applies once every four years for the application fee for TSA PreCheck or Global Entry. This can save you time both at security and immigration, and is something I highly recommend signing up for if eligible. (Enrollment required)

Delta has a Pay With Miles feature, where if you have a Delta co-branded credit card, you can redeem miles for one cent each toward a Delta flight purchase (in increments of 5,000 miles per $50). That’s not the best deal in the world, though this is a feature that’s exclusively available to those with an eligible Delta Amex card.

Some people find this to be useful since they can redeem their miles toward flights, and then they still earn miles and MQDs on the portion of the fare they pay in cash.

With the TakeOff 15 perk (exclusively for those with select Delta Amex cards), you can save 15% on the cost of a SkyMiles award ticket when traveling exclusively on Delta (the discount doesn’t apply to taxes and fees). Delta SkyMiles award pricing is dynamic, and generally you’ll find that each mile gets you a bit over a cent toward the cost of a ticket.

Saving 15% on these awards is valuable, and means that you’ll generally get somewhere around 1.2-1.3 cents of value per mile (or sometimes even more). In many cases this will end up being a better value than using the Pay With Miles option, so it’s a real perk of the card.

One of the great features of Amex cards is access to Amex Offers, which offers savings or bonus points on purchases with all kinds of retailers. There’s huge value to be had in getting as many Amex cards as possible, so that you can get these offers on multiple cards.

Amex Offers could save you hundreds of dollars per year. You can access these offers by logging into your account and scrolling down to the bottom of your account summary page. (Enrollment required)

The Delta Platinum Card gets you complimentary Hertz Five Star status. Enrollment is required, and you receive the following benefits with the rental car company:

The Delta Platinum Amex comes with a handful of coverage benefits that can protect you and your belongings both at home and on the road, including:

Up to $300 per Covered Trip that is delayed for more than 12 hours; and 2 claims per Eligible Card per 12 consecutive month period. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company. Baggage insurance plan: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc. Extended warranty and purchase protection: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

The Delta Platinum Credit Card isn’t necessarily the best card for the casual Delta flyer, and it’s also not a card I’d recommend putting much spending on, unless you value the MQDs that you can earn with the card. Even if you value MQDs, you’re better off with the more premium card, since you can earn them twice as fast.

However, this card has solid perks, ranging from a companion certificate, to free checked bags, to priority boarding, to savings on award flights, to access to exclusive award redemption opportunities, to valuable statement credits, and more.

Bigger picture, is the Delta Platinum Card worth it, though? There are a few things to consider.

If the Delta Platinum Amex sounds interesting to you but you are instead looking for a card for your small business, consider the Delta SkyMiles® Platinum Business American Express Card.

Most of the benefits of the card are the same. The main earning difference is that the business card earns 1.5x miles on transit, at U.S. shipping providers, and on single eligible purchases of $5,000 or more (on up to $100,000 of combined eligible purchases per year), while the personal card offers 2x miles at restaurants worldwide and U.S. supermarkets (both cards offer 3x miles on Delta purchases and hotel purchases).

The business version of the card also offers an annual Delta Stays credit of up to $200, rather than one of up to $150, so it’s arguably more lucrative.

The Delta SkyMiles® Gold American Express Card (learn more) is a good card for occasional Delta flyers who want basic airline perks. It has a $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150. (Rates & Fees) and a smaller list of perks, including:

The Delta Gold Card offers the same discounts you get with the Delta Platinum Card, as well as the rideshare credit, but in this case it only kicks in after your first renewal. The Delta Gold Card doesn’t earn MQDs toward status, so that’s another potential downside to keep in mind.

For the very frequent Delta flyer, there’s the Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card (learn more), which has a $650 annual fee (Rates & Fees). What differentiates this card?

If you are looking to earn Delta SkyMiles through credit card spending then consider using a card earning Amex Membership Rewards points. These points can be transferred to Delta SkyMiles at a 1:1 ratio, and you can in many cases earn points at a much faster rate.

For example, the American Express® Gold Card (learn more) offers 4x points at restaurants worldwide (on up to $50K per calendar year, and then 1x) and at U.S. supermarkets (on up to $25K per calendar year, and then 1x), and 3x points on flights booked directly with airlines or at amextravel.com

Furthermore, earning Amex points gives you more flexibility to redeem in other ways, given all the great uses of Membership Rewards points.

The Delta Platinum Amex offers solid perks for those who fly Delta frequently, especially Medallion members. For many, the annual companion certificate will more than justify the annual fee in and of itself, without even accounting for all of the other perks. Some will also get value from the 2,500 MQDs that are offered annually just for having the card.

The annual fee on this card is potentially quite easy to justify, thanks to all the credits you can earn with rideshares, Resy, and even Delta Stays.

The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card

Earn up to $4,300 in travel value when you spend $120,000 in your first 4 months as a cardholder

As High As 175,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

If you fly United Airlines regularly, the (see rates and fees) can be a powerful way to earn more miles and reduce your out-of-pocket travel costs.

As someone who frequently flies United, I've found that the Quest hits a practical middle ground. It offers meaningful airline perks, including a $200 annual United TravelBank credit, two free checked bags and discounts on award flights, without the hefty annual fee of a premium airline card.

But with a $350 annual fee, the Quest isn't necessarily right for everyone.

Here's who I think can get the most value from the card and who might be better off with another option.

Related: I just changed my airline loyalty — here's how the United Quest Card sealed the switch

New United Quest cardholders can currently earn 500 PQP after their first purchase and 80,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, you can earn another 10,000 bonus miles after adding an authorized user in the first three months from account opening.

Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, which peg United miles at 1.2 cents apiece, the full 90,000-mile bonus is worth $1,080. That's not including the additional value of the 500 PQP, which can help you get closer to United Premier status.

While not the strongest offer we've seen in the card's history, it's still a great time to apply if you've already been considering the Quest, particularly if you have upcoming United travel planned.

There's a lot to love about the . Here's who will benefit most from having the card.

If you fly United several times per year, you'll want to take a closer look at the Quest.

That’s because many of the card’s most valuable perks are tied directly to flying United. Cardholders receive:

One of the card's strongest perks is its earning structure. The United Quest earns a strong 10 total miles per dollar spent on eligible United flights as a United MileagePlus member — that's a whopping 12% return, according to TPG's valuations (mileage earning may differ for basic economy and base option tickets).

As someone who holds Premier Silver status, I can earn a total of 12 miles per dollar spent on eligible United flights when using my Quest, which is an even better return.

But what I find especially valuable are the discounts United cardholders now receive when booking award flights. Eligible United cardholders without Premier status save at least 10% on qualifying United-operated award flights, while cardholders with Premier status save at least 15%.

I take advantage of these discounts pretty regularly. Recently, I booked two tickets from Washington, D.C.'s Dulles International Airport (IAD) to London's Heathrow Airport (LHR) for a mother-daughter trip to Europe. Thanks to my cardholder discount, each ticket cost just 34,000 miles plus $11.20 in taxes and fees, rather than 45,000 miles plus taxes and fees.

That's a savings of 11,000 miles per ticket, or 22,000 miles total, worth $264 according to TPG's valuations.

The Quest also offers two additional award flight discounts: 10,000 miles beginning with your first card anniversary and another 10,000 miles after spending $20,000 on purchases in a calendar year.

I recently used my 10,000-mile award flight discount toward a transatlantic flight from Amsterdam Airport Schiphol (AMS) to IAD. The flight would have cost 34,000 miles, but the credit brought it down to just 24,000 miles plus $112.83 in taxes and fees.

That's another $120 worth of miles saved, based on TPG's valuations.

Between the cardholder award pricing discounts and the annual award flight credits, the Quest gives me several ways to stretch my United miles further, which is why it's a card I plan to keep in my wallet long-term.

Related: United unveils huge MileagePlus shake-up, rewarding cardholders with higher earn rates

This is one of the most underrated — and potentially most valuable — perks of the United Quest Card.

The card includes two free checked bags for you and a companion on the same reservation. On domestic economy flights, United typically charges $50 ($45 if prepaid) for the first checked bag and $60 ($55 if prepaid) for the second bag.

That means you could pay up to $110 per person each way if you check two bags without a card benefit.

If you and a companion each check two bags round-trip on just one domestic flight, that could cost up to $440 total. That alone covers the Quest Card’s $350 annual fee.

Personally, I frequently fly United and regularly check two bags free thanks to my Quest Card. For travelers who often travel with a companion, don’t pack light, take longer trips or occasionally travel with bulkier items like skis or golf clubs, this benefit alone can justify holding the card year after year.

Related: These 27 credit cards can get you free checked bags on your next flight

Each account anniversary, the Quest Card provides $200 in United TravelBank cash. This credit can be used toward United-operated flights and is automatically deposited into your TravelBank account.

I recently used my $200 TravelBank credit to offset the cost of a round-trip flight from San Francisco International Airport (SFO) to IAD to visit family. The ticket originally cost $560, but my TravelBank credit brought my out-of-pocket cost down to $360.

And the TravelBank credit isn't the only statement credit available with the Quest.

Cardholders can also receive other statement credits, including:

I wouldn't go out of my way to use a credit just to justify the card's annual fee, but if you're already spending money with these merchants, they can provide some additional savings.

For me, the TravelBank credit is the easiest to use. When you subtract its $200 value from the Quest's $350 annual fee, that leaves an effective cost of $150 — assuming you can use the credit in full — before factoring in free checked bags, award flight discounts and other benefits.

If you're working toward United Premier status, the Quest Card can also help you get there.

Cardholders can earn 1 PQP for every $20 spent on purchases with the card, up to 18,000 PQP per calendar year.

Those PQP count toward United Premier status qualification, potentially helping you close the gap to your next status tier.

Plus, beginning in 2027, eligible United cardholders will receive a head start on status qualification. United will deposit PQP equivalent to 5% of the amount required for their current Premier status tier into their accounts at the start of the year. That means Premier Silver members, for example, will receive a 300-PQP boost.

I earned United Premier Silver status for the first time last year, and I've already secured it again for next year, thanks in part to the PQP boost I received at the beginning of the year and the PQP I've earned through flying and spending on my Quest.

I generally don't put much spending on the card outside of United purchases, since I have other cards that earn more flexible rewards on everyday expenses. However, I did intentionally increase my Quest spending over the past few months to earn the additional PQP I needed to secure Silver for another year.

For me, that was worth it because I regularly fly United and appreciate the benefits that come with Premier status.

Of course, I wouldn't recommend putting unnecessary purchases on a card just to earn PQP. But if you're already close to qualifying for status, the Quest can give you another way to get there.

The United Quest Card is a strong step up from the (see rates and fees) — especially for travelers who fly United more than once or twice per year.

The Explorer is a great entry-level option, with a $0 introductory annual fee for the first year (then $150) and useful perks like a free checked bag and two one-time United Club passes each year. For occasional United flyers, that may be all you need.

But if you’re booking multiple United flights annually and check bags or redeem miles, the Quest’s incremental perks can quickly outweigh the difference in annual fees and deliver stronger long-term value.

In short, the Explorer fits the occasional flyer. The Quest is designed for frequent United travelers who can maximize its recurring value.

While the is packed with benefits for United fans and frequent travelers, there are a few reasons why the card might not be the right fit. Let's take a deeper look at who the card isn't the right fit for.

While the United Quest Card has many travel-related benefits, it does not come with any lounge privileges, and you don’t get any guest passes.

If lounge access is a priority, the (see rates and fees) may be a better fit. It includes a United Club membership as part of its annual fee, which grants access for the primary cardholder and eligible guests.

And for those who don't want to pay the United Club's steep $695 annual fee, remember that the offers two guest passes annually for a much more approachable fee ($0 introductory; $150 after the first year).

That said, not everyone needs airline-specific lounge access. For example, I personally get lounge access through the Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card, so I don’t need the Quest Card to provide that benefit.

While the number of Capital One lounges is limited, the Venture X also includes a Priority Pass lounge membership (at participating lounges), so I rarely feel short on options.

If you also already have lounge access through another premium travel card, the lack of United Club access here may not matter.

Related: Is the United Club Card annual fee worth it?

The United Quest Card is subject to Chase’s 5/24 rule. If you’ve opened five or more personal credit cards across all issuers in the past 24 months, you’re unlikely to be approved.

If you’re currently over 5/24, you may need to wait — or consider a card from another issuer.

Related: Chase's 5/24 rule: Everything you need to know

The United Quest Card earns United MileagePlus miles. If you don’t regularly fly United — or you prefer more flexibility in how you redeem your rewards — a transferable points or miles card could be a better option.

Flexible points and miles can typically be transferred to multiple airline and hotel partners or redeemed in other ways, giving you more options.

Two strong alternatives with significantly lower annual fees include:

If you value flexibility over airline-specific perks, one of those cards may be a better long-term fit.

If you fly United multiple times per year, check bags regularly and can easily use the $200 annual TravelBank credit, the United Quest Card’s ongoing perks can quickly offset much of its $350 annual fee.

However, if you prioritize lounge access, prefer flexible points or miles over airline-specific miles or only fly United occasionally, another card — either within United’s lineup or outside of it — may be a better fit.

Ultimately, the Quest Card shines for travelers who are loyal enough to United to benefit from its airline perks but don’t need the full premium treatment of a club membership.

To learn more, read our full review of the United Quest Card.

#6199. Peltola campaign loses in court on rejected absentee ballots as she maintains narrow lead

Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy outlines the legal battles plaguing the state's Senate race between incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic challenger Mary Peltola, as vote counting continues.

Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola lost in her legal effort to get access to records identifying rejected absentee ballots during the ongoing count, and then lost some of her narrow lead in the latest ballot drop Wednesday night.

An Alaska judge on Wednesday ruled against the Peltola campaign’s request for the records in the midterm's final uncalled Senate race, ruling the demand was "simply not reasonable" while election officials continue counting votes.

Superior Court Judge Thomas Matthews sided with the Alaska Division of Elections, finding the agency is "currently busy processing ballots from the 2026 general election" and "simply lacks the capacity to generate the report" from the voter registration database.

"Even if the request were otherwise considered reasonable outside the peak election time of year, it is simply not reasonable nor required right now," Matthews wrote, adding that "the timing of the Campaign’s request could simply not be worse."

MARY PELTOLA'S CAMPAIGN, DEMS BACKED COVERT SCHEME TO FIELD SPOILER CANDIDATES IN ALASKA SENATE RACE: REPORT

Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola has been under fire for potentially having knowledge of a campaign or Democratic operative scheme to place spoiler candidates on the ranked-choice voting ballot. (Nathaniel Wilder/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Peltola’s campaign had sued last week seeking information about which absentee ballots were flagged for rejection and why.

Campaign attorney Abha Kelly told the court the process was "going incredibly smoothly" and that the campaign was not seeking confidential data or trying to disrupt the count. She argued the request would simply centralize transparency that observers already have in a decentralized way.

DUNLEAVY CALLS ALASKA VOTING SYSTEM ‘VERY CONFUSING’ AS RAZOR-THIN SENATE RACE FROZEN IN TIME

PELTOLA INSISTS 'I KNEW NOTHING' ABOUT ALLEGED 'DECOY DAN' SCHEME AS SULLIVAN ALLEGES SHE IS 'STILL LYING'

The state also said producing a customized report would impose a significant burden during peak election work.

Matthews added at the Tuesday hearing that the case was "not about who won or lost the election" but about access to public records under the Public Records Act. The Sullivan campaign was allowed to intervene.

With roughly 86% of the expected vote counted and more than 248,000 ballots tallied, Peltola held 121,487 first-choice votes (48.9%) to incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan's 117,512 (47.3%), a lead of 3,975 votes. Neither candidate is above 50%, so the race remains on track for ranked-choice tabulation after absentee counting concludes around Nov. 18, with certification expected Nov. 25.

The race could still come down to the other candidates, including Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., who has 4,100 votes, while Gerald Heikes has 5,426.

Those third- and fourth-place totals exceed the current margin between the top two candidates and could prove decisive when lower finishers are eliminated and second-choice preferences are redistributed under Alaska’s ranked-choice system. The vote to repeal that voting system is failing at 52.5% to 47.5%, which is also still too close to call over a week after Election Day.

Fox News' Melissa Chrise, Matt Finn, The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.

#6198. Why The C-17 Globemaster Can Taxi Backwards Without A Tow Truck

The Boeing C-17 Globemaster III has been explicitly designed to be able to reverse at austere airports and to conduct three-point turns while carrying a full load. This is an important set of features that allow it to be versatile and to operate from forward airstrips where infrastructure is rudimentary, and where the airstrip is as narrow as 75 feet (23 meters).

Reversing under their own power is typically one of the advantages that turboprop transports (including the Airbus A400M) boast over jet-powered airlifters. But the C-17 is not unique as a reversing turbofan transport, as the smaller C-390 and the roughly comparable Il-76 jets also appear to have some measure of reversal capabilities. But what is remarkable is how well the C-17 can do it, including in tight spaces and with a heavy load.

Military cargo aircraft are designed to operate in a fundamentally different environment than commercial freighters. Commercial freighters can count on tow trucks to push them back at airports around the world. Operating in austere and dangerous forward airstrips is another matter entirely. It is more practical for turboprop tactical transports to be able to taxi backwards than large jet transports. The Lockheed C-130 Hercules family is able to go backwards, as is the European Airbus A400M Atlas tactical/strategic airlifter.

But this is not universal for military turboprops. ​​​​​​​The smaller tactical C-295 is powered by two Pratt & Whitney Canada PW127 turboprops with reversible-pitch propellers. This means that the aircraft has the basic propulsion characteristics needed for reverse taxiing, but it is unclear if reverse taxiing is an approved or regularly used feature of the aircraft.

The massive C-5 is equipped with thrust-reversing capability, but it is unclear if it actually can reverse under its own power. The same is true for the Antonov An-124. According to Aviation Week, the tactical KC-390 Millennium comes with reverse taxiing as one of its ground-maneuvering capabilities. Among larger jet-powered strategic airlifters, the Boeing C-17 Globemaster III is unusual for being able to easily reverse under its own power. All the established reversing airlifters are noticeably smaller.

The C-17 Globemaster III is able to combine the reversing capability typically associated with turboprop transports (C-130, A400M) with large jet transport. This is an explicitly recognized C-17 operating procedure and is not just a hack pilots can do with their thrust reversers. Globalmasters are powered by four Pratt & Whitney F117-PW-100 turbofan engines (based on the commercial PW2040).

Those engines are part of the family of ​​​​​​​PW2000 engines that power the Boeing 757, Boeing C-32A, and even the upgraded Russian Ilyushin Il-96M variant. The USAF's Air Mobility Command explains, "Each engine is rated at 40,440 pounds of thrust and includes thrust reversers that direct air flow upward and forward to avoid ingesting dust and debris. Additionally, thrust reversers provide enough thrust to reverse the aircraft while taxiing backwards and create in-flight drag for maximum rate descents."

Anecdotal reporting, reverse thrusters confirmed by Canada

One of the top advantages of the design is that the Globemaster III has the capability to "operate into and out of short runways and austere airfields carrying large payloads." Separately, it is worth noting that the C-17's closest Soviet/Russian analogue, the Ilyushin Il-76, would seem like it can reverse to some extent. One line of evidence of the Il-76's ability to reverse is from the Transportation Safety Board of Canada investigation into a Volga-Dnepr Il-76TD-90VD runway overrun at St. John's.

From the C-141 Starlifter to the C-17 Globemaster III, the USAF's airlift capabilities have evolved over time.

While the Globlemaster III's turbofans are based on those of the Boeing 757, they are not the same. These military variant engines' thrust-reversing system directs airflow upwards and forwards. Conventional turbofans' reverse thrust mostly directs air forwards. The difference is important, as it allows the C-17 to reduce the amount of foreign material like dust and debris that its engines ingest when operating in austere conditions.

The feature also allows the transport aircraft to generate significant backwards thrust without requiring a pushback. All four engines come with thrust reversers. One of the most eye-catching capabilities of the C-17 is that it is able to do this even when operating at very high weights. This includes backing at the maximum ramp weight of 586,000 lb (265,800 kg), on gradients of up to 2%.

Yet another hat trick is that the Globlemaster is able to perform a three-point turn on narrow runways. Pilots have very limited visibility directly behind the aircraft, and so the loadmaster acts as the pilot's eyes when backing up. The loadmaster remains in continuous interphone contact with the pilots, feeding continuous instructions. The loadmaster calls the stopping point. This is similar to having someone outside the car assist in telling the driver how much space the car has, when to turn, and when to stop.

The US Air Force states, "The design of the aircraft (high-lift wing, slats, and externally blown flaps) allows it to operate through small, austere airfields. The C-17 can take off and land on runways as short as 3,500 feet (1,064 meters) and only 90 feet wide (27.4 meters). Even on such narrow runways, the C-17 can turn around using a three-point star turn and its backing capability." The detail of airstrips only 90 feet (27.4 meters) wide is notable.

For reference, the C-17 is only 174 feet (53 meters) long, and the minimum airstrip width is much less than its own wingspan of 169 feet 10 inches (51.75 meters). Its much larger C-5M Super Galaxy counterpart is 247 feet (75.3 meters) long. In November 2026, I flew with Pacific Missionary Aviation to the remote Pacific island of Ulithi, where the tiny landing strip covers the width of the island. I asked the pilot what the largest aircraft that could operate on it was. He said, for commercial aircraft, ​​​​​​​it was the nine-seater Beechcraft Super King Air 200 we were flying.

Taking off, we used almost the whole runway. Incredibly, even this tiny airstrip gets tantalizingly close to what the massive C-17 can use. Generally, the C-17 requires 3,500 feet (1,066 meters) of runway, while Ultithi is 3,000 feet (914 meters). However, the C-17 can get clearance to operate below 3,000 feet, making it possible. The strip is also narrow at 75 feet (23 meters). That said, there is a wider bump at the ends of the airstrip that could make it large enough.

The C-17 Globemaster III's four-engine design holds the key to its unrivaled capabilities, but was this a choice of power or necessity?

The ability of the Globlemaster III to operate on tiny airstrips like Ultithi (a tight fit) is becoming increasingly important ​​​​​​​as the USAF implements its Agile Combat Employment (ACE) doctrine. In the past, the importance was more heavily focused on being able to fly into austere forward bases. This is becoming increasingly problematic as aircraft become vulnerable on the ground.

What is becoming increasingly important is dispersion and mobility. Aircraft need to disperse out of Guam's Andersen Air Force Base and land in various airstrips around the region. Realistically, heavy transports could be pushed back from frontline areas, but these Second Island Chain bases may remain feasible, even if the First Island Chain becomes contested.

The other factor is that to be survivable when deployed forward, aircraft need to move. A C-17 is a prime target and a sitting duck on the ground. When flying into forward airbases, it will need to operate in a fast turnaround time. The more the aircraft is able to operate from dispersed bases, including without infrastructure (like tow trucks), and return to safer bases, the more survivable it will become and the more useful it will be.

Reversing, even with the loadmaster's help, risks bumping into things. Generally speaking, operators elect a pushback if feasible. One notable insight into these large military transports is an investigation of an incident with ​​​​​​​a French A400M during Exercise Pitch Black in Australia. The French A400M operating at RAAF Darwin, where there was only one access route and no space to turn around. The French requested a towing tractor, but it would take hours to arrive. Instead, they opted for a power back.

The aircraft used reverse mode on all four TP400 engines; its rear cargo ramp was opened, and the loadmaster positioned himself on the ramp to guide the pilots. The aircraft hit a mobile light unit located at the edge of the taxiway. Instinctively, the pilot braked, causing the aircraft to tip backward with the auxiliary landing gear lifting and the ramp hitting the ground.

The aircraft was damaged in several areas, with the report stating, "Engine 1 propeller was severely damaged." It notes, "Performing the power-back maneuver repeatedly in similar conditions for three weeks, the crew has developed a representation of the area that had never changed." Put another way, the crew didn't expect the German detachment to position a mobile light unit where they had reversed before and didn't check the surroundings properly.

#6196. Korean Air Adds Newark Flights From Incheon, Joining United & Air Premia

Korean Air has just quietly added a new long haul route, as the airline will be adding service to Newark, New Jersey. What’s interesting is just how competitive this market has become, but it’s logical in the context of what’s going on at the airline (thanks to S_LEE for flagging this).

As of May 22, 2027, Korean Air plans to launch daily nonstop flights between Seoul Incheon (ICN) and Newark. The flight will operate with the following schedule:

KE97 Seoul Incheon to Newark departing 10:00PM arriving 11:00PMKE98 Newark to Seoul Incheon departing 1:00AM arriving 5:15AM (+1 day)

The 6,896-mile flight is blocked at 14hr to the United States, and 15hr15min to South Korea. Korean Air will use a Boeing 777-300ER for the route, featuring 277 seats, including eight first class seats, 42 business class seats, and 227 economy seats.

This technically marks a service resumption, as Korean Air last served Newark through September 2001, but then suspended flights after the 9/11 terror attacks, and never resumed the flights. This new service will complement Korean Air’s existing service to New York Kennedy (JFK), which typically operates twice daily.

On top of that, Korean Air’s destinations in the United States include Atlanta (ATL), Boston (BOS), Chicago (ORD), Dallas (DFW), Honolulu (HNL), Las Vegas (LAS), Los Angeles (LAX), San Francisco (SFO), Seattle (SEA), and Washington Dulles (IAD).

Interestingly, Korean Air faces quite a bit of competition in the market between Incheon and Newark. Going back several years, it’s a route that no airline served.

However, that has changed in recent times. In May 2023, South Korean budget carrier Air Premia launched service in the market using a Boeing 787. Then in September 2026, United Airlines launched flights in the market, also using a Boeing 787. Korean Air’s timing is very similar to Air Premia’s in both directions, which isn’t too surprising.

Some people might be surprised to see Korean Air adding flights to Newark in addition to existing service to Kennedy (with no plans to reduce that service), but this actually seems pretty straightforward to me.

Keep in mind that Korean Air and Asiana have merged, and in the coming weeks, the two airlines will even take on the same brand. Historically these carriers were huge competitors, so of course in some markets they’ll be reducing capacity. In other words, the combined Korean Air won’t have quite as many frequencies to places like Los Angeles, New York, and San Francisco, as the two airlines did separately.

That of course opens up the opportunity to serve more new markets, and clearly Newark was identified as one of those opportunities. Also keep in mind that Korean Air operates as part of a transpacific joint venture with Delta, so the airlines can coordinate fares and schedules, and it’s all about the combined depth and breadth of service.

If you’re looking at this from a Manhattan centric perspective, you might be surprised that the airline is bothering to serve both airports. However, service to Newark goes way beyond that, and the idea is that this flight is useful for serving parts of New Jersey, Pennsylvania, etc. Admittedly those flyers likely aren’t loyal to SkyTeam, but from a Korea point of sale perspective (especially with the number of people studying in the region), it makes sense.

As of May 2027, Korean Air will be launching daily flights from Seoul Incheon to Newark, complementing existing service to Kennedy. This means we’ll see three daily flights between Incheon and Newark on three different airlines… that’s quite the step up from the zero daily flights we saw several years back!

With Korean Air’s takeover of Asiana complete, it’s logical that the South Korean mega carrier would be looking at adding some new markets, given the increased connectivity and scale of the operation.

What do you make of Korean Air launching Newark flights?

New Jersey has a population of nearly 120k Korean/Korean Americans, with nearly half living in northern New Jersey close to Newark Airport. Northern New Jersey is also home to many US divisions of large Korean companies such as Samsung. This addition shouldn't be surprising at all.

As I have said for years, KE as well as its partner DL have been in a very long waiting period for approval of the OZ merger and the ability to add new flights. I believe this is the first new or readded city for KE in years. It is very likely that KE will shift one or more flights from LAX and JFK to DL as they add new flights; KE will most likely be the carrier to add flights to new markets. The JV covers more than just US-S. Korea and DL is adding flights to other parts of E. Asia. The DL pilot agreement requires DL to add flights on its own metal as KE converts OZ flights to KE.. KE is in process of doing that but has not, IIRC, done it for US flights.

Korean Air will actually be adding two additional daily flights to New York (JFK) from December 17, 2026 so between then and the Newark launch, Korean Air will fly four times daily to the New York area, whereas once Korean Air launches Newark flights, it will fly fives times daily, which is actually unprecedented for Korean Air as it has never operated this many flights to the New York area in its history. It will trail British Airways which has the most flights to the New York area of any foreign airline but Korean Air will hold that title for ultra long-haul flying (as normally, it would be impossible to have that many flights for an ultra long-haul due to slot scarcity and extreme distances, even Emirates has many flights but with a catch: only two are nonstop while the others are fifth-freedom routes). Can you please update that on this article to reflect this? Note: Here are the flights that Korean Air will fly to the New York area both after the merger and Newark launch (All 777s here are 277-seater version): KE83: 08:25 - 10:00 777-300ER KE81: 10:00 - 11:10 A380 KE85: 19:30 - 21:00 777-300ER KE87: 21:05 - 23:00 777-300ER (Dec 17 - Mar 27) ; A380 (Mar 28-onwards) KE97: 22:00 - 23:00 777-300ER (May 22-onwards)

As High As 175,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

It's a question we've been diving deep into at The Points Guy this month (and something we've been debating for years now). Not only has it been harder to get upgrades and more expensive to earn status, but redemptions have gotten more expensive and watered-down benefits have made pursuing status less appealing for many of us at The Points Guy.

But not me. Despite my complaints, I'm still a fan of top-tier status and can't quit the hamster wheel, though I'm not trying for quite so many these days.

I've already requalified for World of Hyatt Globalist status this year, and I'll be able to requalify for top-tier American Airlines AAdvantage status. But I will also hold lower-tier status with United MileagePlus, Alaska Airlines' Atmos Rewards program and Delta SkyMiles.

In 2027, I'll continue to hold Platinum Elite status in IHG One Rewards and Marriott Bonvoy, as well as Hilton Honors Diamond status and Air Canada Aeroplan 25K status, just for carrying credit cards.

I even have top-tier status with Starbucks Rewards.

Here's the full breakdown of my elite-status plans for 2027, the credit cards I use to fast-track them, plus some tips to help you achieve your own status goals before the end of the year.

I've held top-tier American Airlines AAdvantage Executive Platinum status on and off for years now. I'm already getting closer to requalifying for 2027, and since the qualification year runs through Feb. 28, I have a few more months to work toward my goal.

So far, I've earned 148,538 Loyalty Points — the metric that AAdvantage members must accrue to earn elite status — toward the 200,000 Loyalty Points required to qualify for the Executive Platinum tier. Once I hit that threshold, I'll requalify for perks like a 120% mileage bonus, Group 1 boarding, complimentary food and drinks when traveling in the main cabin and more.

Related: 5 ways to earn more American Airlines Loyalty Points before February ends

Thanks to the airline's Loyalty Point Rewards milestones, I can also hit a few more reward tiers along the way to Executive Platinum status. For example, once I hit 175,000 Loyalty Points, I can choose from a menu of valuable benefits, including two systemwide upgrade certificates.

I'm likely to choose systemwide upgrades again, but the 25,000 bonus miles and the trip credits are probably the best alternate options.

I've already used two systemwide upgrades from coach to business class on AA's transcontinental flight from San Francisco to New York and back. I also just confirmed two more upgrades for upcoming international trips, including a flight to Paris from New York and another from London back to New York.

Holding the (see rates and fees) makes it easier to rack up Loyalty Points. This card helps me reach my status goal by netting me up to 40,000 additional Loyalty Points per elite status qualification year (10,000 bonus Loyalty Points after reaching 50,000, 90,000, 165,000 and 240,000 Loyalty Points).

Related: How I booked Japan Airlines first class for just 80K American Airlines AAdvantage miles

Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards is now the only major U.S. airline loyalty program that lets you earn elite status from actual flight miles. That means you don't have to spend an outrageous amount of money to earn top-tier status (though you can choose to earn status via spending). Alaska Atmos Rewards members can now also earn points on award redemptions, which has driven my status earnings this year.

I've spent my Atmos Rewards points on award tickets flying Cathay Pacific within Asia and a flight from Seattle to Hong Kong in business class, a Hawaiian Airlines first-class flight from Honolulu to New York and an American Airlines flight from New York to Prague.

So far, I've earned the 40,000 status points required for Gold status this year through a combination of reward flights and spending on my . In addition to earning 1 status point for every $2 spent, with no spending cap, I also earn 10,000 status points each year on my account anniversary and 3 points per $1 on all foreign transactions with this card. This makes it worth the $395 annual fee, to me.

(Cardholders with the $95 annual fee earn 1 status point per $3 spent, also with no spending cap.)

While Alaska's partnership with American Airlines means I can fly Alaska flights with my top-tier American Airlines AAdvantage status, I'm considering pursuing an even higher Alaska status in 2027. One of the main reasons is that Alaska upgrades its top-tier Titanium members (and a companion) to business class on international flights on the day of departure. Those with status are also now eligible for complimentary upgrades on Hawaiian Airlines flights. I've gotten upgraded on Hawaiian a few times with my status.

I'm also putting a ton of spending on my Summit card now, since Atmos Rewards has a partnership with Bilt that gets you 3 Atmos Rewards points for every dollar of rent you put on the card.

All that spending could help get me a good chunk of the way toward top-tier Titanium status, which requires 135,000 status points. I need to make a decision soon about my 2027 focus, but I haven't been able to cut the cord with American Airlines and fully commit to Alaska... at least not yet.

Related: Last-minute strategies for earning Alaska Atmos Rewards elite status

Over the past few years, my status with Delta has been on a steep decline. I enjoyed several years as a Delta Diamond, but it's just become too expensive (28,000 Medallion Qualification Dollars, to be exact) to earn top-tier status.

I only qualified for entry-level Silver last year, which requires 5,000 MQDs. A friend threw me a bone and gifted me second-tier Gold status, which typically requires 10,000 MQDs, but I'm not on track to re-earn it for 2027.

So far, my total spending this year is just 7,338 MQDs. This includes 5,000 MQDs just for holding the and the .

The $650 annual fee (see rates and fees) for the Delta Reserve is steep, but it's often worth it for those chasing status. It's just not enough of a boost to get me even to Gold status.

The Reserve card does give 1 MQD for every $10 you spend on the card. Technically, you could spend your way to status, but there's no way I can put that much spending on my Delta SkyMiles Reserve American Express Card. While I still like the card for all its perks, I'm no longer putting much spending on it.

While I am likely to drop down to Silver for 2027, I'll still fly Delta occasionally.

I've made great use of SkyMiles over the years. Last year, I lucked out with an award from Mexico City International Airport (MEX) to Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) and then to Brisbane Airport (BNE) in Delta One. There was a brief moment when the flight was available for just 73,000 SkyMiles one-way. I jumped at the opportunity to fly in Delta One on the more-than-14-hour flight to Australia.

Despite being what I'd consider the least valuable airline currency, SkyMiles remain appealing, and I'll keep my Reserve and Platinum cards for the long term. I've gotten a lot of use out of the statement credits that come with holding the cards.

Related: Last-minute strategies for earning Delta Medallion elite status

I added another airline elite status to my collection in 2026: Air Canada Aeroplan 25K status, which I received simply for signing up for the (see rates and fees) and carrying the card. This would typically require earning 25,000 Status Qualifying Credits through the airline.

Unfortunately, I haven't had many opportunities to actually fly with Air Canada, and I've even let some of my valuable eUpgrade credits expire unused.

Still, I've become increasingly interested in the Air Canada Aeroplan program, especially because of its extensive network of airline partners and the ability to book some excellent business-class award flights through them.

One of my favorite redemptions using my welcome bonus on that card was booking a business-class flight on Emirates from Rio de Janeiro to Buenos Aires for just 56,000 Aeroplan points. It's a fascinating fifth-freedom route, and I was especially excited about the opportunity to finally experience Emirates.

I was also able to book Swiss Airlines business class from Cairo to Zurich and then on to New York for just 85,000 Aeroplan points.

Looking ahead, I'm particularly intrigued by Aeroplan's generous stopover rules. The program allows travelers to add a stopover of more than 24 hours on eligible international one-way award itineraries for just 5,000 additional points. That's an incredible opportunity to visit two destinations on a single award ticket.

Even though I haven't gotten much use out of my Air Canada elite status, Aeroplan remains one of the most interesting airline loyalty programs in my points-and-miles arsenal. I'm hoping to put more of those points — and perhaps some of those elite benefits — to work in the year ahead.

Related: How to redeem Aeroplan points for maximum value

Another new status for me is United Airlines MileagePlus Premier Silver. I actually did a status challenge with United late last year, and enjoyed a few months of top-tier United Premier 1K status, but I wasn't able to complete the challenge to unlock it for a full year.

Still, I've really enjoyed flying United more. It's easier to get to their hub at Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) from my New York City apartment, and I ended up flying and earning enough this year to earn the entry-level United Silver status, which requires at least 6,000 Premier qualifying points or 15 Premier Qualifying Flights and 5,000 PQPs. (In 2027, United is ditching PQFs, making status eligible only through PQPs.)

Silver status allows me to get priority boarding, extra-legroom seats at check-in 24 hours before flying and standby for earlier flights.

During the brief window I had 1K status, I really enjoyed boarding ahead of Group 1.

Related: 5 last-minute ways to earn United elite status this year

More importantly, during my challenge I signed up for the (see rates and fees), which got me a good stash of United miles that I've used effectively.

I was able to spend just 85,000 United miles for a one-way business-class flight from Tokyo to Chicago and then on to Newark this year, and I've just booked another business-class flight from Sydney, Australia, back to New York for 85,000 United miles.

I've earned a total of 8,640 PQPs toward status this year, but I'm unlikely to earn the more than 3,000 more I'd need for Premier Gold before the end of the year. I think Silver status is just fine for me for now.

I've loved having top-tier World of Hyatt Globalist status again this year. I've been able to use suite upgrades at several stand-out properties this year, including the Grand Hyatt Kauai Resort & Spa in Hawaii, the Grand Hyatt Rio de Janeiro in Brazil and the Hyatt Regency Cairo West in Egypt.

Globalist benefits include guaranteed 4 p.m. late checkout, free breakfast and better upgrade odds.

This year, I've earned top-tier status organically with stays all over the world. I especially loved finally getting to check out the newly renovated Park Hyatt Tokyo and to stay at the Park Hyatts in Shanghai and Beijing.

While earning Globalist status requires 60 nights at Hyatt hotels per year, I've already stayed 79 nights this year. I may try to hit 90 nights in 2026, so I can earn another Milestone Rewards choice.

I also plan on keeping both my (see rates and fees) and my (see rates and fees) to help me get more elite nights toward status each year.

Related: Which credit card should you use for Hyatt stays?

I've also been putting Hyatt stays on my World of Hyatt Credit Card to earn 4 points per dollar spent at Hyatt hotels and resorts. You also earn two elite nights for every $5,000 you put on the personal card.

To me, World of Hyatt is the most valuable hotel loyalty program because I often get upgraded and never have to fight for late checkout. Hyatt points also stretch very far, especially compared with Hilton and Marriott. I already have trips on the books next year for Alila Villas Uluwatu in Indonesia, Park Hyatt Milan and Hyatt Paris Madeleine.

Related: How to redeem Hyatt points for free nights and more

Hilton Honors elite status is one of the easiest achievements to reach. Although I stayed at a Hilton hotel only a few times this year, I maintained Diamond status. How did I manage that? It's a perk of holding .

Related: Last-minute strategies for earning Hilton Honors elite status

The card comes with Hilton Diamond status for as long as you hold it. Despite a $550 annual card fee (see rates and fees), the card is still worth keeping.

There are other valuable inclusions, such as up to $400 to spend at Hilton resorts every year (up to $200 in statement credits from January to June and another up to $200 in statement credits from July to December), up to $200 in statement credits for eligible flight purchases (up to $50 per quarter) and a free night when you open the account and reach your annual card anniversary.

Last year, I used my free night at the chic Conrad Tokyo on a room that would have been more than $1,100. This year, I used it at the Hilton Tokyo in a room that went for more than $650 a night.

I used one of my $200 stay statement credits last year at the Hilton Tangier Al Houara Resort & Spa in Morocco, and the other at Resorts World Las Vegas. In past years, I've also used it at Hilton Cancun Mar Caribe All-Inclusive Resort and Hilton Hawaiian Village Waikiki Beach Resort in Hawaii.

I also use the airline fee credits regularly. When using the Aspire card to pay, you get up to $50 in statement credits for eligible airline purchases each quarter.

Thanks to this card, I've had Hilton Diamond status since 2020.

Related: No suite upgrade but charm aplenty: What it's like staying at one of Hilton's SLH properties as a top-tier elite

While I have had some nice stays at Hilton properties — including the stunning Conrad Bora Bora Nui — over the years, I've rarely been upgraded despite my Diamond status. Still, the statement credits alone justify keeping the Aspire card and my Diamond status for 2027, even if I don't have as much luck getting upgrades with Hilton as I do with Hyatt.

I will earn Platinum Elite status with Marriott again this year just for holding a credit card.

In the past, I've been content with the Marriott Bonvoy Gold Elite status I receive courtesy of the ; it gives status in several hotel programs, including Marriott Bonvoy (enrollment required).

Related: Guide to Marriott and Hilton elite status with the Amex Platinum and Business Platinum

Then in 2022, American Express surprised everyone by announcing that holders of the would get Platinum Elite status for as long as they hold the card. I jumped at the chance to apply for it. As a result, I've held Platinum Elite status since then.

I've spent more than two dozen nights at Marriott properties this year and having Platinum Elite status certainly enhanced my trips with benefits like guaranteed late checkout, lounge access and complimentary breakfast. I even got an upgrade at the Ritz-Carlton in Hong Kong.

I used the annual free night that comes with the Brilliant card two years in a row at the lakefront Hotel President Wilson in Geneva, Switzerland. Last year, I used it for London's Bankside Hotel.

Related: 30 best Marriott hotels in the world that you can book with points

So far, I've booked 46 Marriott nights this year. I won't try to get the higher Titanium status — which requires 75 nights — though the idea of opening the is intriguing. Each year you hold the card, you receive 15 elite night credits toward the next level of Marriott Bonvoy elite status.

At least for now, though, I'll keep the personal Brilliant card open and enjoy Platinum Elite status without worrying about how many nights I need to stay.

Related: Last-minute strategies to earn Marriott Bonvoy elite status

Like my other hotel statuses, I have Platinum Elite status with IHG One Rewards by virtue of holding its hotel-branded card.

Last year, I stayed at several memorable IHG properties, including the Kimpton Fitzroy in London, the InterContinental Porto in Portugal, the Kimpton Overland Hotel in Atlanta and the InterContinental Ljubljana in Slovenia. This year, I've checked into the Hotel InterContinental Bordeaux Le Grand and WM Hotel in Sai Kung (a Vignette property) near Hong Kong.

Despite staying only seven nights at IHG hotels in 2026, I will maintain IHG Platinum Elite status simply by holding the IHG One Rewards Select Credit Card (no longer open to new applicants). In addition to elite status, my favorite perk of this card is its free night award worth up to 40,000 points, which I've used at the Kimpton Armory Hotel in Bozeman, Montana, and the aforementioned InterContinental in Portugal.

The information for the IHG One Rewards Select card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

The new version of the card is the (see rates and fees), which also provides Platinum Elite status. It also comes with a fourth night free on award stays and the ability to add points to your 60,000-point anniversary free night certificate (these perks aren't available on the Select card). The annual fee is $350.

I'll keep my IHG card for status (and a free night) again next year. I'm also sitting on a nice stash of points, so odds are I'll enjoy some great redemptions in the not-too-distant future — though I don't have any IHG stays planned so far in 2027.

Related: Last-minute strategies for earning IHG One Rewards elite status

The last status I'll mention is with Starbucks, since I'm a regular at the cafe near my apartment.

That regularity earned me top-tier Reserve status in the Starbucks Rewards program, which was overhauled earlier this year.

Reserve status earns 0.7 Stars more per dollar spent than entry-level Green status (for a total of 1.7 Stars per dollar) and requires earning an eye-watering 2,500 Stars over a rolling 12-month period to reach. That's 2,000 more Stars than necessary for the next-lowest tier, Gold.

It may not be the most rewarding program in the world — especially if you have a lower status tier — but the savings I get through the program add up and have me just as hooked on it as I am on my preferred hotel and airline programs.

Related: Why I got top-tier status with Starbucks and enjoy it — despite the reduced earnings for some

I've thought about going fully free agent and stopping my pursuit of status. But the truth is, I have fun on the hamster wheel, and the perks really make the game worth playing.

I'll have top-tier status with American, Hyatt and Hilton again next year. I'm excited to use more of my perks in 2027, and I will report back on my 2028 plans next year.

If you're considering going for status, you should really do the math to see if the extra costs are worth the benefits you get. It's harder to earn status these days, and the benefits keep getting whittled down. Don't do it unless you know you will use the perks and that you can do it without spending a small fortune.

It can be more cost-effective to get a credit card that automatically gives you some status perks, like free checked bags and priority boarding.

At least think about it. I'm not sure I'm the best at following my own advice.

#6194. JetBlue’s New First Class Is Missing A Cabin Divider… But Why?!?

In the coming weeks, JetBlue will be introducing a domestic first class product for the first time, which will be known as BlueFirst. This is an exciting and long overdue development, and I trust it will help JetBlue’s revenue performance, especially given how efficiently planes are being reconfigured (by reducing legroom in economy).

The first aircraft has now been retrofitted with the new cabins, and it appears that JetBlue had a media day today for this showing off both the new hard and soft product. We already largely knew what to expect, but what stands out to me is the one thing that’s missing, which I really can’t make sense of.

I don’t want to bury the lede here, so let me get right to it — on planes with BlueFirst, JetBlue won’t have any sort of a cabin divider between first class and the rest of the cabin. It’s not just that there isn’t a curtain, but there’s not even a divider hanging from the overhead bins.

JetBlue unveiled its new domestic first-class seats Wednesday as more of the country’s carriers bet on the premium travel boom to make them profitable again.Read more: https://t.co/5o3k2Ru5R9 pic.twitter.com/1BTcLVOr7s

I guess this also explains the very creative angles of the renderings that have been released up until now, which clearly try to avoid highlighting this reality.

I really can’t make sense of this decision. I know we no longer live in an era where there are real, full bulkheads between cabins, since that’s not efficient. But just installing a small, flimsy divider, along with a curtain, costs very little, doesn’t weigh a lot, etc.

To be clear, this isn’t about “oh, I don’t want to be seen by anyone.” Instead, it’s about managing traffic to and from the forward lavatory. At US airlines, the most common policy is that on domestic flights, you can use any lavatory onboard the aircraft, even in a different cabin. There are some exceptions, including for JetBlue Mint, but that’s also easier to enforce thanks to how the A321 is configured, with a lavatory behind Mint, in front of economy.

I’m not sure if JetBlue intends to reserve the forward lavatory for BlueFirst passengers, but either way, you can expect there will be a steady stream of passengers lining up to use the forward lavatory. So it’s not even about potentially not having a dedicated lavatory, but instead it’s about just constantly having people standing in the aisle right by your seat. This will also make the life of the first class flight attendant more difficult.

Take Aer Lingus AerSpace, for example, which is Aer Lingus’ premium product on short haul flights in Europe. It’s simply the first row of seats with blocked middles, and no divider between that and the rest of the plane. The problem is that if you’re seated in the aisle in AerSpace, you basically just have someone’s butt in your face the entire flight. You’re almost better off not booking the product, just to avoid that.

Anyway, I can’t really make sense of this decision, so I’d be fascinated to know what the logic was. There’s not another US airline with first class that has no separation between first class and economy. Spirit’s “Big Front Seat” didn’t have any divider, but that also wasn’t first class — it was just an, ummm, big front seat.

Similarly, Breeze Airways’ “Nicest” product also doesn’t have a divider, but it’s also not a separate cabin.

CNBC’s Phil Le Beau was onboard JetBlue’s first BlueFirst A320 with CEO Joanna Geraghty. I like Le Beau, but this interview is also the perfect example of why I just don’t really value interviewing airline executives in a traditional sense.

Le Beau asked Geraghty a good question — “did you wait too long to add a first class?” If we are being honest, there’s only one correct answer, which is OF COURSE. Like, unarguably, JetBlue was at least years late, if not a decade late, to introducing first class. That’s not even Geraghty’s fault, it’s that previous CEO Robin Hayes was perhaps one of the least focused CEOs the US airline industry has ever seen.

Geraghty’s answer, though, was “I don’t think we’ve waited too long, we’ve had Mint for a very long time, it just takes time with some of these products to roll them out.” I get it — nobody wants to be, like “we screwed up and waited too long, but I mainly blame the guy before me.”

Seriously, though, if she really doesn’t think JetBlue waited too long to commit to introducing first class, then I’d question how observant the executive team has been of the industry. I mean, Frontier announced it would introduce first class before JetBlue, which should tell you all you need to know. Oh, and Frontier will even have divider, even if it doesn’t have recline, food, or drinks!

Also, the below screen grab from the interview gave me a chuckle…

JetBlue’s BlueFirst class is entering service soon, which is exciting. I’m a huge fan of JetBlue, and I think historically they’ve done a great job with both their hard and soft product, and have great attention to detail. So I’m just a bit puzzled as to how they came to the conclusion that there was no need to introduce a cabin divider between first class and economy.

JetBlue will be the first airline in the US with first class to not have any sort of a cabin divider, and I can’t make sense of that.

What do you make of JetBlue’s odd cabin divider decision?

Lack of a divider between First and Main cabin will just mean "fair game" for seat stealers from Y. They'll plop down in an F seat and then create a problem removing them.

I don't like the flimsy dividers/see-thru curtains as it is so I'd probably hate the no-dividers, not that it would stop me from flying BlueFirst. It's a minor thing but I understand people don't like prying eyes into the exclusivity plus also the dividers reduce noise and like somebody pointed out maybe JetBlue wants economy people to see what they are missing. 🙄

It's been awhile since I've flown JetBlue outside of mint but do they still do the economy service by tray service, like Southwest? I find the biggest reason economy passengers go use the front lav is because the service cart is blocking the aisle to the back ones.

Why are they missing a divider? Because they're evil, low-rent, and disgusting, like everything related to Noo Yawk. And Mint Is Shint.

As one of the 2.1k 25for25ers who's flown a lot of Jetblue in the back and in Mint, I think dividers like that for BlueFirst are unnecessary. As someone who finds himself at the first row of econ often, curtains are f'ing annoying and do very little to stop the flow of passengers from econ to go to the front lav. Just prewarn passengers not to congregate by the front lav, and if an econ is hanging out there, just give a stern warning. I like that there aren't curtains in the current Mint configs. If an econ in EMS needs to go and no one's in the front lav, then why stop them? Plus curtains seem like a safety hazard.

#6193. United Airlines Bans “AI Agents,” Claims It’s To “Protect Customers”

United Airlines has just banned travelers from using “AI Agents” to book or service tickets (thanks to TravelinWilly for flagging this). That’s an interesting stance for United, easily the country’s most tech savvy airline, to take. So what’s actually going on here?

United Airlines has today updated its contract of carriage, which are the terms that passengers have to agree to when they book a ticket. In the section about prohibited practices at the airline, the carrier added the following:

The use of AI Agents to make, modify or service a Ticket, and/or to purchase any service or product.

The “AI Agents” term is defined by United as follows:

AI Agent means any software or service, including but not limited to an AI assistant, AI agent or AI-enabled browser that takes autonomous or semi-autonomous action, whether or not Passenger or another individual supervises or approves its actions, to discover, search for, book, purchase, ticket, service or manage any product or service offered by or through United, including flights, seats, upgrades, ancillary products and partner products, on behalf of or at the instruction of Passenger or other individual. AI Agents include but are not limited to: (i) AI assistants built into social media, messaging, search or other consumer platforms; (ii) AI-enabled browsers and standalone AI agents; and (iii) any third-party AI assistant that accesses United through a tool, application or connection provided by a travel agency or other intermediary.

United even put out a press release about this change, claiming that it’s making the change to “protect” customers. Here’s part of the explanation:

Sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles. Plus, these automated AI actions have the potential to violate FAA and DOT regulations – as an example, flight check-in requires human acknowledgment that bags do not contain banned substances like explosives.

United claims it’s taking steps to restrict this kind of access, both directly within its digital platforms, and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators, to prohibit use by unauthorized, third party personal AI agents or assistants.

It goes without saying that use of AI is becoming exponentially more popular in recent times, and is a force to be reckoned with. It’s anyone’s guess just how far it goes, in terms of how much the average person uses it in their everyday life.

There are certainly aspects of AI that are incredibly annoying, whether you look at it as an individual or a business. Admittedly I’m biased, but I’m so tired of feeling like half of what I’m reading online (whether on social media or websites) is written by a computer and not a human. It even extends to things like TripAdvisor reviews.

It’s also frustrating how many people write 30 paragraph emails nowadays, which are clearly 90% AI. I don’t really understand how that makes anyone’s life better. As far as I’m concerned, just give me the bullet points you fed your AI buddy, and we’ll all be better off for it. Anyway, rant over, back to United…

I suspect United’s real motive here is that it doesn’t want AI automatically being able to track and reprice flights (and then issue vouchers for passengers), or being able to too closely compare overall value on different airlines. For that matter, it probably just doesn’t want a third party getting that much data on the airline, not to mention that all of this can take a considerable toll on servers, if this scales.

But here’s what I find most interesting — the way this rule is written strikes me as being incredibly broad, no? Not to repeat the quote again, but this is the part I’m referencing, in particular:

AI Agent means any software or service, including but not limited to an AI assistant, AI agent or AI-enabled browser that takes autonomous or semi-autonomous action, whether or not Passenger or another individual supervises or approves its actions, to discover, search for, book, purchase, ticket, service or manage any product or service offered by or through United, including flights, seats, upgrades, ancillary products and partner products, on behalf of or at the instruction of Passenger or other individual.

Any software that automatically “discovers” or searches for any product or service offered by United would include all award search tools (along with all kinds of other businesses), no? Is that actually the intent here, or does United just plan to selectively enforce rules? We did see Air Canada engage in a battle over this a few years back, so is United planning something similar?

United Airlines has today updated its rules to ban “AI Agents,” and the airline even put out a press release about it. The company claims it’s making this change to protect customers and their accounts, as AI bots could have unintended consequences.

Many people are understandably skeptical of that explanation, as I imagine the airline also wants to ban these kinds of things to help people reprice tickets, get better fares, etc. For that matter, based on how broadly the definition is written, it seems that even things like award search engines would be banned.

The comments on this page have not been provided, reviewed, approved or otherwise endorsed by any advertiser, and it is not an advertiser's responsibility to ensure posts and/or questions are answered.

I think this is likely a combination of pricing data protection (there are sites today that have a lot of access but there are limits to how it can be leveraged individually, whereas you could have your own agent do data scrapes specific to flights you want to book), and getting ahead of the potential for thousands of individual agents scraping airline websites and either causing stability issues or running up their hosting costs. They also want to protect their own ability to create their own agents that have unique access to their data (and potentially charging for that). Amazon has done the same thing - and went as far as to limit the descriptions and details they provide in order emails now so Google can't scrape the data from Gmail accounts.

It's pretty clear that when an AI agent books a ticket for the user, United is not liable for mistake. What's more interesting, though, is if there's a third party service like cheapflights.ai or something that the user can pay to book them a good flight. If the website screws up, is the user or cheapflights.ai liable? More abstractly, in an agentic SaaS scenario, does the agent owner or the agent operator bear liability?

AI agents would have a terrible look to book ratio, which will drive up costs for the airline. This has been around for travel agents for years. If we shop too much but book to little, we'll get reprimanded. Since that can't be done with bots, they have to be stopped somehow from shopping around too much. A human can perform only a limited number of searches at a time, whereas bots theoretically could search indefinitely. That would bring server and CRS costs go through the roof.

This seems pretty clear to stop an AI agent that would auto rebook the flight as it gets cheaper.

Horse has bolted. UA might as well get used to the flood and find a way to integrate such searches into its business. we are quickly heading to a future where your personal bot will be shopping from the merchants' bots.
